The input “table” is an excerpt from the Table of Contents of the BEMESS manual (Service Pack 2025-4 Build 146) by SOFiSTiK AG and covers the section entitled “Theoretical Principles.” It is organized as a two-column layout in which the left column lists section and subsection titles (with hierarchical numbering) and the right column gives the starting page number in the manual. Below is a structured description suitable for ingestion in a RAG-style vector store:

1. Table Title and Context  
   – Title: “Theoretical Principles” (appears on page 2-1).  
   – Manual context: BEMESS is a design program for reinforced concrete plates and shells; this chapter lays out the underlying theory and design procedures.  

2. Column Definitions  
   • Column 1 (“Section Heading”):  
     – Contains main headings (e.g. “1 Principles, compare of different design strategies”) and nested subsections indicated by decimal numbering (e.g. “2.2.3 Concrete compression stress”).  
   • Column 2 (“Page Number”):  
     – Indicates the page on which that section or subsection begins. Page numbers follow the format “2-n,” denoting Chapter 2 pages.  

3. Hierarchical Structure  
   – Level 1 sections:  
     • 1 Principles, compare of different design strategies (page 2-1)  
     • 2 Bending Design of Reinforced Concrete (page 2-1)  
     • 3 Service Load Checks (page 2-13)  
     • 4 Shear Checks (page 2-16)  
     • 5 Punching Checks (page 2-19)  
     • 6 Linear Stress Determination (page 2-32)  
     • 7 Disk structures (page 2-33)  
     • 8 Volume elements (page 2-34)  
   – Level 2 subsections under section 2 (“Bending Design of Reinforced Concrete”):  
     • 2.2.1 General Comments (2-1)  
     • 2.2.2 Reinforcement Meshes (2-2)  
     • 2.2.3 Concrete compression stress (2-2)  
     • 2.2.4 Compression reinforcement (2-2)  
     • 2.2.5 Minimum reinforcement of the pressed cross sections (2-4)  
     • 2.2.6 Tendons (2-4)  
     • 2.2.7 Procedure of design according to Baumann (CTRL LAY 0) (2-6)  
     • 2.2.8 Procedure of the layer design (CTRL LAY 1) (2-8)  
     • 2.2.9 Sandwich design according new Eurocode prEN Annex G (CTRL LAY 2) (2-9)  
     • 2.2.10 Steel fiber Concrete (2-11)  
     • 2.2.11 Other Design Codes (2-12)  
   – Level 2 under section 3 (“Service Load Checks”):  
     • 2.3.1 Minimum Thickness Check of the Compression Zone (2-13)  
     • 2.3.2 Crack Width Control without Direct Calculation (2-13)  
     • 2.3.3 Crack Width Control with Direct Calculation (2-14)  
     • 2.3.4 SLS stresses, stress range, fatigue (2-15)  
   – Level 2 under section 4 (“Shear Checks”):  
     • 2.4.1 Other Design Codes (2-17)  
   – Level 2 under section 5 (“Punching Checks”):  
     • 2.5.1 General Informations (2-19)  
     • 2.5.2 Column Input and Control Parameters (2-20)  
     • 2.5.3 Inner, Edge and Corner Columns (2-20)  
     • 2.5.4 Shear and Bending Design at the Column (2-22)  
     • 2.5.5 Special Features at Wall Ends (2-23)  
     • 2.5.6 Special Features at Wall Corners (2-24)  
     • 2.5.7 Punching at Foundations (2-25)  
     • 2.5.8 Consideration of the Prestress during Punching Check (2-25)  
     • 2.5.9 Punching Check at a Three-Dimensional System (2-25)  
     • 2.5.10 V-Ed analysis out of MAXIMA superposition loadcases (2-27)  
     • 2.5.11 Other Design Codes (2-28)  

4. Observations and Usage Notes  
   – The numbering resets at each major chapter; sub-subsections are denoted by three-level decimals.  
   – The table provides a complete breakdown of design procedures (bending, shear, punching), serviceability checks, and special element types.  
   – Page references facilitate rapid navigation and can be used as metadata fields (“page_start”) in a RAG database.  
   – Section titles often reference program control flags (e.g. CTRL LAY) and design standards (e.g. Eurocode), which could be indexed as keywords.

The table shown is “Input Description” (section 3) from the BEMESS Design of Plates and Shells manual. It serves as a concise index of every input record—i.e. keyword-based command or data block—that the BEMESS program recognizes. Each line associates:

• A section number (3.1 through 3.25)  
• The record keyword plus its descriptive title  
• The page on which the record is explained in detail

By scanning this table, a user or a downstream ingest process (e.g. a RAG vector store) immediately knows what kinds of instructions can be fed into BEMESS and where to find their syntax and semantics. Below is a breakdown of how the table is organized and what each record does:

1.  Input Language (3.1, p. 3-1)  
    – Describes the overall syntax rules, free-format vs. fixed-format input, delimiters, continuation rules and comment conventions.

2.  Input Records (3.2, p. 3-1)  
    – Introduces the concept of record-oriented input, i.e. each data block begins with a keyword and follows a defined format.

3.  NORM – Default Design Code (3.3, p. 3-3)  
    – Selects the national or international code (e.g. Eurocode, ACI, DIN) that governs all design checks.

4.  CTRL – Control of the Design (3.4, p. 3-26)  
    – Switches on or off individual design features (ultimate limit state, serviceability, reinforcement override, etc.).  
    4.1. CORE – Parallel Computation Control (3.4.1, p. 3-34)

5.  REIN – Title of the Design Case (3.5, p. 3-36)  
    – Assigns an alphanumeric label to each reinforcement calculation run.

6.  CRAC – Control of Service Load Checks (3.6, p. 3-37)  
    – Enables crack-width verification, deformations, stress limits under service loads.

7.  MREI – Minimum Reinforcement (3.7, p. 3-40)  
    – Defines lower bounds for steel ratios to satisfy code-mandated minimums.

8.  SHFT – Offset Value for Shift Rule (3.8, p. 3-42)  
    – Sets a global offset for element centroids or reinforcement layers.

9.  NSTR – SLS Checks (3.9, p. 3-43)  
    – Specific serviceability limit state criteria (deflection, crack-width, stress at service loads).

10. MAT – Input of Material Properties (3.10, p. 3-47)  
     – Concrete grade, steel grade, shell material parameters, creep and shrinkage data.

11. GEOM – Input of the Cross Section (3.11, p. 3-49)  
     – Section geometry definitions: plate thickness, shell curvature, varying thickness, openings.

12. DIRE – Orthogonal Two-Course Reinforcement (3.12, p. 3-51)  
     – Defines primary and secondary reinforcement layout at right angles.

13. THRE – Skew 2- and 3-Course Reinforcement (3.13, p. 3-53)  
     – Allows angled reinforcement layers (e.g. 45 deg mesh, three-directional grids).

14. DI3D – BRIC Reinforcement (3.14, p. 3-55)  
     – Brick-type 3D reinforcement elements for thick slabs or blocks.

15. LAY – Multi-Layer Reinforcement (3.15, p. 3-57)  
     – Stacks more than three layers, specifies layer spacing and cover.

16. PARA – Design Parameter (3.16, p. 3-59)  
     – Global or record-specific parameters (partial safety factors, load factors, rounding rules).

17. PUNC – Punching Design (3.17, p. 3-62)  
     – Controls punching shear checks at discrete support points, corners and wall ends.

18. LC – Selection of Design Load Cases (3.18, p. 3-65)  
     – Picks which ASE or MAXIMA load cases enter the reinforcement design.

19. GRP – Selection of Groups (3.19, p. 3-66)  
     – Filters subsets of elements/nodes by group labels (e.g. slab zones, shell patches).

20. ELEM – Selection of Elements (3.20, p. 3-67)  
     – Further refines which finite elements are included in the design.

21. NODE – Selection of Nodes (3.21, p. 3-68)  
     – Point selections, supports, hinge points for localized checks.

22. SELE – Selection of Punching Points (3.22, p. 3-69)  
     – Identifies column or wall corner nodes for punching.

23. S – Input of External Forces and Moments (3.23, p. 3-70)  
     – Overrides or supplements load effects from ASE/MAXIMA with user-defined values.

24. EXPO – Export of the Design Parameters (3.24, p. 3-71)  
     – Writes out reinforcement areas, stress summaries, shear forces to auxiliary files.

25. ECHO – Control of Output (3.25, p. 3-72)  
     – Adjusts verbosity: detailed per-element tables, summary reports, graphics exports.

Together, these 25 record types give the user full control over code selection, load application, geometry, materials, reinforcement detailing, punching checks, and output formatting. A RAG system ingesting this table will tag each record keyword, link it to its procedural context (section and page), and allow users to jump directly to the section that describes syntax, parameters, allowed value ranges, default settings, and example calls.

 1 Task Description
 The program BEMESS is used to design forces of the analsis programs ASE or superimposed forces of MAXIMA according to various codes.
 It is also capable to extract extreme stresses from a set of loadcases according to the linear elastic theory.
 When the design is performed for several load cases, the result of the design calculation repre- sents the maximum reinforcement amount which is calculated from these load cases. BEMESS does not perform any load case superpositions. This is the task of the program MAXIMA.

It is also capable to extract extreme stresses from a set of loadcases according to the linear elastic theory.. When the design is performed for several load cases, the result of the design calculation repre- sents the maximum reinforcement amount which is calculated from these load cases. BEMESS does not perform any load case superpositions. This is the task of the program MAXIMA..
 Additionally to the ultimate limit design, serviceability checks can be done. This can be crack width control, minimum reinforcement, stress and fatigue checks.
 The compression reinforcement for shells and disks is calculated according to the stress state. The appropriate parameters are preset according to each code.
 For circular plates, cylinders or similar structures a circular reinforcement can be defined.
 The program performs a punching check at point supports (columns) as well as at wall corners and wall ends.

Special effects in a concrete shell design were published by SOFiSTiK on the Munich Concrete Seminar 2017. A short video shows the subject and different design strategies, see:
 YOUTUBE Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wIzO8YNLCn4
 The following design strategies have been compared:
 • Baumann design (SOFiSTiK since 1987)
 • Wood-Armer method (uniaxial design in 2 directions)
 • Capra Maury (uniaxial design every 5 degree)
 • Sandwich-Modell according EN-1992-2 attachment LL
 • SOFiSTiK Layerdesign (consistent iteration of strain)

content:
Three design cases are distinguished: Disks, plates and shells.
 Also BRIC volume elements can be designed.

The image is a three-part schematic, rendered in simple blue linework with black arrows and a single red arrow, illustrating how an initially orthogonal reinforcement mesh in a concrete slab deforms under skew tension and how an additional concrete compression strut restores load-carrying capacity.

1. Left sub-figure (“orthogonal mesh”):  
   • Depicts a perfect square mesh of two orthogonal reinforcement runs—one horizontal, one vertical—drawn in bold blue lines.  
   • At mid-span on each mesh bar is a small perpendicular black tick indicating the reinforcement cross-section.  
   • Two black diagonal arrows originate from the lower left and point toward the upper right, both labeled “n–I,” denoting the local principal force direction (normal to the first principal axis).  
   • This state represents an unloaded or ideally aligned mesh where main tensile stresses coincide with bar directions.

2. Center sub-figure (“deformation to a rhomb”):  
   • The same four‐bar mesh is now a parallelogram (rhombus) with the top and bottom chords skewed rightward and the side chords skewed inward.  
   • The black diagonal arrows labeled “n–I” remain in the same orientation relative to the original square but now indicate that the principal stress direction is misaligned with the deformed bar directions.  
   • This illustrates how, under significant skew‐tension loading, the concrete cracks open along n–I, and the reinforcement alone is sheared, causing the mesh to “rhomboidize.”

3. Right sub-figure (“compression strut”):  
   • The skewed parallelogram mesh is repeated in blue.  
   • A bold red arrow is drawn diagonally from the top-left node down to the mid-point of the bottom bar, representing the additional concrete compression strut that forms between cracked edges.  
   • This red diagonal strut carries the shear component that the reinforcement bars cannot resist in tension alone, effectively “triangulating” the mesh to reestablish a load path for the skew shear force.  
   • The tick marks on the mesh bars remain visible, emphasizing that the steel mesh still takes tensile load while the concrete strut resists compression.

Caption below the three sketches reads: “Reinforcement mesh on skew tension, deformation to an rhomb, compression strut.”

Overall, the sequence visualizes:

- How the main stress direction (n–I) often does not align with an orthogonal reinforcement layout in slab and shell finite elements.
- Under skewed tensile loading, the steel grid deforms into a rhombus and cannot carry the shear component by tension alone.
- Only by developing an inclined concrete compression strut (red arrow) between cracked edges can the composite system safely transfer the skew tension and shear forces.

This illustration underscores the need for considering skew or multi-course reinforcement meshes—or additional compression struts—in automated design programs (ASE, BEMESS) that compute element forces in local coordinate systems (“upper” and “lower” reinforcement layers relative to the positive z-axis).

In slab and shell elements the direction of the main forces usually does not fit to the direction of the reinforcement. The main stresses often load the reinforcement mesh with a skew angle. So a shear force appears in the reinforcement mesh. In case the concrete fails due to tension, the reinforcement allone cannot carry this shear and would deform to a rhomb. Only with an additional compression strut in the concrete the reinforcement mesh can carry the skew tension force, see the following figure:
 You can use an otogonal mesh or a three-course and/or skew two-course reinforcement mesh (record THRE). For circular plates a radial and a tangential orthogonal reinforcement can be selected through the input of a centre point.
 The program ASE determine the internal forces and moments in the local coordinate systems of the plane finite elements (see appropriate manuals). In BEMESS both the directions of the reinforcement layers and the terms ’upper’ and ’lower’ are oriented at the local coordinate
 systems; ’lower’ is at the side of positive z axis. Particularly in spacial systems the user should realize the characteristics of the local coordinate axis definition.
 The design of the necessary reinforcement cross sections occurs according to the material strengths and laws of the respective code.

The image presents a schematic, cross-sectional view of a reinforced concrete element subjected to horizontal loads and braced by a two-course, skewed reinforcement mesh. Rendered as a light-gray rectangle, the concrete block spans the full width of the frame. Black arrows placed just outside the left and right faces of the rectangle point outward, indicating the application of tensile (pull-apart) forces along the horizontal axis.

Within the concrete, two identical “diamond” patterns of blue lines run side by side. Each diamond is formed by two bars oriented at +45° and –45° to the horizontal, crossing at the center to define the skewed two-course mesh. This arrangement illustrates how, under horizontal tension, steel reinforcement placed at ±45° to the load will develop tensile forces most efficiently by aligning with the principal stress directions.

Bisecting each diamond vertically is a single, bold red line. These red members represent the compressive “strut” provided by the concrete: as the reinforcement bars carry tensile forces along their skewed trajectories, the concrete core in between must carry the corresponding compressive stresses. Because the mesh is symmetrically skewed at 45°, the principal compressive stress acts vertically, giving rise to these vertical struts. The two units together demonstrate a repeating pattern: tension along the blue, skewed reinforcement and compression along the red, orthogonal concrete strut.

Key features and their structural roles:
- Light-gray background: the concrete continuum, which must accommodate both tension (via steel) and compression (via its own stiffness).  
- Black arrows (left & right): external horizontal tensile loads causing an elliptic/hyperbolic stress state.  
- Blue lines at ±45°: skew two-course reinforcement mesh aligned with principal tensile stresses to resist cracking.  
- Red vertical lines: compression struts inside the concrete, transferring compressive forces that arise where the reinforcement mesh cannot carry compression.  
- Two repeating cells: illustrate how multiple mesh modules can be laid in sequence to span longer members.

This diagram corresponds to Figure 2.2 in the accompanying text. It visualizes how, in hyperbolic (simultaneous tension and compression) stress states, a two-course skewed mesh at 45° can be “radically minimized” by omitting the least-effective layer and substituting a stiffening compressive strut of concrete.

In most stress situations the orthogonal two-course reinforcement mesh is the optimum solution of the design task.
 Skew two-course reinforcement meshes are chosen mostly due to constructive considerations. They are static generally less effective than orthogonal nets. The steel requirement increases more than linearly with the skewness of the reinforcement mesh. A two-course reinforcement is only allowed for 90 up to 60 degree skewness. For higher skewness a third layer is necessary to avoid large crack width.
 Three-course reinforcement meshes are the best statical solution for the case of an elliptic stress state (universal tension or compression): The required steel amount is minimal, i.e. it corresponds to the required cross section of an orthogonal reinforcement mesh laid parallel to the principal stresses. On the other hand there is no three-course solution for the case of the hyperbolic stress states (simultaneous tension and compression). For this a radically minimised two-course solution is sought. This is done via breaking off of this reinforcement layer which is used least statically. The stiffening compressive concrete force which generally must be assigned to another direction, however, is set at this place.
 The loading of the heterogeneous reinforced concrete continuum is transformed according to the compliance of the internal force equilibrium along the reinforcement directions (tension or compression) and the stiffening compression strut of the concrete (Figure 2.2).

In case the permissible compressive concrete stress is exceeded, a compression reinforce- ment is inserted if possible. The permissible compressive concrete stress is reduced in case of transverse tension - EN 1991-1-1 6.5.2(2). For lateral compression 100% are approved. In the region of 0.0 to 0.1 N/mm2 transverse tension the compressive strength is reduced linearly from 100 % to 80 % (or 75% according to the code). This reduction can be switched off with CTRL TENS 0.

The image consists of three schematic, side-by-side diagrams of a rectangular column section illustrating how a 45° reinforcement mesh interacts with applied compressive loads, and how the CTRL PFAI 2 control option alters load transfer. All three sketches share the same overall gray-filled rectangle representing the concrete column cross section. Superimposed on each rectangle is a blue, diamond-shaped pattern of reinforcement bars inclined at ±45 degrees. Above each column, a downward arrow labeled “P” (or “P > βc”) indicates the applied axial load.  

1. Left diagram (“Column with 45 degree reinforcement mesh”):  
 • The gray rectangle stands on a flat baseline.  
 • Two downward black arrows at the top corners are labeled “P,” showing a uniaxial compressive load within the concrete capacity (P ≤ βc).  
 • Inside, a blue rhombus formed by two crossing bars at +45° and –45° to the horizontal illustrates the reinforcement mesh.  
 • No additional arrows appear along the mesh, implying that the concrete alone carries the load and the reinforcement remains stress-free.  

2. Middle diagram (“P > βc” case without CTRL PFAI 2):  
 • The top arrow is now labeled “P > βc,” indicating that the applied compressive force exceeds what the concrete can carry by itself.  
 • Two blue horizontal arrows, one on each side of the rhombus, point outward toward the vertical faces. These arrows symbolize a tensile (splitting) force in the transverse reinforcement caused by the mesh tending to deform into a more flattened shape under uniaxial compression.  
 • No external support arrows are shown, signifying that the splitting force cannot be braced by the concrete alone. The mesh cannot develop compressive capacity because it would have to be braced by a tensile force that concrete can’t provide.  
 • The caption under this sketch notes that with a 45° mesh and no CTRL PFAI 2, the reinforcement deforms to a rhombus and cannot resist extra compressive load.  

3. Right diagram (same load P > βc, with CTRL PFAI 2 enabled):  
 • The top arrow again reads “P > βc.”  
 • Four blue diagonal arrows appear at the midpoints of the left and right faces (two per side), each directed outward and downward away from the column, terminating on small red base symbols depicting neighboring elements or supports. These arrows are labeled “CTRL PFAI 2.”  
 • This indicates that any compressive force not absorbed by the concrete is directly transferred into the compression reinforcement and then assumed to be carried off into adjacent elements (shown by the red supports).  
 • With this control option active, the column can sustain the higher axial load because the non-absorbable portion of the compressive force bypasses the concrete and is anchored in neighboring structure.  

Overall Visual Features:  
• Gray fill denotes concrete volume.  
• Blue lines depict reinforcement bars at ±45° orientation, forming a continuous mesh.  
• Black arrows at the top show the applied load magnitude relative to concrete capacity (P versus βc).  
• Middle sketch adds blue horizontal arrows to show unbraced splitting forces in the mesh.  
• Right sketch introduces blue outward-pointing arrows ending on red support icons, illustrating how CTRL PFAI 2 reroutes excess compression into adjacent elements.  

Labels and legends at the bottom clarify that this is a “Column with 45 degree reinforcement mesh” (left), the “right process with CTRL PFAI 2” (right), and the failure case when P exceeds βc without CTRL PFAI 2 (middle). The diagram succinctly contrasts the natural inability of an unbraced 45° mesh to carry extra compression with the mechanically exact workaround provided by the CTRL PFAI 2 control directive.

The figure comprises two side-by-side schematic cross-sections of a reinforced concrete element, each set against a light gray background and annotated as “Figure 2.4.” Below the drawing is the caption:  
“Figure 2.4: left: window opening (PFAI 2 useful) – right: wall girder (PFAI 2 problematic).”

Left-hand diagram (“window opening”):  
• Concrete domain is shown as a rectangular block filled with light gray.  
• A re-entrant corner (window opening) is formed by two perpendicular blue lines representing the orthogonal reinforcement mesh in both horizontal and vertical directions.  
• A principal compressive force (red arrow) approaches the inner corner at a 45° angle to the horizontal bar. This arrow is labeled “σ > βc” at its entry point, indicating that the compressive stress exceeds the concrete’s capacity βc.  
• Two bright green vectors labeled “D” emanate from the corner along the directions of the reinforcement bars. One green arrow points up along the vertical bar; the other points right along the horizontal bar. These denote the compression reinforcement taking up the overload that concrete alone cannot resist.  
• Red arrows along the blue lines but away from the corner indicate the redistributed principal stress pathways within the reinforced element.  
• This layout illustrates how PFAI 2 can be activated: the excess compressive load is shifted into the reinforcement directions and assumed to transfer to neighboring elements, thus avoiding an “angle too large” design error.

Right-hand diagram (“wall girder”):  
• Another gray-shaded rectangle depicts a concrete wall-girder cross-section with the same orthogonal blue mesh.  
• A red diagonal arrow indicates the principal compressive force entering the element and pointing toward the outer support corner.  
• Instead of green reinforcement vectors, a single brown arrow labeled “(D)” points horizontally out of the element toward a free boundary.  
• The red arrow shows that the force would need to be carried into the horizontal bars. However, because these bars abut a free edge with no anchorage, they cannot develop the necessary compressive capacity.  
• This configuration demonstrates why invoking PFAI 2 here is problematic: the reinforcement mesh cannot brace itself against a free boundary, and the required anchorage is missing.

Together these sketches contrast a favorable scenario—where compression reinforcement at a re-entrant corner can be assumed to transmit loads—and an unfavorable one, where free-edge geometry prevents the compressive force from being anchored, making PFAI 2 inappropriate.

If the principal compressive force can not be carried by the concrete alone, the possibility of compression reinforcement must be checked.
 If reinforcement is available with a smaller angle, for example an angle with a 10 degree de- viation to the principal compressive force, then this reinforcement can take up a compressive
 force. The transverse reinforcement then gets a tensile force which can be interpreted as a splitting force. For the equilibrium of the external loads nx, ny, nxy with the inner forces of the concrete compressive force and the forces in the reinforcement directions it is now necessary, that the concrete compressive force is set a little bit skew (from the compression reinforcement away). Now the concrete compressive force is not in line with the external principal normal force. If the angle reaches 45 degrees between the new concrete compressive force and the principal compression reinforcement, then no further loads can be taken up anymore. Now it is not possible to design the cross section. Then the error message ’Angle between compressive force and compression reinforcement too large’ is printed.
 CTRL PFAI 2 can be used to alleviate this mechanically exact procedure and therefore to avoid the error message. The non absorbable concrete compressive force is then fully taken up by reinforcement without further checks of compatibility and it is assumed, that the compressive force of this inserted compression reinforcement is transferred to the neighbouring elements. Usually this is possible at singular points and at re-entrant corners, but not possible at free edges!
 To clear this effect following a column that is loaded uniaxially over βc. If only a reinforcement mesh on 45 degrees is available, also a high reinforcement can not hold the uniaxial principal compressive force, since the reinforcement mesh is deformed stressfree to a rhombus, see Figure 2.3 middle. To brace the reinforcement mesh a stiffening tensile force would be nec- essary but the concrete cannot carry that. On the right side the behavior with CTRL PFAI2 is shown. Here the same load can be carried because the force not be carried by concrete is just transformed inco compression reinforcement with the assumption that the neighbour elements can support this reinforcement compresssion.

To brace the reinforcement mesh a stiffening tensile force would be nec- essary but the concrete cannot carry that. On the right side the behavior with CTRL PFAI2 is shown. Here the same load can be carried because the force not be carried by concrete is just transformed inco compression reinforcement with the assumption that the neighbour elements can support this reinforcement compresssion..
 After this theoretical example now two practical ones. In Figure 2.4 a window opening is shown on the left. In case the concrete compression strength is exceeded in the element right above the corner, the reinforcement can help and carry a part of the loading. A compression force in the reinforcement in this element can be transfered to neighbouring elements and anchored there. So in this example an input CTRL PFAI 2 can help to design this singularity at the re-entrant corner using compression reinforcement.
 But in general this method is not allowed. E.g. at the support of a wall girder, the support compression would point to the support under 45 degree and the ortogonal reinforcement mesh could not carry additional compression. The horizontal bars point to a free boundary where a bar compression (D) could not be anchored. In this example the input of CTRL PFAI 2 would be wrong or at least problematic.
 The stress in the compression reinforcement is limited to a stress at 2 o/oo, that gives -400
 N/mm2 in most cases. Reason:
 In the shell design the forces are converted to a normal force in an upper disc and a normal force in a lower disc (Baumann method) - see Figure 2.7
 Then these discs are treaded as centric loaded parts and we limit the stress according EN- 1992.1.1 6.1 (5) to a stress at 2 o/oo.
 This is not exactly the meaning of the code but it is on the safe side.

Walls designed with BEMESS are considered always as ”reinforced walls”.
 A minimum reinforcement can be demanded, e.g. 0.8% of the statically necessary cross sec- tion (see record MAT ... AM3) . The minimum reinforcement calculation occurs in the direction of the principal stresses. The skew reinforcement is considered with the square of the cosine of the angular deviation.

The image is a screen‐capture from a SOFiSTiK post‐processing window illustrating how prestressing tendons interact with a concrete element in a decompression (SLS) or ultimate‐limit‐state (ULS) check. It is captioned “Figure 2.5: Tendons in decompression check” and shows a single 3D hexahedral (quad‐based) finite element (element 132) under its critical load case (loadcase 2101).  

Key visual components and annotations:  
1. Concrete Block  
  – The central object is a light beige, rectangular prism representing one finite element of a concrete slab or girder.  
  – On its top face a red-blue orthogonal grid (red in one principal direction, blue in the orthogonal) indicates the orientation of the (smeared) tendon directions on the analysis face.  

2. Tendons (Smearing Volume)  
  – Two large, semi-transparent blue cylinders run longitudinally through the lower third of the block, representing the “smeared” bonded tendon zone. These are the main prestressing tendons whose decompression effect is being checked.  
  – A black arrow labeled “deco check” points at the line where the tendons enter the block, emphasizing that decompression (zero‐tension in the concrete) is verified along that region.  

3. Stress/Strain Values (Left Text Box)  
  – On the left side of the image, a white text box lists the computed concrete strain (εc) and tendon strain (εs) at top and bottom faces:  
    • Top ε:

The figure is a schematic cross-section through a reinforced concrete shell or slab, illustrating Baumann’s “fictitious‐disk” concept and the definition of the lever arm z. Key features are:

1. Overall thickness division  
   - The total shell or slab thickness (denoted D) is split into three horizontal layers:  
     • Top fictitious disk: 0.35·D  
     • Central core:          0.30·D  
     • Bottom fictitious disk: 0.35·D  

   These are marked on the left by a vertical dimension chain: 0.35 D, 0.30 D, 0.35 D.

2. Fictitious disks at outer faces  
   - At both the top and bottom faces of the shell are two “disks” of thickness 0.35·D.  
   - Each disk is rendered as a pair of thick black lines (representing the disk boundaries) with a row of black dots just inside—these dots symbolize the integration points or the location of the equivalent membrane forces (Ax, Ay, Axy) acting within the disk.  

3. Lever arm z  
   - On the right side of the cross-section, a two‐headed arrow spanning from the mid‐plane of the bottom disk to the mid‐plane of the top disk is labeled “z.”  
   - This distance z is the effective lever arm used to decompose bending moments into equivalent membrane forces in Baumann’s method. It is computed based on full utilization of the concrete compression zone in the direction of the principal bending moment and principal normal‐force axes (whichever yields the smaller lever arm).

4. Force indicators  
   - An arrow labeled “DB” at the top disk indicates the resultant concrete “brace” force needed to support the reinforcement mesh against shear and compression.  
   - An arrow labeled “Z” at the bottom disk marks the analogous location for the tensile reinforcement resultants.  

5. Boundary outlines  
   - Vertical dashed lines at left and right represent the lateral extent of the shell element under consideration (the “quadrilateral” or “quad” over which local forces are gathered).  

Contextual role in the Baumann design workflow:  
• The bending moments (m-xx, m-yy, m-xy) and membrane forces (n-xx, n-yy, n-xy) from the shell analysis are converted into equivalent membrane forces acting in these two fictitious disks of thickness 0.35·D.  
• For centrally loaded (low‐eccentricity) shells where the 0.35·D disk thickness would underutilize the section, Baumann allows increasing the disk thickness up to 0.5·D·SC1/SC2, interpolating between 0.35 and 0.5 as eccentricity drops below 0.2·D.  
• Once the equivalent disk forces Ax, Ay, Axy are established (see equations Ax = Nx/2 + Mx/z, etc.), principal disk forces AI, AII and their deviation angles to the reinforcement directions are found, enlargement factors fx/fy are applied, and required bar areas (fas1, fas2) are derived. Concrete compression forces (“DB”) also appear in the moment‐design tables to check whether concrete alone can carry the compression or if additional compression reinforcement is needed.  
• The same fictitious‐disk decomposition is then used for service‐load checks (SLS) under optional control flags (CTRL SLS V2.0/V2.1) or for storing “woodarmer” design forces in 3D shell results (CTRL DMOM).

By visualizing the shell’s thickness split and the lever arm z between the two disks, Figure 2.7 encapsulates the core of Baumann’s sandwich‐model approach to bending‐moment decomposition and mesh‐reinforcement design in shell elements.

This reinforcement design is based on the method described by Baumann (Der Bauingenieur 47 (1972), pages 367-377). It looks a little bit similar to the sandwich-modell of EN-1992-2 annex LL.
 The moments m-xx, m-yy and m-xy as well as the membrane forces n-xx, n-yy and n- xy are converted to effective membrane forces acting on fictitious disks with a thickness of 0.35·construction element thickness at the outer shell side, see figure. The image is a single page from the SOFiSTiK “BEMESS | Theoretical Principles” manual, specifically section 2.2.8 entitled “Procedure of the layer design (CTRL LAY 1)”. At the very top of the page appear the module header (“BEMESS | Theoretical Principles”) and the section title in bold. Directly beneath the heading is a short “See also” reference to a YouTube video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i3dVC6tCSH8).  

Below this, a multi-paragraph description explains the so-called “layer design” method introduced in version 2018.  Key points in the text are:  
• The method computes an exact iterative solution for the strain state by balancing six mechanical variables (three in-plane strains εx, εy, εxy and three curvatures κx, κy, κxy) against the six corresponding internal forces (nx, ny, nxy, mx, my, mxy).  
• Nonlinear constitutive models for concrete and steel are employed; inside reinforcing regions concrete stress is set to zero.  
• Under biaxial compression a Poisson ratio is applied; under uniaxial compression with transverse tension it is omitted to reflect crack-parallel behavior. Concrete tensile strength is not modeled directly—crack widths are of primary interest.  
• Compatibility of strain and curvature tensors is enforced in a manner analogous to the classical Baumann design, so oblique tension forces produce corresponding compression struts in the concrete.  

Interspersed in the text are two small parameter boxes keyed “top ε:” and “bottom ε:”, each listing numerical strain and stress extremes (for instance maxec = 8.387 ‰, minec = 0.037 ‰, maxσs ≈ 435.6 MPa, minσc ≈ –19.8 MPa, etc.), along with a reminder that in biaxial compression minec = (εll + γ·εlt)/(1–μ²).  

Following the descriptive text is a 3-dimensional color figure (Figure 2.8) depicting a cubic element under the layer‐design stress state. The cube’s top face shows a stylized reinforcement mesh (blue lines) overlaid with red crack patterns. The front (right) vertical face presents a scalar stress plot in the direction of maximum principal concrete compression, while the back (left) face displays combined transverse and skew compression stresses. A small legend points out “Right face: stresses in direction of the max. main concrete compression strain”. The three spatial axes are lightly implied by the cube edges.  

Below the figure sits its caption—“Figure 2.8: Real stress distribution as a result of the layer design (kink due to mue analysis)”—and, at the bottom of the page, further elaboration on SLS versus ULS workflows. These paragraphs describe the iteration strategy (Chrisfield method), automatic insertion of reinforcement via penalty functions when strains exceed limits, and explain how lever arms (‘zl’ and ‘zu’) are subsequently extracted for reporting by locating centroids of compression and tension stress distributions at top and bottom of the section.

See also YOUTUBE Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i3dVC6tCSH8
 This method was completely new implemented in version 2018 and works with an exact itera- tion of the strain state. This method is called ’layer design’ in SOFiSTiK. It can also be used in the ULS design but it is not the default because it requires much more calculation time.
 In the layer design the 6 strain parameter (3 strains εx, εy, εxy and 3 curvatures κx, κy, κxy) are calculated iteratively to achieve equilibrium between the 6 inner forces and the 6 external forces nx,ny,nxy,mx,my,mxy. Thereby nonlinear work laws are taken into account for concrete and steel. Inside the reinforcement area no concrete stress is applied. On biaxial compression of concrete the poisson ratio is used. On uniaxial compression with transverse tension the poisson ratio is not taken into account, because the concrete only works uniaxial parallel to the crack. A further crack opening happens without poisson ratio effect. A concrete tensile strength is not taken into account - not even in the crack design as we are interested in the calculated crack width in the crack section.
 As all components are taken into account using the strain and curvature tensor, also the com- patibility is observed as in the Baumann design. So a tension force acting under 45 degree on a reinforcement mesh causes a necessary compression strut in the concrete.

The stresses in this direction are shown at the right face of the plot cube. At the left face the maximum of the corresponding concrete transverse stress and a possible skew compression is plotted. This is favorable to recognize a skew compression strut stiffening the reinforcement mesh as the direction of main compression may turn over the height. The left concrete stress plot may also have a kink due to the effect that the poisson ration is only taken into account in case of biaxial compression!
 In case enough reinforcement is already defined coming from the ULS, the SLS procedure is relatively clear: with 6 target forces the 6 variable strain parameter are tuned. The iteration is controlled using a Chrisfield iteration method based on residual forces.
 In the ULS design the procedure is much more complex because a starting reinforcement is missing. In the beginning of the iteration the strains increase significantly, the cracked concrete cannot carry the loading. Then the program inserts reinforcement using panelty functions. An additional target appears to meet strain limits. If reinforcement is increased usually a strain limit of 25 Promille is the optimum. In case of compression problems at the compression face the tensile strain must be reduced. On further loading also compression reinforcement can be inserted to achieve equilibrium.
 Summary: Using the consistent strain iteration, the layer design can replace the up to now successful Baumann design. Mainly in the limit range of ULS design the layer design can deliver more accurate results.
 In the SLS the layer design delivers more accurate results than the up to now used uniaxial Capra-Maury method. Especially in post tensioned structures the Capra-Maury method cannot well map the real biaxial stress state.
 Tendons can now be integrated realistic in the strain analysis also in the analysis ot the lever arm (waste-product of the iteration of the strain state) - see tendons.

 Lever arm in the printout:
 A lever arm is not used in the layer design itself, only the balance of the internal stresses with the external internal forces is achieved. But for printing and information purposes a lever arm is extracted from the stresses. For this the center of gravity of the concrete compression stress is determined at the top of the section - see next figure left. Then the center of gravity of the iron tension on the bottom of the section is determined in this direction. The distance is then printed as lever arm ’zl’ = averaged lever arm of lower reinforcement. Should the concrete compressive strain transversely be more than 80% of the concrete main compressive strain at the top, the center of gravity of the iron tensile force at the bottom is averaged without direction, e.g. in the middle of a slab with m-I = m-II. The same procedure is then used for the main compressive strain at the bottom with the iron tensile force at the top for ’zu’ = averaged lever arm of upper reinforcement:

The upper half contains detailed running text on concrete‐slab and shell design according to various annexes of the upcoming Eurocode (Annex G), while the lower half shows a three‐dimensional schematic (Figure 2.10) illustrating lever arms for reinforcement under a twisting moment mxy.

Key textual elements (upper half):

Key graphical elements (lower half, against a light blue background):  
• A beige, rectangular block representing a slab or “sandwich disc.” The block is semi‐transparent so that internal reinforcement layers are visible.  
• On the top surface sits a grid of blue lines—symbolizing the principal reinforcement mesh (cross‐direction and primary direction bars).  
• On the bottom face an orthogonal set of blue rods indicates the lower reinforcement layer.  
• At the block’s mid‐section, a wedge‐shaped brown “slice” has been cut out and pushed aside, emphasizing the interior where reinforcing bars pass through the thickness.  
• From each of the four reinforcement layer locations, colored arrows denote the “lever arms” to the neutral axis:

• Below the graphic, the caption reads:  
  “Figure 2.10: 4 leverarms of 4 reinforcements on twisting moment mxy, calculated with woodarmer, only illustrated with the SOFiSTiK layer method.”

Overall, the screenshot fuses explanatory text on cutting‐edge Eurocode Annex G rules for sandwich and shell design with a color‐coded 3D visualization of how reinforcement lever arms (z‐distances) are determined and how stress and strain distributions are reported for each reinforcement layer. sections: 2.2.9 Sandwich design according new Eurocode prEN Annex G (CTRL LAY 2)

content:
The figure is a three‐dimensional “corner” slice through a reinforced‐concrete shell, sketched to illustrate the so-called Annex G “sandwich disc” model used in the new Eurocode layer‐design approach. It is annotated as Figure 2.11: Annex G sandwich disc model (for shells) and shows three distinct material layers plus all pertinent stress resultants acting on a small square disc at the shell corner.

Description of geometry and numbering  
1. Top reinforcement layer (number 1): this thin plate at the very top of the slab carries the positive bending (tension) in the shell’s top fiber.  
2. Bottom reinforcement layer (number 2): the symmetric layer at the bottom face of the slab, carrying the negative bending (tension) at the bottom fiber.  
3. Mid‐plane (“core”) of the concrete disc (number 3): this represents the neutral‐axis region of the sandwich model, where transverse shear and membrane actions are assembled.

Overall slab thickness is denoted by t (shown by vertical double‐arrows at the left), and the disc model itself spans a small square element at a 90° corner—one face oriented in the x-direction, the other in the y-direction.

Stress and force resultants shown  
• Normal stress components σ′_Edy and σ′_Edx (prime indicating top layer, and unprimed on the bottom): arrows along the slab faces indicate membrane or bending‐induced normal stresses in the local x- and y-directions.  
• Shear stresses τ′_Edxy and τ_Edxy: diagonal arrows on the faces show in‐plane shear stresses on the disc element.  
• Vertical shear forces V_Edy and V_Edx: large arrows pointing down on the upper face edges reflect transverse shear resultants per unit length, transferred into the sandwich disc.  

Each arrow is labeled with a subscript “Ed” (design value) and either “x,” “y,” or “xy” to distinguish directional components. The “prime” notation on the top‐face stresses (σ′, τ′) distinguishes them from the bottom‐face stresses (σ, τ) of the lower reinforcement layer.

Context and use in Annex G layer design  
– Under the forthcoming 2027 Eurocode update, if Annex G is activated (either automatically via the new standard selection in SOFiSTiK GZT or manually with command STEU LAY 2), this sandwich disc model replaces the classical shell‐element approach for design checks.  
– The model employs a rectangular stress block in the concrete pressure zone and evaluates crack widths according to Annex G.5, which generally predicts larger widths in slab corners under torsional moments m_xy.  
– Disk forces (membrane forces and shear forces acting on the disc) are then checked against the design resistances (f_y/1.15 for steel, f_cd reduced per G.9 for concrete in transverse tension), with lever arms z determined from the minimum of the four wood-Armer‐based lever arms or the outer‐layer center distance (see G.2 and G.3).

By assembling the top, mid, and bottom layers in this way, Annex G’s sandwich disc model captures bending, membrane, and shear interactions locally—particularly important at slab corners and curved shells—yielding a more accurate stress distribution and crack‐width prediction than the older simplified shell model.

sections: 2.2.9 Sandwich design according new Eurocode prEN Annex G (CTRL LAY 2)

content:
If the new Eurocode is likely to be introduced in 2027 and the corresponding standard is then selected in Sofistik, the design in the GZT will then be carried out according to the new annex G. You can also activate this manually by entering STEU LAY 2.
 For stress analysis, layer design is always used as the default setting, as this provides much more accurate stresses. With the sandwich model, annex G only uses a rectangular stress block in the pressure zone. Crack detection is then carried out in the default setting using the Baumann design, which provides comparable disk cutting forces. However, the new calculation of crack widths according to Annex G.5 is used, which provides significantly higher crack widths than the old Eurocode, especially in corner areas of slabs with torsional moments mxy. You
 can also manually request crack evidence using this new method with RISS...SAND 11. See a1_single_span_girder.dat Singe span girder with 90 and 45 degree bars.
 Without normal forces and at mxy<0.07*dˆ2*fcd, the procedure is based on Table G.2 and uniaxial design according to 8.1.3 (works like the woodarmer method). Depending on the utilization of the pressure zone, the lever arm is optimally determined and the permissible steel tension is utilized up to the trilinear range of the working line. The design moments are stored - but are 100% identical to Baumann. A reduction in the concrete compressive strength does not take place according to Annex G, as this is only stated in Annex G.3 (membrane). A reduction according to 8.5.2 Compression struts and pressure fields is not necessary for plates. If the cross section cannot carry the force without compression reinforcement, BEMESS switches to SOFiSTiK layer design. As with the Eurocode shell model, the concrete compressive strength is also reduced for slabs. If necessary, BEMESS then attempts to achieve equilibrium with compression reinforcement.

metadata.sections: 2.2.9 Sandwich design according new Eurocode prEN Annex G (CTRL LAY 2)

content:
A reduction according to 8.5.2 Compression struts and pressure fields is not necessary for plates. If the cross section cannot carry the force without compression reinforcement, BEMESS switches to SOFiSTiK layer design. As with the Eurocode shell model, the concrete compressive strength is also reduced for slabs. If necessary, BEMESS then attempts to achieve equilibrium with compression reinforcement..
 Shells:
 Even if a shell only has a small normal force, it is dimensioned according to G.3 (membrane). It also explicitly states that the steel stress can only be applied with fyd (G.1) - i.e. without a trilinear work law. In advance, the most unfavorable lever arm is determined for each iron using a simple woodarmer method, but with strength reduction on transverse tension. The MXY is added to the moment in the iron direction. But the NXY is added in such a way that it delivers a compressive force, because that provides the most unfavorable lever arm.

content:
In case the minimum lever arm of all 4 irons (z-top-1,z-top-2,z-bot-1,z-bot-2, calculated with the woodarmer method) is greater than the center distance of the outer reinforcement layer, this center distance of the outer reinforcement is used. Otherwise the minimum lever arm of all 4 irons is used for the lever arm z of the sandwich disc distance according annex G figure G.2. This method with the outer reinforcement comes from the old Eurocode EN 1992-2:2005, Annex LL (informative)..
 The disk forces are then designed according to annex G, normally with fy/1.15 = 500/1.15 = 435 N/mm2.
 The concrete compressive strength on transverse tension is reduced according to annex G (G.9). If the concrete compressive strength is initially exceeded, BEMESS attempts to reduce the elongation eps1 by increasing the inserted reinforcement in order to increase the concrete compressive strength according to G.3(7)d). If the increase is more than 20%, BEMESS first tries to reduce the lever arm in order to increase the layer thickness t in order to reduce the concrete stress (more pressure zone, especially with normal pressure force).
 If the discs cannot carry the stress without compression reinforcement, BEMESS switches to the SOFiSTiK layer design. There the strain eps1 is not calculated with fyd according to (G.10) and G.4(7)a) but is determined exactly from the strain plane transverse to the compressive stress. If the reduction in compressive strength is high, BEMESS tries to limit it by reducing the steel elongation. You can also activate this new reduction in concrete compressive strength according to (G.9) according to old standards with CTRL TENS ’prEN’.

content:
Up to now, the design of Steel fiber Concrete is only implemented according the german DAfStb-Richtlinie Stahlfaserbeton Ausgabe Juni 2021 and is used in this way also for other EN codes (a corresponding warnung is printed).
 - ULS bending design with the ULS worklaw from AQUA
 - Shear design with VRd,cf according (R.6.2d)
 - Punching with VRd,cf according (R.6.47.1) incl. u-out in equation (6.54)
 - SLS Checks with the SLS worklaw from AQUA
 - Analysis of crack width with αƒ according (R.7.8)
 In case steel fibers cannot be used for a design, e.g. for the dynamic stress range, or if a check is not implemented, a corresponding error message occurs.
 You can then run an AQUA without steel fiber input in advance to get a normal check without steel fibers.
 After the plotted worklaws the tension stress points of the work law are printed. Example see steelfiberdesign.dat

Depending on the country, different boxed values are set. Important is the factor α-cc (fcd=α- cc*fck/γc). Please check the BEMESS material output!
 - Special values for v1 acc. 6.2.3(3) (6.10.aN)
 Important is here the additional safety coefficient gamma-n in dependence on the safety class (1,2 or 3). The safety class is defined in program AQUA via record NORM at CAT:
 NORM S BBK-04 CAT 1: gamma-n=1.00 CAT 2: gamma-n=1.10 CAT 3: gamma-n=1.20
 To change the safety class, an AQUA run with only an input for record NORM can be set in front of the BEMESS.
 - Bilinear material curve for reinforced concrete according to
 3.1.2-(3)P + 3.1.4-(3)P
 Concrete safety factor 1.90 [ with alfa-cd = 1.0]
 Crack check: in 4.4.2 it is recommended to reduce the steel stress accordning figure 31. This can be done in BEMESS with an input of PARA-SSO and a check with CRAC WK TAB. If the user inputs a specific crack width (e.g. CRAC WK 0.15), the analysis of crack width according EN-1992 7.3.4 is done. If this is not possible, shear reinforcement is in- serted. According SIA 262:2013, 4.3.3.4.3 the compression strud angle is analysed between 25 − 45◦.
 Hint
 Please note that in BEMESS, β = 90◦ → snβ = 1.0
 The concrete strength FC (Rb) and FCTK (Rbt) (see program AQUA record CONC) are re- duced with an additional factor for short term/long term loading that can be set with CTRL SNIP, default is 0.9 (long term loading). Steel is only used bilinear up to FY, for shear FP is used for Rs.

The concrete strength FC (Rb) and FCTK (Rbt) (see program AQUA record CONC) are re- duced with an additional factor for short term/long term loading that can be set with CTRL SNIP, default is 0.9 (long term loading). Steel is only used bilinear up to FY, for shear FP is used for Rs..
 According ACI 318-14 a strength reduction factor of 0.65-0.9 according Tabelle 21.2.1 is used, depending on the situation bending, bending+compression or compression alone.
 The strength reduction factor SRF is taken into account according to the table 2.3 AS 3600. bending SRF=0.6 - 0.8, shear SRF=0.7
If requested with the input, the following checks are performed after each other. If necessary the reinforcement is increased which is requested statically by the appropriate amount.

The check for a compression zone height can be done specially on slabs. In spacial systems with tensile normal forces the check usually failes in many elements because in the region of zero bending moment the sections are fully tension stressed.
 Therefore the check is done using a simple slab without normal force. Then the check gives a minimum reinforcement out of geometrical restrictions:
 Assuming a strain at the compression face, a well defined strain in the reinforcement appears using XMIN
 - With this strain in the reinforcement and the E-modulus of steel we get an allowable steel
 stress
 - With the concrete strain and the concrete E-modulus we get a compression force on XMIN
 - The reinforcement must carry this force with the allowable steel stress
 - The first assumed strain is cut away
 So the necessary minimum reinforcement is independant of the first assumed strain and only depending on the Geometrie and the ration of E-moduli.
 (Only CTRL LAY 0 uses the old method of BEMESS version 2016 - see manual of 2016)
 The check is requested with an input XMIN in the record CRAC.

metadata.sections: 2.3.1 Minimum Thickness Check of the Compression Zone

content:
The check limits the available steel stress in the serviceability state to a permissible value. The permissible value comes from a code depending table depending on the bar diameter or
 can be input directly in PARA-SSU! With PARA-SSU a check can be done for the table of bar spacing! Usage:
 If a permissible steel stress is input via PARA-SSU, this value is taken. Otherwise the permis- sible steel stress is calculated based on the tabel bar diameter.
 If the check for the bar diameter table is not implemented vor a specific code, the check can always be done by direct input of the steel stress in PARA-SSU.
 It is assumed a crack formation through load. A crack internal force e.g. for a minimum rein- forcement must be requested in MREI.
 For thick plates the limit diameters are increased according to the standard. For arbitrary crack widths an interpolation inside the table is done.
 In the Baumann design CTRL LAY 0 tendons are not taken into account in the crack design. In the layer design a stress increase of bonded tendons is taken into account in the iteration of the strain state (can be switched off with CTRL SIGZ 0).
 In case a stress increase in bonded tendons occured in the tensile zone in the effective tension area Ac,eff, in the german DIN EN 1992-1-1 the steel stress of the reinforcement in this direc- tion is increased according (NA.7.5.3) - in all other codes not! In the crack design itself, for all codes bonded tendons in Ac,eff are taken into account according EN 1992-1-1 7.3.4 (7.10), in- dependant of 150mm rule of 7.3.2(3). This rule is written for the minimum reinforcement but for the minimum reinforcement tendons are not taken into account in BEMESS. The bond values are taken from 6.8.2 table 6.2.
