metadata.sections: 2.3.2 Crack Width Control without Direct Calculation

content:
The image is titled “Figure 2.12: Crack width design on multilayer reinforcement” and consists of three distinct but related sketches arranged side by side under a single rectangular concrete beam cross-section:

1. Concrete Cross-Section with Two Reinforcement Layers  
   - A simple outline of a rectangular beam cross-section, viewed in elevation.  
   - Near the bottom face of the rectangle are two thin, horizontal lines representing two layers of tensile reinforcement.  
   - The lower (outermost) layer is annotated as “as1 = 20 cm²/m,” and the inner (deeper) layer as “as3 = 10 cm²/m.” (These values denote steel area per meter of beam width.)  
   - No crack lines are shown here; the purpose is purely to locate the reinforcement.

2. Strain and Steel Stress Diagrams  
   Immediately to the right of the cross-section are two schematic plots, one above the other, sharing the same depth axis:
   a) Strain (ε) Diagram  
      - A right‐leaning triangular line indicating a linear strain distribution from zero at the top fiber down to a maximum at the bottom fiber.  
      - The top of the triangle is labeled “ε” (zero strain), and the bottom tip corresponds to the maximum tensile strain in the concrete/steel.  
   b) Steel Stress (σ) Diagram  
      - Two small horizontal bars placed at the depths corresponding to the two reinforcement layers.  
      - The upper bar (at the shallower depth) is labeled “σ1,” the deeper bar “σ3.”  
      - A lightly sketched, nearly rectangular stress block shows that the steel stress in the outer layer (σ1) is higher than that in the inner layer (σ3).  
      - To the right of this block is a vertical axis labeled “σ.”

3. Dimensional Sketch of Bar Depths and Cover  
   On the far right is a simplified cross-sectional detail focusing solely on the positioning of the bars:
   - A vertical line indicates the concrete face; two horizontal dimension arrows point rightward from that face to mark the depths of each reinforcement layer.  
   - The distance to the first (outer) bar is “d1 = 40 mm.”  
   - The deeper bar sits at “d3 = 80 mm.”  
   - Between the face and the first bar is a small double arrow denoting the concrete cover “c” (not numerically labeled here but implied as the clear cover).  
   - Two small arrowheads between the first and second bar show the spacing or additional cover inside.

Overall, the figure illustrates how, in a multilayer reinforcement layout, the individual layer areas (as1, as3) and their respective depths (d1, d3) feed into both the strain distribution and the resulting steel stresses (σ1, σ3). These inputs are then used—via a direct‐calculation crack‐width formula—to compute an “effective” reinforcement depth (d_eff) and an “averaged” bar diameter, which in turn govern permissible crack widths according to Eurocode 2 (EN 1992-1-1 §7.3.4(3)) or default national tables. The figure visually supports the text’s example calculation of d_eff = 50.4 mm, obtained by weighting each layer’s depth with its area and stress, as well as the determination of maximum crack spacing using the outer‐layer cover.

sections: 2.3.3 Crack Width Control with Direct Calculation

content:
If the simple check according to the tables is not sufficing, a direct calculation can occur with the default of the permissible crack width. For EN codes also equation 7.14 of EN 1992-1- 1 7.3.4(3) is taken into account (except Germany and Austria). If the check is not explicitly programmed in BEMESS for a specific code, the check is done based on eurocode. For this please check the protocol of the design parameters in the output.
 The method of direct calculation of crack width should be used especially in bridge design. For normal buildings, the limitation of the crack width without direct calculation according to the tables is recommended.
 In case of a LAY multilayer reinforcement, the layers are averaged with their force com- ponent. May be the most outer layer (d1=40mm) with as1=20 cm2/m has a steel stress of 200 N/mm2 und the next inner layer with same direction (d3=80mm) with as3=10 cm2/m has a steel stress of 140 N/mm2, the center of the tension force is at d-eff= 50.4 mm = (40mm*20cm2/m*200N/mm2 + 80mm*10cm2/m*140N/mm2)/(20cm2/m*200N/mm2 + 10cm2/m*140N/mm2). The crack width is then calculated according to the crack formulars with the (in the same way) averaged bar diameter. For the stell stress the maximum stress in this area is used. This is usually the steel stress in the most outer layer (can be changed with CRAC AIMA -10[mm] to the stress in the force center). To calculate the crack distance sr,max,
 the concrete cover c from the most outer reinforcement is used.
 The direct analsis of crack width is requested with an input WK PARA in the record CRAC.

metadata.sections: 2.3.3 Crack Width Control with Direct Calculation

content:
The illustration shows a simplified 3-D isometric view of a rectangular concrete slab or panel (rendered as a light gray block) whose top face is overlaid by a blue, orthogonal grid of reinforcement bars. These blue lines form a regular mesh running in two perpendicular directions, representing the steel reinforcement layout in the slab. No tendons or prestressing strands are shown here—only the primary reinforcing bars in a two-way slab grillage.

At one point on the slab’s top surface, a set of four green radial lines (numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4) fan out from a common origin. Each of these green rays indicates one of the discrete directions in which the Capra-Maury method evaluates the uniaxial strain and stress state. The rays are labeled in ascending order (1 through 4) simply to illustrate the idea of stepping through successive orientations.

Above the center of the green fan, a thick red curved arrow sweeps clockwise through approximately 90°, implying the continuous rotation of the assumed principal stress or strain direction across the full 360° in 5° increments (36 steps total). The red arrow’s head points downward toward the slab, emphasizing that the uniaxial check rotates about an axis normal to the slab surface.

The edges of the slab are drawn with bold black outline to give perspective: the longer sides run front-to-back, while the shorter sides run left-to-right. The blue reinforcement grid lines are inset slightly from these edges, suggesting a concrete cover zone around the periphery.

Beneath the diagram, the caption reads “Figure 2.13: Capra-Maury design,” indicating that this visualization pertains to the Capra-Maury uniaxial design variant (CTRL SLS V2 = 1) of the SLS stress‐check routines. In this method, the slab is analyzed by iterating the biaxial strain state in successive uniaxial orientations rather than by simplified interaction formulas. The graphic succinctly conveys:

 • A two-way reinforced concrete slab block  
 • An evenly spaced, orthogonal rebar mesh (blue)  
 • A rotating uniaxial analysis direction (red curved arrow)  
 • Discrete directional steps (green rays numbered 1–4)  

Overall, the image encapsulates the core concept of Capra-Maury design: performing separate uniaxial stress‐strain iterations at regular angular increments (every 5°) to capture the most unfavorable combination of stresses in any orientation, rather than relying on approximate interaction curves or single‐direction checks.

With NSTR various SLS stress checks can be done.
 Without input to CTRL LAY the SLS stress analysis uses the layer design with the mechanically consistent approach of the iteration of the biaxial strain state. This method does not use sim- plifications or modified analysis methods like Baumann or Capra-Maury but is based only on structure mechanical basics and the material work laws. Then all 6 forces nx,ny,nxy,mx,my,mxy are brought to equilibrium with the corresponding 6 strains in one iteration.
 With CTRL SLS V2 also the old methods can be set:
 V2=0 : SLS with substitute forced according Baumann
 V2=1 : uniaxial design every 5 degree according Capra-Maury
 In each element the stresses in concrete and steel are calculated for all loadcases with a uniaxuial iteration of the strain state in 36 directions (all 5 degree)
 V2=2 : mechanically consistent layer design (default)
 In the Baumann and Capra-Maury method tendons are not taken into account in the stress analysis. In the layer design a stress increase of bonded tendons is taken into account in the iteration of the strain state (can be switched off with CTRL SIGZ 0).
 In the layer design also the different bond behaviour of prestressing and reinforcing steel is taken into in the steel stress range according EN 1992-1-1 6.8.2 (6.64). For this tendons are taken into accound inside 2.5*d1 with d1=axis surface distance of the bar.
 With CTRL SIGZ 999 V2 0.45 the value xi (Ratio of bond strength between tendons and rein- forcing steel 6.8.2 table 6.2) can be set e.g. to 0.45. With CTRL SIGZ 999 V2 0 the increase of reinforcement stress due to tendon bond can be switched off.

The image is a simplified, schematic cross‐section of a haunched beam or slab illustrating how the overall shear V is decomposed into the shear parts of the internal inclined compression and tension forces (the so–called truss model). It is labeled “Figure 2.14: Shear force parts in a haunch” and shows the following key elements:

1. Geometry of the Haunch  
   • The section tapers from a smaller depth on the left to a greater depth on the right, drawn as a trapezoid in elevation.  
   • The left end is the “support” or point of application of the external shear V, and the right end is where the section is cut (vertical line) for internal force equilibrium.  

2. External Shear V  
   • At the far left, a single upward‐pointing arrow indicates the applied external shear force V (sometimes denoted VED).  

3. Internal Force Arrows (Truss Model)  
   • Near the top of the haunch, a thick solid arrow slants from right to left, representing the inclined compression strut in the concrete.  
   • Near the bottom of the haunch, a thick solid arrow slants from left to right, representing the tension tie in the reinforcement.  

4. Shear‐Component Wedges and Vertical Force Parts  
   • Next to each internal‐force arrow is a small, white, right‐triangle “wedge” symbolizing the lever arm between the compression and tension lines of action.  
   • Adjacent to each wedge is a straight vertical arrow pointing downward:  
     – The upper vertical arrow is labeled “Vccd” (the shear part contributed by the concrete compression strut).  
     – The lower vertical arrow is labeled “Vtd” (the shear part contributed by the tensile tie).  

5. Interpretation of the Diagram  
   • The figure shows that the total external shear V is shared between the two internal truss members: the concrete strut and the steel tie. Each member’s vertical component (Vccd and Vtd) is “extracted” from V to yield a reduced effective shear VED*.  
   • In practical design (e.g. in BEMESS or other EN 1992 implementations), these reductions can be switched off (CTRL VLEV 0 V2 0), letting the program ignore haunch effects if desired.  
   • Once Vccd and Vtd have been determined, the remaining shear demand (VED*) is divided by the internal lever arm to compute the effective shear stress τ0 used for checking against VRd,c and VRd,max.  

6. Relation to Code‐Based Shear Check  
   • By accounting for the inclined internal forces, the haunch increases the capacity VRd,c before shear reinforcement is needed.  
   • If VED* exceeds VRd,c (which itself depends on longitudinal reinforcement), either shear links must be provided or the longitudinal reinforcement ratio must be increased (CTRL ro_v or PUNC ro_v in punching checks).  

Overall, Figure 2.14 is a clear visual representation of the classical truss‐analogy for shear in a section of varying depth (haunch). It breaks down the external shear into the contributions of the concrete strut and the steel tie, which is fundamental to EN 1992 shear design with variable compression‐strut inclination.

A shear check is performed for plates and shells. The critical shear force V is determined from the shear forces VX and VY as main shear force VED in this vector direction.
 In haunched sections die shear parts of the inclinded compression and tension force are taken into account. In the printout you then find VED as external force and VED* as shear force after the Vccd and Vtd reduction (or increase). The haunch reduction can be switched off with CTRL VLEV 0 V2 0.
 This shear force, divided by the lever arm of the internal forces (see bending design), results in the effective shear stress τ0.
 The output includes the shear zone, the existing shear stress τ0 and possibly the shear stress τ which has to be considered. Perpendicular links are assumed during the calculation of the required shear reinforcement. The shear reinforcement can be output in reference to an area (cm2/m2) or to the elements (cm2).
 The shear design according to EN-1992 and most modern codes is based on two design values of the sustainable shear force:
 • VRd,c:
 Design value of the sustainable shear force without shear reinforcement
 • VRd,m:
 Maximum design value of the sustainable shear force with shear reinforcement, which can be sustained without failure of the fictitious compression concrete strut. If this value is exceeded by the existing shear stress Vsd, the cross section can not be designed.
 If shear links are necessary, a minimum shear reinforcement is calculated according to the
 code.
 In BEMESS the method with variable compression strut inclination is implemented. The com- pression strut inclination is determined in this case according to the utilization degree.
 As VRd,cdepends on the longitudinal reinforcement, for first V>VRd,cthere are two possibilities - either compute shear reinforcement or increase longitudinal reinforcement to increase VRd1. This can be controlled with CTRL ro_v for the overall slab or with PUNC ro_v for punching regions. Example of an input ( bemess6_design.dat ):

As VRd,cdepends on the longitudinal reinforcement, for first V>VRd,cthere are two possibilities - either compute shear reinforcement or increase longitudinal reinforcement to increase VRd1. This can be controlled with CTRL ro_v for the overall slab or with PUNC ro_v for punching regions. Example of an input ( bemess6_design.dat ):.
 CTRL RO_V 0.5 $ The program attempts not to use any shear reinforcement $ up to this bending reinforcement ratio. The shear check $ increases perhaps the bending reinforcement up to this value. PUNC ro_v 1.50 $ for punching desing
 During the calculation of VRd,c and the compression strut inclination the available longitudinal tensile and longitudinal compressive reinforcement as well as the normal force to be included in the principal shear force direction are considered. Reinforcements are considered in this case with the square of the cosine of the angular deviation to the principal shear force direction.

Following boxed values are used depending on the code:
 - 6.2.2(1) Shear VRd,ct analysis
 - 6.2.3(2) max. compression angle cot0
 - No minimum shear reinforcement.
 - Minimum value for vrdc: vmn+k1*σcp according to 6.2.2(1) (6.3N)
 in normal shear design
 The shear design according to the old British Standard (not BS-EN1992) occurs like the check according to old EC2. The from the concrete alone sustainable shear stress v-c is determined in this case in dependence on the bending reinforcement in principal shear force direction according British Standard Table 3.9.
 Unlike the original EC2 the standard method in the shear design which shows a smaller shear reinforcement at weak loaded cross sections may not be employed here. The compression strut inclination beta is limited to 0.6 (according to B4700 equation 23).
 Shear design ass = γs · (τ-u-0.3ftj · k)/(0.9fe) max. shear stress 0.2fcj/γb or 5 MPa (compression strut)
 Plates without shear design are allowed to
 VSd ≤ 0.25 · ƒƒcd · r · (1.0 + 50 · ρ) · b · d · δ
 otherwise shear design with VSd ≤ Vcd + Vd with Vcd = 0.60fctd · b · d · δ max. shear force 0.3fcd· b · d minimum shear reinforcement min-Vd = 0.5 · Vsd
 In shear design, without increase of longitudinal reinforcement it is possible that bending rein- forcement plastifies, so an increased epsv acc. 4.3.3.2.3 (39) is used. Dmax is set to 32 mm. Value kc is set to 0.55 (4.2.1.7).

In shear design, without increase of longitudinal reinforcement it is possible that bending rein- forcement plastifies, so an increased epsv acc. 4.3.3.2.3 (39) is used. Dmax is set to 32 mm. Value kc is set to 0.55 (4.2.1.7)..
 In case the shear check needs longitudinal reinforcement up to ro_v (see ctrl ro_v) , equations 4.3.3.2.2 (38) and 4.3.3.2.1 are used. Then an elastic behavior of the longitudinal reinforce- ment is assumed as more than necessary longitudinal reinforcement is present. If this is not possible, shear reinforcement is inserted. According 4.3.3.4.3 the compression strud angle is analyzed between 25-45 degree. If shear reinforcement is necessary, a minimum shear reinforcement is used according 5.5.2.2 (110) (see 5.5.3.3). The maximum shear strength is checked acc. 4.3.3.4.6.
 For shear check of plates no shear reinforcement is used up to Qb according to equation (8.57). For this c is taken to 1.0·h0. On higher shear force, links are provided according to (8.58) with variable compression (c = 2.0·h0 , controllable with CTRL COTT). The minimum shear links are considered with qs ≥ 0.25·Rbt·b. The maximum shear capacity is limited with equation (8.55).
 The shear check is done according to the alternative model which is described in BBK 04-3.7.3.7. As for DIN-Fachbericht a minimum value vmin is used for the concrete bearing capacity. For the shear check the program attempts to increase the member resistance VRdc via an increase of the longitudinal reinforcement up to RO_V (see CTRL RO_V) in order to refuse a shear reinforcement. If a shear reinforcement is necessary, an optimal inclination compression strut is determined according to 3.7.4.3d. However, this compression strut inclination becomes not smaller than cot-teta≤1.5 due to BBK 04-figure 3.7.4.3b. If shear links necessary, they are designed to fs=fst according to 3.7.4.3f. A minimum shear reinforcement is not checked.

However, this compression strut inclination becomes not smaller than cot-teta≤1.5 due to BBK 04-figure 3.7.4.3b. If shear links necessary, they are designed to fs=fst according to 3.7.4.3f. A minimum shear reinforcement is not checked..
 In the shear design according ACI 318-14 a strength reduction factor of 0.75 for shear is used (ACI 318-14 Table 21.2.1). A minimum shear reinforcement is taken into account if necessary according ACI 318-14 Table 9.6.3.3.
 For shear design BEMESS tries to avoid, if possible, the shear reinforcement by increasing the longitudinal tension reinforcement up to CTRL RO_V.
 If this is not possible, for V>0.5*SRF*Vuc the shear reinforcement is designed with a variable concrete compression angle according to AS 3600 8.2.10. The minimum shear reinforcement is taken into account according to AS 3600 8.2.8. SRF is here the strength reduction factor (for shear SRF=0.7).
 - Without shear reinforcement: if τSd < β * τ0d according to 6.2.2(1) similar to EC2-vrdct
 - Otherwise full shear design with optimum compression angle via compression capacity acc. 6.2.2.1(14)P - (17)P
 - Minimum compression angle cot-theta: according to 6.2.2.1(9)(a):
 2.0 for curtailed reinforcement = default in BEMESS MAT-K1S
 2.5 if not curtailed: input in BEMESS-MAT-K1
 - Without minimum shear reinforcement for slabs (6.4.3.1 (4)P only for beams)

Load cases with support reactions have to be contained in the indicated load cases. If the internal forces and moments from the program MAXIMA are designed, the program BEMESS has to be informed also about the load case of the extreme support reactions (record LC). The use of boundary elements for linear wall support is the precondition for the automatic identification of wall ends and wall corners. An elastic edge support is recommended. The stiffness of this linear edge support results to c=E·D/h (with h=wall height) in this case and can be input generally with approximate 500000 kN/m for the usual building constructions. Indeed a PZ support with an additional output edge element is possible, however, high singular corner moments which depend on the element mesh strongly are calculated then at the re-entrant corners!
 The program searches then single support nodes (single columns) and wall ends as well as wall corners and performs a punching check for these points.
 The punching force at single support node uses the technique of connecting forces according Figure 2.21. At wall corners or edges a perimeter cut is analyzed, see section wall ends.
 Nodes with less than 5 kN support reaction are not considered! This has to be considered for the control of the punching points (with program WING ”QUAD ASPS SCHH 0.20”)! Within the punching area the plate shear design is replaced then by a punching check. The elements lying within this area get then at least the for the punching check necessary upper longitudinal reinforcement. If the bending design shows a higher longitudinal reinforcement, this becomes determinent. A normal plate shear design occurs outside of the punching area.
 Studrails: see PUNC KPU.
 In case of a column head the program verifies the punching in the inner and outer part. Exam- ple see bemess7_columnhead.dat.
 With ECHO PUNC EXTR a plot ot the punching sitiuation can also be requested if no shear reinforcement is necessary.
 So that a necessary shear reinforcement will not forget in the graphics, all points have the shear reinforcement in the punching area, also the points directly about the column!

Exam- ple see bemess7_columnhead.dat.. With ECHO PUNC EXTR a plot ot the punching sitiuation can also be requested if no shear reinforcement is necessary.. So that a necessary shear reinforcement will not forget in the graphics, all points have the shear reinforcement in the punching area, also the points directly about the column!.
 If no column dimensions are input, BEMESS uses a rectangular column with d=b=plate thick- ness (however, not larger than 30 cm) as default. Column dimensions possibly defined in the data base are accepted (Slabdesigner).
 With ECHO PUNC FULL a detailed output is printed per column.

Usually the column parameters are set in the graphical input of a structural point in SOFIPLUS. These parameters are used in BEMESS.
 In special cases they can be modified in a manual input PUNC where the columns can be assigned by means of the supporting coordinates X and Y (mesh-independent). But also a node number can be input on TYPE.
 The program attempts to perform first of all the punching check without shear reinforcement. If bending reinforcements more than REIN (default 1.5 %) results, so the program changes to punching check with shear reinforcement.
 Control parameters on punching can also be input in a separate TEDDY task in front of a SSD Task design, example see SELE

The image is a black-and-white schematic, labeled at its top left “Segment Method:”, illustrating how discrete radial segments around a column are used to locate the effective (or “active”) punching-shear perimeter in a flat slab. Below the sketch is the caption “Figure 2.15: Segment method to find the active perimeter.”

Main Geometry  
• At the center sits a square column cross-section, drawn in plan view as a small square.  
• Concentric about this square are two circles:  
  – The inner (light) circle represents the theoretical 2d perimeter (at a radial distance equal to the slab’s effective depth d from the column face).  
  – The outer (thin) circle marks the maximum search radius, here denoted “6*” (i.e. 6·d or 6·effective depth) beyond the 2d line.  
• A series of radial lines subdivide the annular ring between inner and outer circles into equal angular “search segments” (in the actual implementation, 72 segments of 5° each).

Identification of Edges and Openings  
• A horizontal straight line across the upper part of the diagram is labeled “Boundary of slab,” showing where the slab edge cuts the search ring. Two adjacent segments (numbered “1” and “2”) intersect this slab boundary and are shaded to indicate they are not fully intact.  
• In the lower-right quadrant, a rectangular notch or “Opening” is drawn just outside the inner circle; that cut also removes material from certain search segments (here illustrated by a darker shade in segment “4”). Segment “3” (mid-right) is shown partly shaded but still intact within the slab material.  
• The fact that more than one segment is truncated (segments 1, 2 and 4 in the example) signals to the algorithm that an opening exists in the slab, so the smaller, “caught” perimeter u around the column is adopted rather than the full interior boundary.

Callouts and Labels  
• “Search segment inner radius” is indicated by an arrow to the inner circle (distance = d).  
• “Search segment outer radius” is pointed to the outer circle (distance = 6·d).  
• “u” is drawn from the column square to the inner circle, twice, showing the active perimeter location around the full column cross-section.  
• A dimension line below the sketch shows “6*” spanning from the inner circle to the outer circle, and “dS” (between inner circle and column face) with a sub-dimension labeled d.

Interpretation in Context  
The figure concretely demonstrates the “segment method” described in the accompanying text: the program automatically checks consecutive angular segments for the presence of slab material (plate elements). If all sub-areas of a segment are present, that segment is counted toward the punching perimeter. Segments cut by a slab boundary or by an opening are flagged as “inactive,” reducing the effective perimeter u. By identifying which segments are lost to edges or openings, the software determines whether a column behaves as interior, edge or corner (based on the ratio u/u₀), and applies the appropriate punching-shear checks—including the increased stress factor β for eccentric loads.

The image is a clean, white-background header and caption snippet extracted from a SOFiSTiK BEMESS manual or theoretical‐principles document. At the very top, flush left in a medium‐weight sans‐serif font colored deep blue, sits the word “BEMESS,” followed by a vertical divider (“|”) and then the subtitle “Theoretical Principles” in black. A thin horizontal rule runs beneath this header, visually separating the title bar from the body of the page. On the upper right corner, aligned with the header, is the SOFiSTiK corporate logo: a stylized, segmented, spherical grid motif in blue, accompanied to its right by the SOFiSTiK wordmark in gray, set in a modern, geometric typeface.

Below the dividing line, and centered horizontally, is the figure caption text. It reads, in a standard black sans‐serif font:  
“Figure 6.21N for edge and corner columns (by default). This behavior can be controlled with CTRL BETA.”  

Within this line, the label “CTRL BETA” is highlighted in the same deep blue used for the “BEMESS” text, drawing the reader’s eye to the program command that overrides default behavior. The caption line is neither boxed nor accompanied by any graphic illustration in this snippet; it stands alone as a descriptive title for a figure presumably found elsewhere in the full document.

Visually, the page section conveys a professional, technical style: minimal color palette (blue, black, gray), ample white space, and clear typographic hierarchy. The header bar and logo firmly establish document branding, while the subsequent figure caption succinctly informs the user that Figure 6.21N pertains to the way edge and corner columns are handled by default in the punching‐shear analysis module. In the broader context of the punching shear perimeter and β-factor discussion, this caption indicates that the segment method’s adjustment for reduced perimeters at slab edges or corners can be manually toggled via the “CTRL BETA” input in BEMESS.

For edge and corner columns the effective perimeter is reduced based on a segment method. In addition the punching force is increased by a beta factor.
 BEMESS determines itself the effective round cut automatically, when it is controlled whether in individual segments around the column blockouts or edges are to be found. It applies in this case individual segment areas like for the block load analysis. If for a segment area plate elements are used with 100%, the segment is considered as effective for the punching. Currently 72 segments are arranged with 5 degrees per segment. The search segments extend from dS/2 to dS/2+6·effective depth.
 In fig. 2.15 the segments 1,2+4 are not covered completely. Segment 1+2 finds the boundary, segment 4 finds the opening. The program can not differ between boundary and opening but the fact that two active segments u occur indicates that there must be an opening. Then the catched u is taken as the active perimeter. Without opening the active perimeter may be elongated up to the real boundary according EN 1992-1-1 figure 6.15. You find this in the full punching listing marked with ”+ boundary spacing”.
 The segment method delivers the effective perimeter u of the punching round cut. The ratio
 u/u0 is output in % in the result list.
 A column is considered as an inside column from 1.00·u0 to 0.80·u0., as an edge column from 0.80·u0 to 0.50·u0, as a corner column smaller 0.50·u0.
 In case a point lies exactly on the boundary we assume that this is only done to simplify the analysis model and the outer column face is alligned with slab boundary in reality. So the perimeter is elongated by 2*half column width in that case, see EN 1992-1-1 figure 6.15. In case the point lies a little bit inside the slab, the length of an exact perimeter at distance 2d is used.

In case a point lies exactly on the boundary we assume that this is only done to simplify the analysis model and the outer column face is alligned with slab boundary in reality. So the perimeter is elongated by 2*half column width in that case, see EN 1992-1-1 figure 6.15. In case the point lies a little bit inside the slab, the length of an exact perimeter at distance 2d is used..
 According to the standard the shear stress in the perimeter cut determined with u is increased with a beat factor for the rough consideration of not axisymmetric bending loading. Using CTRL WINT 0 the program calculates this eccentricity value beta according EN 6.4.3 (6.39). BEMESS extracts a restraint column bending moment also in case of a simple pz-supported slab using the shear force distribution around the punching node. If the column is really restraint with a rotational spring or a column beam the real restraint moment is used to calculate the beta value according EN 6.4.3 (6.39). The loadcase with the maximum product of Vz*beta will be designed for punching. This beta method is performed for all design codes - even if they do not note it explicitely.
 Usually we have a biaxial bending moment MX+MY. Thus also for international codes the extended german formula (NA 6.39.1) is used to combine both Mx and My. The function W1 according (6.40) is analyzed for the active part of the perimeter, also for edge and corner columns. In general the beta value is limited to 1.80 to avoid unrealistic high values. At edge and corner columns often high beta values are computed. But as the perimeter is already highly reduced at these columns, BEMESS uses the flat (approximate) values according EN 6.4.3(6)
 The beta value can also be set manually for every punching node with PUNC ... BETA but for security on edge and corner columns at least the flat value is used.

The drawing (Figure 2.16) shows two simplified, vertical cross-section sketches of a reinforced-concrete plate (slab) at two types of interior support nodes—a central column node on the left and a wall-end or wall-corner node on the right. Both sketches illustrate how the slab thickness is locally increased during the bending-and-punching-shear design for the central support:

1. General layout  
   - The upper horizontal element represents the slab (plate) itself.  
   - A heavy dashed vertical line marks the geometric centerline of the support.  
   - Below the slab, thin vertical lines (left figure) denote the column profile; in the right figure, a stepped outline indicates a wall or corner support.  
   - The thickness of the slab at the node is indicated by the dimension “d” in the left sketch.

2. Central-column node (left sketch)  
   - Instead of performing a detailed regular plate-shear design around the punching perimeter, the software omits that region and substitutes a punching-shear check.  
   - A frustum-shaped “thickening” zone radiates from the column face into the slab. Its boundary is drawn with a serrated line to highlight the local increase in plate depth.  
   - The slope of the taper is 1 vertical : 3 horizontal (i.e. for every 1 unit of thickness added at the column, it extends 3 units outward toward the slab).  
   - This local “node thickness” increase is only applied for the bending design of the central node; when the default plate thickness from the GEOM record covers walls ends and corners, no additional thickening occurs.  
   - If the user activates ECHO REIN FULL, the software will explicitly print the geometry of this increased-thickness region for each node.

3. Wall-end or wall-corner node (right sketch)  
   - A similar step-and-taper profile is shown, with the thicker slab zone beginning directly at the wall face and tapering away.  
   - The punching-shear check zone is outlined in a dotted profile to indicate the portion where regular shear design is bypassed in favor of the punching check.  
   - At corners or ends of walls, shear forces can flow around the critical perimeter. Therefore, if stirrups for punching shear are required, the software will recommend increasing the design shear force by 15 percent to account for external shear flow beyond the critical cut. This adjustment is SOFiSTiK’s own handling and may be suppressed via the CTRL WINT 0 V2 0 switch.

4. Contextual design notes (from the accompanying text)  
   - To reduce the high bending moment at a singularly supported node, a moment reduction Δm = (A/8)·(bmin/bmax) is applied, where A is the maximum support reaction and bmin/bmax the smaller/larger column dimensions. Under equal biaxial loading (mI = mII and bx = by), each moment is reduced by A/16, capped at 20 percent overall.  
   - These reductions also apply when punching shear checks (PUNC NO) are active, unless specifically turned off (e.g. PUNC NO D 0.01 B 0.01 to disable punching or SELE commands to exclude certain nodes).  
   - The figure’s legend refers to Load Area “Aod” and the determinant sections of the critical round cut in accordance with German and Austrian punching-shear code conventions.

Overall, Figure 2.16 graphically conveys how SOFiSTiK locally thickens the slab around central and wall supports—omitting the regular shear plate design in favor of a punching check, incorporating bending and shear adjustments, and providing user controls to switch these provisions on or off.

sections: 2.5.4 Shear and Bending Design at the Column

content:
The provided graphic is a two-dimensional schematic of a critical perforation (punching) shear perimeter around a loaded column or wall element, as used in German/Austrian design practice. It combines a hatched rectangular “load area” at its center with a smooth, rounded outer loop that marks the “determinant sections of the critical round cut.” Key geometric dimensions, notation and legend items appear around and inside the drawing. The following points describe its layout in detail:

1. Central Load Area (Label “1”)  
   • Shaded by diagonal hatching, this central region represents the plan projection of the loaded area—typically the column or wall footprint—subject to punching shear checks.  
   • It is a rectangle of width b and length a, with a clear stipulation beneath: “a ≥ 2 b,” indicating that the longer side a must be at least twice the shorter side b.  

2. Critical Perimeter Loop (Label “2”)  
   • Surrounds the hatched rectangle with a continuous bar—or frame—shaped line. At each of the four mid-sides, the frame bows outward in a half-cylinder form (semi-circular bulge).  
   • This loop denotes the locus where punching shear is evaluated: a critical round cut that encircles the loaded area at a certain offset.  

3. Dimensional Annotations  
   • Offset from the rectangle to the inner face of the loop: 1.5·d (where “d” is the effective depth of the slab or plate). This is shown on the left side by a horizontal leader ending in “1,5 d.”  
   • On the top and bottom horizontal edges, the total height of the loop above/below the load area equals b (the shorter side of the rectangle). Mid-way along each of these edges a short vertical arrow marks “b₁/2,” indicating half of a special width b₁ that defines the bulge’s radial thickness. Just outside that, another arrow marks “b₁/2” on the opposite side, summing to full b₁.  
   • On the bottom, directly under the hatched rectangle, two small horizontal dimensions of a₁/2 appear at each half-width location of the rectangle, labeling the distance from the rectangle’s vertical edge to the point where the bulge begins.  

4. Legend and Caption  
   • A keyed legend in the corner reads:  
     – “1 Load area A_od”  
     – “2 determinant sections of the critical round cut Germany and Austria”  
   • Beneath the figure is the caption “Figure 2.17: Determinant sections of the critical round cut Germany and Austria.”  

5. Graphical Style  
   • All lines are uniformly thick, with the load area hatched at 45° to distinguish it from the steel-tube style frame of the critical perimeter.  
   • Arrows and leaders use solid thin lines to connect numeric labels to features without obscuring geometry.  
   • Text is set in a clear sans serif font, with subscripts (e.g. b₁, a₁) and multiplication dots (1,5 d).  

Contextual Notes (from accompanying specification text, not shown on the drawing):  
– Within the punching area the usual plate-shear reinforcement is suppressed in favor of a direct punching check.  
– To limit high nodal bending moments at singular supports, a moment reduction Δm = A/8 · (b_min/b_max) is applied (with further splitting into Δm_I = A/16, Δm_II = A/16 under biaxial loading when b_x = b_y), capped at 20 %.  
– Special options (PUNC NO, SELE, CTRL WINT) allow turning off punching checks or moment reductions for specific nodes.  
– An increased plate thickness (tapering out from the column edge at a 1:3 slope) is adopted for central column node bending checks, visible in ECHO REIN FULL outputs but omitted under default GEOM settings.  
– When punching-shear stirrups are required at wall ends/corners, a 15 % force increase is recommended (user-toggleable) to account for shear flow entering from outside the critical perimeter.

sections: 2.5.4 Shear and Bending Design at the Column

content:
The illustration is a 2-D plan view of a wall-end condition showing how the punching-shear perimeter and load area are defined when a rectangular column sits flush against the end of a wall.  The wall is drawn as two long, parallel horizontal lines (representing the top and bottom faces of the wall).  In the center of that span is a rectangular column (shown as a narrower pair of parallel lines) bearing onto the wall end.

On the right side of the column the “punching check” region is sketched by a U-shaped, rounded contour that traces a distance b1/2 away from the column face along the wall’s thickness (above and below).  This curved outline represents the critical perimeter used in punching‐shear design.  A pair of dimension arrows mark that offset: one vertical arrow on the right of the wall indicating b1/2 from the column edge up into the wall, and a matching arrow indicating b1/2 down into the wall.  Likewise, a small horizontal arrow below the contour marks a1/2, the distance the critical perimeter extends in front of the wall face.

A leader arrow points to the central region of the column interface and is labeled “1.”  In the accompanying legend this “1” is defined as the load area Aod (the area over which the column reaction is assumed to act).  Legend item “2” (not explicitly called out by arrow in the sketch) refers to “determinant sections of the critical round cut” used in Germany and Austria for punching design.

Beneath the drawing is the caption:
“Figure 2.18: Wall end, a1 and b1 see inner columns.”

Key graphic elements:
• Wall represented by two parallel horizontal lines.  
• Centered column represented by narrower parallel lines.  
• Curved or rounded U-shape around the right-hand column face outlining the punching‐shear perimeter.  
• Dimension arrows:
   – b1/2 vertical offsets above and below the wall thickness  
   – a1/2 horizontal offset in front of the wall face  
• Leader arrow to the column face labeled “1” (load area).  
• Legend entries identifying “1” as Load area Aod and “2” as the determinant sections of the critical round cut.  
• Caption stating Figure number, describing that a1 and b1 relate to inner columns at a wall end.

Overall, the graphic communicates how the punching shear perimeter is established for a column at a wall termination, with clear half-width offsets (a1/2, b1/2) and a rounded critical perimeter conforming to regional design practice.

sections: 2.5.4 Shear and Bending Design at the Column

content:
Within the punching area the regular plate shear design is omitted and replaced by the punch- ing check.
 The high node moment in a singular supported node is reduced with delta-m = A/8·bmin/bmax (A = maximum support reaction, bmin, bmax = smaller, larger column dimension). It is con- sidered, that for biaxial moment loading (mI=mII) the support pressure can be determined only in each case to a half for a mI and a mII support moment reduction, therefore delta-mI= A/16 and delta-mII= A/16 for bx=by. The moment reduction is limited to max. 20 %. This reduction also works on switched off punching PUNC NO. With PUNC NO D 0.01 B 0.01 the moment reduction can be switched off. With SELE this can be switched off for specific nodes.
 In addition a larger thickness is used during the bending design of the central column node. In this case the thickness is increased from the column edge with 1:3. With the default of a plate thickness in the record GEOM as well as at wall ends and wall corners this increase does not occur. The increased thickness is printed in the case of ECHO REIN FULL per node.
 Legend 1 Load area Aod
 2
 determinant sections of the critical round cut Germany and Austria
 In case punching shear stirrups are necessary at wallends or wallcorners, a recommendation is printed to increase the force by 15 o/o for an external studrail design as shear forces also flow to the corner from outside the critical perimeter (passing the end of the critical perimeter). This increase is a SOFiSTiK own handling and can be switched off with CTRL WINT 0 V2 0.

metadata.sections: 2.5.4 Shear and Bending Design at the Column

content:
The drawing is labeled “Figure 2.19: Wall corner” and presents a plan-view detail of a corner in a reinforced-concrete wall or slab element where a concentrated load is applied near the interior corner of the wall. Key features of the sketch are described below.  

1. Geometry of the wall corner  
   - Two perpendicular wall segments meet at a right angle. The vertical segment on the right is dimensioned with a thickness or width “b.” The horizontal segment on the left has the same cross-section thickness, but only the right side of the horizontal arm is shown in detail.  
   - The intersection of these two wall segments defines the interior corner of the structure, and just inside that corner a small, square or rectangular “load area” is indicated.  

2. Load area (Aod) and legend  
   - The small square immediately adjacent to the corner is marked with the numeral “1.” In the accompanying legend, “1” is defined as “Load area Aod.” This denotes the plan-area over which the concentrated force is assumed to act.  
   - A dimension line adjacent to the load area shows half of its side length, labeled “a1/2.” By symmetry, the full side length of the loaded patch would be “a1,” with the “/2” dimension indicating the distance from the wall faces to the load area boundary.  

3. Punching-shear perimeter  
   - Although not explicitly outlined in a heavy line on this particular sketch, the context notes that the punching-shear perimeter at wall corners is placed at a side length of 1·d from the edges of the loaded area. In other words, one moves a distance “d” out from each loaded-area edge in plan, forming a square or rectangular shear perimeter.  
   - The figure caption and text clarify that this 1·d perimeter rule applies irrespective of the overall wall width “b.” Unlike some earlier code provisions, the width of the wall does not influence the punching-shear boundary at corners.  

4. Reference to analytical approach  
   - The accompanying text specifies that the method used to compute the punching force at a corner is the same as that applied at a free wall end. The EN-1991-1-1 provision (or equivalent national code) has modified the punching-perimeter definition so that the critical shear path lies at a constant offset d from the loaded area, regardless of how large the wall is.  

5. Overall intent of the sketch  
   - By isolating the corner region and carefully dimensioning the load patch and wall geometry, the drawing underlines that punching shear checks at corners can be carried out in exactly the same way as at straight or free edges once the 1·d perimeter rule has been adopted. This simplifies design checks and removes the need to consider the full wall width in corner shear verifications.

The punching at wall corners was improved according EN-1991-1-1 and is also valid for other codes.
 At wall corners the side length of the punching perimeter is set to 1.·d (depending on the code). The wall width has no effect now! The analysis of the punching force used the same method than at wall ends.
 Legend 1 Load area Aod
 1

For EN-1991-1-1 codes the critical perimeter distance is searched iteratively. Other codes often use a distance 1.0·d . The distance to the slab boundary is not valued as critical as for normal slabs (the critical distance to the boundary is taken to 1.2-1.8·d depending on the slab thickness (6·d for normal slabs/openings). A higher boundary β value is then taken for a relation u/u0 < 0.95 (0.80 for normal slabs).
 Reduction of the soil pressure according EN-1991-1-1 is allowed with 100% area of the critical reduced design cut. PUNC LC_P reactivated to input a fixed loadcase for soil pressure reduc- tion. Futhermore now at least 90 % of the maximum soil pressure is taken for the reduction, also in case of lower minimum soil pressure, because usually the maximum punching force corresponds with maximum soil pressure (is not clear in priory).
 With ECHO PUNC 4 you can get the punchung force V-Ed without bedding reduction in the WINGRAF plot.

Depending on the code prestress normal stresses are taken into account for punching design, but only the part of real defined slab tendons crossing the punching zone. Normal forces of a normal 3D analysis without tendons are not taken into account!
 The vertical component of tendons is considered for the analysis of VED in all design codes. BEMESS searches for each punching perimeter the tendons which cross this perimeter. For a horizontal deviation of the tendon to the perimeter greater than 60 degree a tendon is not taken into account for this perimeter. Up to 40 degree the cosine is used, between 40 and 60 the contribution is interpolated. Creep and shrinkage are considered with a constant loss of CTRL VPDC - default VPDC=0.12 (=12%). With ECHO PUNC EXTR all used tendons are listed with their single effect.
 Instead of the automatic calculation of Vpd, Vpd can also be input manually for each punching node with PUNC...VPD (positive = relieving effect). The input value is then taken constant for each punching perimeter.

metadata.sections: 2.5.8 Consideration of the Prestress during Punching Check

content:
The image presents a three-dimensional finite-element model of a multi-storey reinforced-concrete structure, viewed in perspective so that three slab levels, their supporting columns and wall ends are all visible. The intent of the illustration is to show automatically determined critical punching shear perimeters (in red) around each column and wall termination. Below is a detailed breakdown of what can be seen:

Overall geometry and color coding  
- Slabs are shown as thin wireframe surfaces in blue (top, mid and foundation levels) with grid lines outlining the finite-element mesh.  
- Vertical supports consist of slender columns drawn in magenta lines and broader rectangular walls outlined in a lighter cyan or blue line.  
- The viewer is looking from a corner angle so that two exterior sides of the building frame are in the foreground.

Critical punching shear contours  
- At each slab-to-column junction, one or more concentric red closed “rings” mark the positions of critical punching shear perimeters (i.e. the loci where shear reinforcement is required).  
- The intensity of the red contour indicates the maximum shear stress zones immediately adjacent to the column cross section, tapering off outward.  
- Some columns (particularly at the foundation slab) display two nested red rings, indicating two shear-reinforcement perimeters that the analysis has determined are necessary. At upper storeys only a single perimeter is shown.

Wall-end punching details  
- Along the slab edges where walls terminate, semi-circular (reduced) punching perimeters are visible in red. These “half-rings” illustrate that the slab edge reduces the punching perimeter in those directions.  
- The walls themselves are visualized as thicker, continuous vertical plates, and the associated red contours hug these ends rather than fully encircle.

Numeric annotations  
- Adjacent to each red perimeter a small block of black text gives the key design values. Typical lines read:  
   • “VEd = 280.2 kN” (the factored punching shear force to be checked)  
   • “Perm = 21.12 cm²” (area of required shear reinforcement around that perimeter)  
   • Sometimes also “kr = 2x4” or similar notation indicating the number and arrangement of reinforcement legs.  
- These labels are oriented so they hover just outside each ring, making it clear which data apply to which perimeter.

Finite-element connection logic  
- The diagram implicitly reflects the procedure described in the accompanying text: at each column-slab node, the software sums the connecting forces of the adjacent four quad-elements and uses the resulting punching force, rather than integrating elemental shear stresses around a path. This approach remains accurate even when higher-level column loads arrive as concentrated nodal loads.  
- By automatically extracting column cross-section dimensions and wall thicknesses, the software establishes the correct radii for each round cut and wall-end cut, then omits the normal plate-shear check within the excluded circular zone.

Caption and figure reference  
- At the very bottom of the image is the label “Figure 2.20: Critical punching and shear reinforcement perimeters,” tying the graphic back to the text.  

In summary, this 3D wireframe view emphasizes how an FEM-based tool (in this case BEMESS) identifies, contours and annotates all critical punching perimeters at slab-column and slab-wall interfaces across multiple floors—providing the engineer with immediate visual feedback on where and how much perimeter shear reinforcement is required.

sections: 2.5.9 Punching Check at a Three-Dimensional System

content:
The image presents a three-dimensional finite‐element model of a reinforced concrete slab, rendered in varying shades of blue to highlight the underlying quadrilateral mesh. The slab surface spans almost the entire field of view, with uniformly spaced grid lines delineating individual plate elements. Toward the right edge of the slab one can see a gently curved boundary, suggesting an architectural feature such as a terrace or a circular opening. Two slender, light-cyan columns penetrate vertically through the slab at distinct locations: one closer to the left-centre area, the other nearer the curved edge. Each column is represented as a smooth cylindrical shaft rising perpendicularly above and below the slab plane.

At the precise nodes where the columns intersect the slab, striking red “star” markers denote the critical punching‐shear perimeters automatically determined by the analysis software (BEMESS). These markers take the form of small radial arrows or crosses encircling the column axis, indicating the round cut beyond which the normal plate shear check may be omitted. In the instance closest to the curved slab edge, the red perimeter lies partially truncated by the slab’s curvature, emphasizing the software’s ability to adapt the shear‐reinforcement geometry to irregular floor outlines.

The viewpoint is set at an oblique angle above the slab, affording a clear perspective on both the horizontal surface mesh and the vertical alignment of columns. Subtle color gradients—from deeper blues in the distance to lighter tones near the foreground—enhance depth perception and clearly differentiate element boundaries. The mesh is sufficiently fine to show individual quadrilateral elements, each connecting to the column node; in fact, four such quads meet at each column penetration.

Beneath the visualization, the figure caption reads: “Figure 2.21: Connecting forces to calculate the punching force at columns.” This underscores the methodology illustrated: the software sums the nodal “connecting forces” from the four adjacent plate elements around each column node to compute the punching shear force. By integrating these forces through the element shape functions, the program achieves greater precision than traditional perimeter‐based shear‐force integration, and can correctly handle single‐load cases or combined superposed maxima. Overall, the image conveys both the geometric layout of slab‐column interactions and the automated detection of critical punching zones used in three‐dimensional finite‐element design.

sections: 2.5.9 Punching Check at a Three-Dimensional System

content:
In increasing measure high-rise buildings are analysed according to the Finite Element Method also for three-dimensional systems. The singular column points and wall end points are a problem in the design especially for the shear design. The decisive punching points of column connections and wall ends are identified automatically also at inserted slabs and checked.
 Within a round cut the normal plate shear check can be omitted then. The bending moments are reduced at the columns. The decisive shear force results from the difference of the column forces over and under the slab. Because these parts are not anymore understandable from the column forces after a superposition with the partial safety factors, the punching force is integrated about the shape functions at the punching node from the bordering plate elements. The punching dimensions are extracted automatically from the column cross sections and the wall thicknesses.
 In the same manner a punching check is performed for columns and wall ends at elastic bedded
 foundation plates with deduction of the minimum soil pressure.
 In the illustration the automatically determined critical punching round cuts are plotted in red. Some punching points require multiple shear reinforcement perimeters. Here this is the case particularly in the foundation slab. The in each case reduced round cut is recognizable at the wall ends.
 The following Figure 2.21 shows how BEMESS calculates the punching force:
 Procedure: at the column node in the slab here 4 quad elements attach to the node. The connecting forces of these 4 quad elements are summed up and give the punching force.
 These connecting forces are much more precise that the quad shear forces that could be integrated in a perimeter around the column. Furthermore this method also works in case the column forces of a higher level are only applied as single loads. A problem is that usually only the MAXIMA superposed loadcases are used - see problemm of Figure 2.23
 A differnce of the column force above and below the slab is not used in BEMESS as the Max- Min column forces are separate results and sometimes not even analyzed.
 Punching is only performed on horizontal slabs but not at vertical walls!

metadata.sections: 2.5.9 Punching Check at a Three-Dimensional System

content:
The drawing is a highly simplified 3‐D “slab on column” submodel used to illustrate how BEMESS derives a punching shear design action from its MAXIMA superposition of single‐load‐case results.  It consists of a rigid slab element spanning across a single central column, which in turn is founded on a fixed support (shown by the standard ground‐fixing symbol under the column foot).  Three sketches (a, b and c) are laid out left to right, each corresponding to one of the relevant load situations:

1. γ * g (Dead Load)  
   - Two identical downward point loads of 200 kN each are applied to the slab, one on each side of the column.  
   - These loads represent the characteristic dead weight (self‐weight plus any permanent finishes).  
   - The column carries these two 200 kN reactions straight down into the support.

2. γ * w (Wind Load)  
   - One side of the slab is subjected to a downward wind pressure of 70 kN, while the opposite side is uplifted by –70 kN (shown as an upward arrow).  
   - This gives a net overturning couple about the column and illustrates the worst‐case eccentricity of the wind action alone.  
   - In isolation, the column base reactions would be unequal: +70 kN on the loaded side and –70 kN on the unloaded side.

3. γ * g + γ * w (Superposed Maxima from BEMESS)  
   - BEMESS does not have a single combined γ*g+γ*w loadcase in its linear‐elastic solver.  Instead it computes separate support reactions and bending moments for each fundamental loadcase, then forms envelope MAXIMA of these results.  
   - On the left side of the column the envelope picks up the larger downward reaction (200 kN + 70 kN = 270 kN), while on the right it picks the larger “uplift” magnitude in absolute value (200 kN – 70 kN = 130 kN down in envelope, although that came from a different single‐load‐case scenario).  
   - From these enveloped point loads BEMESS derives a punching shear design force V_Ed = 470 kN.  Applying the default β‐factor (β = 1.08), the controlling punching shear becomes β · V_Ed = 508 kN, which closely matches the manually computed value of β · V_Ed = 512 kN obtained from the actual γ*g+γ*w combination.  

Key observations:  
- The MAXIMA‐superposed reactions mix effects that never occur simultaneously (wind up on one side, wind down on the other).  
- Despite that, the enveloped punching shear force β·V_Ed ≃ 508 kN remains on the conservative side relative to the true combined loadcase (512 kN).  
- Note: BEMESS normally enforces a minimum β = 1.15 by default.  To use β = 1.08 you must override with the command “CTRL BETA –2.”

Figure 2.22 thus demonstrates how BEMESS’s MAXIMA superposition approach yields a reasonable—and in practice safely conservative—punching shear design action even when the actual worst‐case combination is not available as a single loadcase in the 3D analysis.

sections: 2.5.10 V-Ed analysis out of MAXIMA superposition loadcases

content:
The image is a three-part schematic (labelled “Figure 2.23: Punching force, extracted from MAXIMA quad superposition forces”) showing how BEMESS treats slab-on-column punching loads under different loading scenarios and after superposition (“MAXIMA-min-mxx”). Each part is a simple side-elevation sketch of a flat slab element on a single central column, with support at the base, and with arrows indicating the reaction or applied loads at the slab‐column interface.

1. Left Sketch (γ * g):  
   - Captioned “γ ∗ g.”  
   - A rectangular slab panel is drawn atop a slender column. The column base is shown with hatch marks indicating a fixed support.  
   - Two vertical arrows point downward onto the slab—one on the left side labelled “200 kN,” the other on the right side simply “200.”  
   - These arrows represent the factored dead‐load reaction at the column under permanent (dead) loading with partial safety factor γ applied.  

2. Middle Sketch (γ * w):  
   - Captioned “γ ∗ w.”  
   - Same slab‐on-column geometry.  
   - On the left edge of the slab a downward arrow labelled “70” indicates wind pressure acting downward, while on the right edge an upward arrow labelled “–70” indicates suction (lift) from wind.  
   - This idealized pair of loads shows the factored wind action (uplift and downward pressure) at the column interface.  

3. Right Sketch (MAXIMA ‑ min ‑ mxx):  
   - Captioned “MAXIMA – min – mxx.”  
   - Geometry again identical.  
   - Two downward arrows represent the extreme superposed reactions extracted from BEMESS’s MAXIMA quad force envelope:  
     • Left arrow labeled “270” (kN downward)  
     • Right arrow labeled “200” (kN downward)  
   - Next to the column are design quantities:  
     • “V – Ed = 470 kN” (ultimate punching shear force extracted)  
     • “M = 30 kNm” (bending moment)  
     • “β = 1.08” (punching shear strength modification factor chosen)  
     • “β ∗ V – Ed = 508 kN” (design controlling shear after applying β)  

Below these three sketches is the figure title explaining that the punching force is extracted from the MAXIMA quad superposition forces—which, in a 3D system, represent envelope forces that do not correspond to a single real loadcase but can be used for design.  

Overall, the composite figure makes visually clear that:
- Individual factored loadcases (γ g, γ w) produce column forces of 200 kN and ±70 kN respectively.
- The MAXIMA superposition algorithm then combines results (even from non-simultaneous actions) to produce an envelope of shear forces (270 kN at one side, 200 kN at the other), leading to an extracted V-Ed of 470 kN.
- Applying the chosen factor β = 1.08 yields a design shear of about 508 kN, closely matching a manual combination check (γ g + γ w = 512 kN).
- The note in the surrounding text emphasizes that BEMESS’s default β is 1.15 (conservative), and that using β = 1.08 requires the user to input “CTRL BETA –2.”

sections: 2.5.10 V-Ed analysis out of MAXIMA superposition loadcases

content:
In the design of a normal slab or shell structure BEMESS only gets the MAXIMA superposition loadcases. The superposed support reactions don’t help because in a 3D system they do not give an information at the punching node. Lets now study an example, showing a slab on a column with dead load and wind. In a manual calculation you would check the combination γ ∗ g + γ ∗ and design punching with β ∗ V − Ed = 512kN:
 But the combination loadcase γ ∗ g + γ ∗ does not exist as a single loadcase in a normal analysis. There you only have the single loadcases and the MAXIMA superposition quad forces, e.g. min-mxx. From this BEMESS must extract a punching force and gets:
 The force V-Ed= 470 kN does not really exist but the design controlling value β ∗ V − Ed = 508kN is quite close to the manual value.
 Conclusion: the superposed MAXIMA quad forces can contain results from actions that cannot occur in parallel (left of the column force with wind, right of the column force without wind), but
 the design controlling value β ∗ V − Ed = 508kN is OK.
 Remark: by default BEMESS uses a minimum β of 1.15. So BEMESS would be on the save side here. To use the value β =1.08 you must input CTRL BETA -2.

metadata.sections: 2.5.10 V-Ed analysis out of MAXIMA superposition loadcases

content:
The image is a plan‐view sketch illustrating how the punching‐shear control perimeter “u” is defined for both square (or rectangular) and circular column cross-sections. It is captioned “Figure 2.24: Control perimeter u.”

General layout  
• Two subfigures are shown side by side.  
• The left subfigure shows a square column of side lengths “a” (horizontal) and “b” (vertical) in plan view. The column core is hatched or filled in gray.  
• The right subfigure shows a circular column (filled gray) of diameter “s,” also in plan view.  

Control perimeter for square column (left)  
• Around the gray square is drawn a dashed‐and‐dot loop representing the perimeter at a distance d_v/2 from the column face. Here d_v denotes the effective depth (often equal to the slab thickness minus cover).  
• Along the top and bottom edges of this loop, horizontal dimension arrows mark the column’s half‐spacing plus clearance: each arrow between the square face and the loop is labeled d_v/2.  
• Above the loop, two arrows bracket the total clear span between adjacent columns in the horizontal direction and are labeled “a.” To the left and right horizontally on the loop, small arrows mark the slab span “b.”  
• Beneath the subfigure is the formula for the total control‐perimeter length:  
  u = 2·a + 2·b + d_v·π  
  This expression acknowledges that the four straight‐edge segments each extend a plus b, and the four semicircular corners sum to a full circle of radius d_v/2, giving π·d_v.  

Control perimeter for circular column (right)  
• A circle shaded gray represents the column core of diameter “s.”  
• A concentric dashed‐and‐dot circle lies at a radial distance of d_v/2 around it. A radial dimension arrow between the two circles is labeled d_v/2.  
• Under this subfigure is the associated perimeter formula, shown in the form “u = (s + d_v)·π,” reflecting that the diameter of the control circle is the column diameter plus d_v.  

Caption and styling  
• Below both sketches is the figure title: “Figure 2.24: Control perimeter u.”  
• Linework is clean and schematic; all arrows are thin, with arrowheads at both ends and labels in plain text.  
• The hatched fill of the column cores contrasts with the white background and the dashed control perimeters, making the distinction between the column outline and the control loop immediately clear.

The image is a plan-view sketch (Figure 2.25) illustrating how the “reduced” punching‐shear control perimeter u* is formed around a square column in a slab when that basic perimeter would otherwise exceed the maximum allowed by the code.  At the center of the drawing you see the column cross-section represented by a thick‐lined square.  Around that square is a shaded, cross-shaped band: this grey region is the locus of points at which the shear-control perimeter is taken once the standard (full) control perimeter has been truncated because it would be larger than 12·d (where d is the slab effective depth).

Key graphical details:

 • Column: a solid‐line square in the center.  
 • Reduced perimeter u*: shown in grey, forming four “arms” that extend out from the midpoints of each face of the column.  At each arm the outline is straight for a distance of 1.5·dv from the face, then curves gently back in toward the adjacent arm, intersecting at a point that lies dv/2 from the face in the orthogonal direction.  The result is an inward‐curving, rounded‐corner cross.  
 • Dimension callouts:  
    – On the left side of the column, a leader line points to the shallow recess in the grey band and is labeled “dv/2.”  
    – On the top and right sides, leader lines mark the length of each protruding arm and are labeled “1.5·dv.”  (The same 1.5·dv dimension appears at both the top and the right outer edge of the shaded band.)  
 • Dashed outline (light dashed square around the shaded region): indicates the original basic control perimeter that, if unmodified, would lie at a uniform distance d from the column faces.  Because that basic line lies further than the code allows (exceeding 12·d), the algorithm instead adopts the inner, reduced shape shown in grey.  

Caption (underneath):  
Figure 2.25: Reduced control perimeter u*  

Contextual interpretation with respect to punching‐shear design:

According to SIA 262:2013 (and similarly in many national adaptations of EC 2), when a column is situated well inside a large slab, the full control perimeter (a closed loop located at a distance d from the column face) may exceed the limit (typically 12·d).  In such cases the code permits—or requires—use of a reduced perimeter l₁,red.  This sketch shows exactly how that reduction is carried out for a square column:

1. From the midpoint of each column face you move outward a distance of 1.5·d (dv in the figure), instead of the full 3·d that a uniform loop would require.  
2. From each arm’s tip you draw a smooth, curved transition back into the orthogonal arm at the point which lies d/2 from the adjacent face.  
3. The resulting shape (the grey cross) encloses exactly the portion of slab where the punching shear capacity must be checked without exceeding the permitted loop length.

By using this reduced control perimeter u*, the punching‐shear check remains conservative (smaller u* gives smaller VRd,c, making design safer) but avoids an unbounded increase in perimeter length in very large slabs.

The illustration titled “Figure 2.26: Reduced control perimeter u” consists of two half‐plan views of a slab–column intersection, showing how the critical punching shear perimeter is “cut off” when the supporting column lies near an edge or in a corner of the slab. In both sketches the column is rendered as a solid grey rectangle; the surrounding slab is white, and the critical perimeter is traced in a heavier continuous black line. Dimension lines in light grey indicate how far the perimeter extends from the face of the column: 1.5 · d_v in every direction that is not already bounded by a free slab edge.

Left Sketch (Column Flush with One Edge)  
• Column geometry: a rectangular column of width b, its near face coincident with the slab’s top edge (the free boundary).  
• Control perimeter: begins 1.5 · d_v inside the slab from the free edge, runs parallel to that edge for a length equal to the column width b, then turns around two semicircular ends of radius d_v/2 and returns along a second straight segment also at 1.5 · d_v from the free edge.  
• Dimension callouts: two opposing short dimension bars labelled “1.5 · d_v” mark the offset from the free edge to the control line; a vertical callout labelled b marks the column width; a further note “1.5 · d_v” appears on the opposite (inner) side.  
• Formula beneath the sketch:  
   u = 2 · 1.5 · d_v + b + (d_v / 2) · π  
  This sums the two straight runs (each 1.5 d_v), the column width b, and the combined length of two half‐circles (i.e. one full circle of radius d_v/2).

Right Sketch (Column in a Corner)  
• Column geometry: same grey rectangle, now snug into two orthogonal free edges of the slab (top and right edges).  
• Control perimeter: truncated on both adjacent slab edges so that it begins 1.5 · d_v from each free boundary in two directions, runs parallel to each column face, and closes with a single semicircular arc of radius d_v/2 connecting the two offset lines.  
• Dimension callouts: two dimension bars on each side are labelled “1.5 · d_v,” marking the horizontal and vertical offsets from the slab edges.  
• Formula beneath the sketch:  
   u = 2 · 1.5 · d_v + 2 · 1.5 · d_v + (d_v / 2) · π  
  Here the sum comprises four straight segments (two on each face, each of length 1.5 d_v) plus the semicircular connector.

Key points illustrated:  
- When the column is away from edges, the standard control perimeter at a distance 1.5 · d_v all around is continuous.  
- When a free edge or corner truncates the slab, the control perimeter is reduced by omitting those portions that would lie outside the slab.  
- In practical punching‐shear design (per EC2, SIA 262:2013, etc.), this reduced perimeter u replaces the full‐enclosure perimeter to compute VRd,c.  
- The radius d_v/2 corresponds to the effective slab depth or lever arm used in punching shear checks, and π · (d_v/2) accounts for the curved segment.  
- This figure supports the algorithm by which software (e.g. BEMESS) automatically trims the basic punching perimeter whenever columns lie near edges or openings, thereby reflecting the lower available shear path.

Punching design is done with the critical perimeter at 2.0*d. An additional check at the column face is added depending on the country code.
 - Minimum value for vrdc according to 6.4.4(1) (6.47) for punching
 In punching design the effective steel stress value fyd_ef is taken into account.
 - According to 6.4.5(3) (6.53) a maximum punching resistance is taken into account.

The image presents a schematic 3-D view of a rectangular solid (likely representing a structural element or plate) whose top surface is subdivided into a uniform square grid of blue lines. Centered on that gridded face is a stress‐rosette or “point” where multiple directional probes are illustrated to explain how surface stresses are sampled at incremental angles. Below is a breakdown of the key visual elements and how they relate to the accompanying text on stress-range determinations:  

1. Global Geometry and Grid  
   • A block drawn in isometric perspective, with three visible faces (top, front, right).  
   • The top face carries a blue grid (five columns by five rows of equal squares), suggesting finite‐element or measurement nodes where stress data could be mapped and contoured (e.g. isolines of stress).  

2. Stress-Probe Rosette at a Single Grid Cell  
   • At the approximate center of the grid, four green arrows radiate outward. Each arrow is labeled 1, 2, 3 or 4 in black numerals. They represent four distinct probe directions where normal stress is evaluated.  
   • A red curved arrow around the rosette indicates that this set of directions is rotated incrementally (in this illustration perhaps by 3° or another small angle) to sweep through a full 360° measurement. This embodies the Capra‐Maury or rosette technique described in the text, which samples stress every few degrees to find maximum stress range on the surface.  

3. Labeling and Directional Context  
   • Arrow 1 points roughly toward the upper-left corner of the top surface, arrow 2 toward the top edge, arrow 3 toward the right edge, and arrow 4 toward the lower-right corner.  
   • The sequence 1→2→3→4 implies successive stress gauges oriented at angular offsets (often 0°, 45°, 90° and 135°, though here the exact values are schematic).  
   • The red rotation arrow shows how, for each grid node, the entire four-probe rosette is rotated in small increments (every 3° if following the text) to capture the extreme tensile or compressive stress across all possible directions.  

4. Relation to BEMESS/WINGRAF Workflow  
   • The underlying grid hints at where BEMESS computes stresses per element for each load case or superposed load.  
   • After isolating “permanent” or envelope stresses (via CTRL STRE in BEMESS), the extreme values get plotted in WinGRAF—either as isolines on this grid or as cut plots.  
   • The rosette technique then identifies the maximum stress range at each node and records the associated angle, just as the image’s rotating arrow suggests.  

5. Key Take-Away from the Visualization  
   • This drawing clarifies how normal stress directions are systematically sampled over the full 360° by rotating a multi-gauge rosette.  
   • By stepping the probe every 3° (per Capra-Maury), the software can pinpoint the worst-case orientation and magnitude of stress range, which is essential for fatigue and strength assessments.  
   • The final output (in WinGRAF) will typically show, for each grid node, the maximum positive and negative normal stresses, the range between them, and the angle at which they occur—information that underpins envelope plots and isoline maps of critical stresses.
