The table defines a set of input “records” for a SOFiSTiK FEA/structural‐design file.  Each record has a unique keyword (CTRL, CRAC, MREI, … DIRE) and an associated list of permissible items (parameters) that control various aspects of the analysis or design.  Below is a structured description of its contents and its intended use in a RAG‐vector‐store context:

1. Overall Structure and Context  
   • Records may appear in any order, except that an END record must always conclude the file.  
   • Standard records—HEAD, END, PAGE—are covered in the SOFiSTiK general manual; they do not appear here.  
   • Default values apply automatically for any item not explicitly supplied.  
   • ELEM or NODE records (not shown) trigger design computations using the last‐defined parameters.  
     – Any subsequent GEO, DIRE or THRE record applies to the next ELEM/NODE block.  

2. Record Summaries  
   2.1 CTRL  (Control parameters)  
     • Governs global solution and output controls  
     • Key items include:  
       – TYPE  (analysis type)  
       – RMOD  (reinforcement model)  
       – SYST  (coordinate system)  
       – WALL, AUGM, THIC  (wall and augmentation settings)  
       – TENS, WARN, RADP, BUBB  (tension checks, warnings, crack‐width defaults)  
       – LCR/LCRI, VF70, SNIP, WINT/WEND  (crack‐width extraction and integration)  
       – PFAI, RO_V, COTT, FACH, REDN, REDM, VPDC, SIGZ, LCRP, WTEN  (miscellaneous control flags)  

   2.2 CRAC  (Crack‐width parameters)  
     • Defines cracking behavior when RMOD indicates cracked analysis  
     • Items include:  
       – MUEZ (fracture‐parameter exponent)  
       – XMIN, DDES, STAN (limit, detailing and standard crack specs)  
       – WK/WKB (characteristic crack‐widths)  
       – BETA, BET1, BET2 (shape‐factor coefficients)  
       – K1, DDEB (stress‐distribution modifiers)  
       – BOND (bond‐slip control)  

   2.3 MREI  (Reinforcement‐interaction)  
     • Governs interaction between steel and concrete  
     • Items: FFCT, KC, K, ROBU, PARA  

   2.4 SHFT  (Shifting)  
     • Single item: TYPE  (defines element‐shift scheme)  

   2.5 NSTR  (Nonlinear‐stress record)  
     • For defining multi‐linear stress–strain charts or limit states  
     • Items include: SIGS, SIGT (tensile/compressive strengths);  
       CHKC/CHKR (check flags), FATC (fatigue control);  
       LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, LS_P (limit‐state factors upper/lower);  
       FACU, FACL, FACV, FACP (reduction factors); SIGP (peak stress);  
       LOCP (location parameter)  

   2.6 MAT  (Material properties)  
     • Defines concrete and steel characteristics  
     • Concrete items: CONC, MINC, N, BETZ  
     • Steel items: STEE, FC, FY, MSTA  
     • Other: K (stiffness exponent), AM3 (multiaxial factor), TU0 (initial temperature),  
       T011, T02, T03 (temperature coefficients), TUGR, TRD (time‐dependent creep parameters),  
       SC1/SC2, SS1/SS2 (shrinkage/creep curves)  

   2.7 GEOM  (Geometry modifiers)  
     • Alters section geometry for design checks  
     • Items: H, HA, DHA, HB, DHB (flange/web depths); DDHA, DDHB (effective depths); HPRE (prestress depth)  

   2.8 DIRE  (Reinforcement orientation)  
     • Specifies reinforcement or principal stress directions  
     • Items: UPP, LOW (upper/lower layer control); TYPE (orientation type); X, Y, Z (direction cosines)  

3. Usage Notes for RAG‐Vector Store  
   • Each record/item pair forms a searchable metadata key.  
   • Arbitrary ordering means the vector store must index records independently of sequence.  
   • Default‐value logic: if an item is missing in the file, assume its built‐in default when querying.  
   • Downstream queries can look for specific records (e.g. “CRAC”) or items (e.g. “wk” or “CONC”) to retrieve design settings or to cluster similar designs.  

This description allows a RAG‐enabled application to understand the schema (records ↔ items) and to map natural‐language queries (“show me all concrete strength definitions” → MAT: CONC, MINC, etc.) into the correct vector‐indexed fields.

The table in question serves as the master definition of all “input records” that the SOFiSTiK RAG‐vector‐store parser will recognize.  Although we only see the first few entries here, its overall structure and logical conventions can be described in detail:

1.  Overall Layout  
    •  The table is arranged in rows, one per record‐type, and (typically) five to seven columns.  Common column headings are:  
       – Record identifier (e.g. “ECHO”, “OPT”, “VAL”)  
       – Field positions or format (e.g. character columns or Fortran‐style I/F descriptors)  
       – Data type or unit (integer, real, text, “–” when not applicable)  
       – Default value (if omitted by the user)  
       – Semantic comment or “remarks” explaining precisely what the record does  
    •  A footnote (“Table continued on next page”) indicates that there are more records defined beyond the excerpt shown.

2.  Key Records Defined in the Excerpt  
    •  ECHO  
       – Controls whether the input lines are echoed back in the listing or log file.  
       – Typical format: one integer flag (0 = off, 1 = on).  
       – Default: usually “1” (echo enabled).  
    •  OPT  
       – A multi‐flag record that turns on/off various solver or print options.  
       – May accept a bit‐mask or a series of single‐letter codes.  
       – Defaults to a safe set of options enabling basic convergence and warnings.  
    •  VAL  
       – Defines numerical values or “design parameters” that can later be referenced by ELEM or NODE.  
       – Format: parameter name (4-character text), real value.  
       – If omitted, a zero or another built-in default is assumed.  

3.  Sequencing Rules  
    •  The input records may appear in any order—there is no strict requirement that you must define ECHO before OPT, for example.  
    •  Exception: the END record must always be the very last line of the input deck.  This tells the parser “stop reading.”  
    •  HEAD and PAGE are special control records described elsewhere in the SOFiSTiK “FEA/STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics” manual.  

4.  Dependencies Between Records  
    •  Whenever an ELEM or NODE record is encountered, the software immediately “freezes” the current set of parameters (from all prior ECHO/OPT/VAL records) and uses them for that element or node.  
    •  Any GEO, DIRE or THRE record placed immediately after ELEM or NODE serves only to modify the *next* design entry.  In other words, GEO/DIRE/THRE do *not* apply retroactively.  

5.  Default‐Value Behavior  
    •  The documentation notes that “A reasonable analysis is possible even without data.”  
    •  If any parameter is never explicitly set, its default in‐software value will be used.  This ensures—especially in early modeling stages—that the parser will not fail outright.  

6.  Cross‐References  
    •  More exhaustive definitions of HEAD, PAGE, END (and any global setting records) live in the SOFiSTiK general manual.  
    •  The table here is a concise summary of those records that most directly influence “design‐type” input (elements, nodes, geometry flags, thresholds, etc.).  

In practice, you would scroll or click to the “next page” to see the remaining records (GEO, DIRE, THRE, ELEM, NODE and so on), each laid out in the same columnar format.  Taken together, this tabular definition is the backbone of any RAG vector‐store ingestion: it tells parsers exactly how to tokenize, interpret, default, and sequence each kind of line in a structural‐analysis input deck.

   • Parameterization record for detailed element or node-based design settings.
   • Items include:
     NOG, NOEL, DU, DU2, DU3, DL, DL2, DL3

     BSU, BSU2, BSU3, BSL, BSL2, BSL3  
     TYPE  
   • These cover degrees of freedom upper/lower adjustments, shear parameters, axial/sliding stiffnesses, buckling soils, and a TYPE flag.

5. PUNC
   • Punctual or point-based load record.

   • Load Case record.
   • Items: NO, PERC, FACT

7. GRP
   • Load Group record—bundles multiple load cases or load case sequences.
   • Items: NO, ENVA, ENVB, WKU, WKL, SIGU, SIGL

   • Element-based design invocation.

   • Node-based design invocation.

The source “NORM” table is a master‐lookup for structural design codes and their country-specific variants. It serves two main purposes: (1) define which international or national standard is in force and (2) provide the metadata needed by SOFiSTiK (via INI‐files) to pick default material properties, safety factors, combination rules, units, etc. The table can be thought of as having three logical sections:

1. Global Definition Fields  
   • NORM (record name)  
   • DC (Design code family): abbreviated code (EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, etc.)  
   • NDC (Designation): specific standard edition (e.g. EN1992-1-1, DIN 1052-1988, OEN B 4300)  
   • COUN (Country code): when an EN‐family code has national annexes or boxed values (e.g. “HK/852” for Hong Kong, “00” for General EN)  
   • UNIT: choice of unit set for global input/output (only active in AQUA/TEMPLATE modules)  
   • d_LANG, PAGE: auxiliary formatting (not central to design selection)  
   • LON, LAT, G: optional local geographic parameters (longitude, latitude, gravity acceleration) – used by modules that account for altitude, wind, snow or seismic loads  

   Notes on Usage:  
   – Defaults for materials, combination rules and load cases are pulled from “DC_NDC.INI.” Changing NORM after defining actions or loads is discouraged.  
   – National variants (boxed values) may be overridden via TVAR records.  
   – If a code allows classification or safety class (CAT), those options appear in its INI‐file.  

2. Per‐Standard Entries  
   Each row in this section enumerates one available standard. Key columns are:  
   • COUN: country or region code (e.g. US, SP, IS, UNE, NZS)  
   • CAT: category or safety class (when required by the code) – e.g.  
     – For Sweden (SS EN1992-1-1/EKS 12:2022): CAT A1, A2, A3 for building safety classes  
     – For Denmark (DS EN-series): CAT LE/NE/HE/LN/NN/HN/etc. denoting “Low/Normal/High safety” × “Extended/Normal/Reduced control”  
     – For bridges: specialized CAT codes such as B1-B4 for road bridges, C1-C4 for footbridges, D1-D4 for rail bridges  
   • Description: full name of the code (e.g. “Design of concrete structures SS EN 1992-1-1/EKS 12:2022”)  
   • UNIT: rarely populated in this extract, but where present it forces units for that code  
   • Design: numeric or letter flag indicating which modules implement it (e.g. “5 A,B” means implemented in both AQB and BEMESS modules)  

   Example snippet:  
     – DIN 1052-1988 “Holzbau (Timber design)” → Category A only, implemented in AQB  
     – OENORM B 4750 (2000) “Spannbeton” → steel‐prestressed concrete, no category  
     – US AASHTO-2014 → maps to US ACI 318-14 for bending, shear, punching, crack controls  

3. Concrete‐Design Feature Table  
   At the end is a small cross‐reference of which concrete checks are supported under AASHTO editions (2004, 2010, 2014, 2020), all of which map to ACI 318-14. The supported checks (column “where”) are:  
   • DESI: bending and shear design  
   • PUNC: punching‐shear check  
   • CSIG: crack‐width via permissible stress method  
   • CT: crack‐width via table lookup  
   • CW: crack‐width via calculation  

Overall, this table drives which design code configuration (.INI file) SOFiSTiK loads, what national parameters apply, which safety classes or categories the user may choose, and which modules (AQB, BEMESS) actually implement the chosen code’s provisions.

The table shown is the “general parameters” section of the NORM record in SOFiSTiK’s input format. It defines a small number of global settings that must be specified at the very start of a project—before any load cases, materials or design checks are defined—because many downstream defaults (materials, load combinations, safety factors, national variants, etc.) are derived from them. Any change of these values after the fact can lead to inconsistencies and is therefore discouraged.

1. Columns  
   • Item – The keyword used in the input deck.  
   • Description – A brief English label describing the purpose of the parameter.  
   • Unit – The physical unit or data type expected. In many cases “Lit4” indicates a code‐defined category or class (i.e. one of a small predefined list). A dash (—) means “no physical unit” or “free text/choice.”  
   • Default – The built-in default value if the user does not explicitly override it. An asterisk (*) signifies “use whatever default the matching INI file provides for this design code and country variant.”

2. Rows  
   1. ALT: Altitude above sea level  
      – Unit: m  
      – Default: 0.0  
      – Notes: The user may override the default gravity/self‐weight factor G by assigning a true local elevation here. Altitude can affect snow combination factors in some codes.  
   2. WIND: Wind zone  
      – Unit: Lit4  
      – Default: *  
      – Notes: Refers to a code‐specific wind region (e.g. Exposure Zones in Eurocode). The actual numeric values or labels are defined in the NORM INI‐file or national annex.  
   3. SNOW: Snow zone  
      – Unit: Lit4  
      – Default: *  
      – Notes: Snow load region selection, again driven by boxed values in the INI‐file for the chosen standard.  
   4. SEIS: Seismic zone  
      – Unit: Lit4  
      – Default: *  
      – Notes: Seismic design category or zone, where supported by the selected design code.  
   5. WCAT: Terrain category for wind  
      – Unit: Lit4  
      – Default: *  
      – Notes: Roughness/obstacle class for wind calculations (e.g. open terrain, suburban, city).  
   6. UNIT: Selection of a set of units  
      – Unit: —  
      – Default: *  
      – Notes: Controls the global unit system (e.g. SI, US‐inch, kips). Only valid in AQUA or TEMPLATE modules; influences both input parsing and output formatting.  
   7. LANG: Selection of an output language default  
      – Unit: —  
      – Default: *  
      – Notes: Chooses the default language (e.g. EN, DE) for printed reports and screen messages. Also only active in AQUA or TEMPLATE.

3. Usage and Context  
   • As soon as you specify NORM with these items, the software reads the corresponding INI file—named DC_NDC.INI (where DC is the design code and NDC may be a country code)—to load all code‐specific parameters, safety factors, material defaults and combination rules.  
   • The asterisk (*) default means “take the code’s built-in value.” If you truly want to force “no wind checking,” for instance, you could enter WIND=NONE.  
   • Any subsequent change of these parameters after defining load cases or materials risks violating the built-in code assumptions—SOFiSTiK warns against this practice.  
   • For “legacy” or historic codes without INI files, some parameters still work in a semi‐automatic way, but you may need to define boxed values manually via TVAR records.

In short, this table is the very first “project‐wide settings” block. It ensures that site‐specific environmental loads and user‐preferences for units/language are all captured in one place and that downstream modules can reliably derive their own defaults from this information.

The source table is a master list of all “NORM” (design‐code) records that SOFiSTiK supports.  Each row defines one design code (or family of codes) together with the ways the software will:

• pick default material and load parameters  
• interpret country‐specific “boxed values”  
• choose units and design modules (AQB, BEMESS, etc.)  

Structure of the table:  
– First column: NORM code identifier (e.g. “EN 199X-200X”, “EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE”, “DS EN 199X-200X”, “US AASHTO-2014”, “CSA S6-19”, etc.)  
– Second column (“Description”): Full name and scope of the code, sub‐parts included (concrete, steel, composite, timber, brickwork, aluminium), references to EN 1990, EN 1991-1-x, national annexes, and—where applicable—country codes (COUN) or categories (CAT).  
– Third column (“UNIT”): Index of the unit‐system default (almost always “5”, representing SI units).  
– Fourth column (“Design”): Letter codes A and/or B showing which design module(s) implement that code (A = AQB, B = BEMESS).

Key fields and parameters (to be specified when first setting up a project):  
– DC (Design code family): EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, BS, IS, US, CSA, NF, SS, DS, NEN, NBN, NBR, ZA, NZS, etc.  
– NDC (specific design‐code variant, e.g. “1992-1-1”, “1993-1-1”) and optional boxed country code (COUN, e.g. “IL/972” for Israel train loads, “HK/852” for Hong Kong deviations).  
– CAT (category or class): a short code that further refines the standard (e.g. bridge type, safety & control class).  The available CAT values (–, A, B, …, D1–D4, LE/NE/HE, etc.) come from the matching INI-file.  
– Geographic parameters: LON (longitude, default 0°), LAT (latitude, default 45°), ALT (altitude, default not shown), gravity G (m/s², default local code value).  These feed wind, snow, earthquake, self‐weight, and combination‐coefficient calculations in later modules.

High‐level blocks in the table:

1. EN Eurocodes – Building (EN 199X-200X)  
   • EN 1992-1-1 (concrete), EN 1993-1-1 (steel), EN 1994-1-1 (composite)  
   • Actions & combinations per EN 1990, EN 1991-1-x  
   • Materials per EN 1995-1-1 (timber), EN 1996-1-1 (brick), EN 1999-1-1 (aluminium)  
   • COUN = IL/972 for train loads in Israel  
   • UNIT 5, Design A & B

2. EN Eurocodes – Bridges (EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE)  
   • EN 1992-2 (concrete), EN 1993-2 (steel), EN 1994-2 (composite)  
   • Actions & loads per EN 1990, EN 1991-2  
   • Materials per EN 1995-2, EN 1996-1-1, EN 1999-1-1  
   • CAT B/C/D for road, foot, rail bridges  
   • UNIT 5, Design A & B

3. Other European National Annex codes:  
   – SS (Sweden), DS (Denmark), NS (Norway), SFS (Finland), NEN/NBN (Netherlands/Belgium)  
   – Each has CAT values for safety & control levels (LE, NE, HE, LN, NN (default), HN, LR, NR, HR) or bridge‐type safety classes (B1–B4, C1–C4, D1–D4).  
   – Actions & combinations via DS EN 1990/NA, DS EN 1991-1-x/NA, materials per DS EN 1995-1-1, DS EN 1996-1-1, DS EN 1999-1-1

4. Other international codes:

   – UNIT always “5”, Design mostly A only

5. NZS (New Zealand)

6. US AASHTO → US ACI 318-14 mapping

   – Implemented features for concrete design:

If you redefine NORM after actions/load cases exist (or by editing INI files), you may violate SOFiSTiK’s expected workflow—always choose code, country, CAT, geographic settings up front.  The matching INI file is named DC_NDC.INI and supplies all defaults and allowable boxed values.

Below is a high‐level, field‐by‐field description of the “Design Code” table as it is used in SOFiSTiK (for RAG‐style indexing or vector storage). The table drives all automatic defaults for materials, load combinations and design routines via matching INI‐files. It is assumed the reader is familiar with the basic project setup in SOFiSTiK (records NORM, CAT, UNIT, etc.).  

1. Table Purpose and Scope  
   – Enumerates every supported structural design code (concrete, steel, composite, timber, etc.).  
   – Each row maps one “NORM + NDC” pair to:  
     • A detailed textual description of which parts and national annexes are covered.  
     • A default unit‐system index.  
     • The design modules in which it is implemented (AQB, BEMESS).  
   – Some rows also supply a CAT enumeration (building class, safety class or bridge class).  

2. Key Columns  
   1. NORM  
      • The code family identifier (e.g. “DIN”, “US”, “SS”, “DS”, “NZS”).  
      • Matches the first part of the INI‐file name.  
   2. NDC (Designation)  
      • A more specific label, typically an umbrella name for multiple parts:  
        – e.g. “DIN EN199X‐200X” for general building codes,  
        – “DIN EN199X‐200X-BRIDGE” for bridge annexes.  
      • Forms the suffix of the INI‐file:  DC_NDC.INI.  
   3. Description  
      • Multi‐line text describing exactly which Eurocode (or other codes) parts and National Annexes are included.  
      • Lists each standard part in chronological or numerical order, for example:  
         – “DIN EN 1992-1-1/NA:2013 Stahlbetontragwerke”  
         – “DIN EN 1993-1-1/NA:2018 Stahlbauten”  
         – “DIN EN 1994-1-1/NA:2010 Verbundtragwerke”  
         – Followed by “einschließlich Einwirkungen nach …” and “einschließlich Materialien nach …”  
      • For bridge codes, includes a CAT line such as  
         “CAT B/C/D Straßenbrücken / Fußgängerbrücken / Eisenbahnbrücken mit Einwirkungen und Bemessungswerte für Brücken (boxed values).”  
   4. UNIT  
      • A small integer (0, 5, etc.) selecting the default unit‐system group in the global UNIT record.  
      • Value “5” typically means SI‐units with kN, m, etc.  
   5. Design  
      • One or two letters denoting modules that support this code:  
         – “A” if implemented in the AQB concrete/steel module,  
         – “B” if implemented in BEMESS,  
         – “A,B” if both.  

3. Optional Columns (in some variants)  
   – CAT (Category/Class): if the code requires classification (e.g. safety class, building use, bridge type).  
     • Enumerated values like “A1”, “A2”, “B1”, “C2”, “D3”, etc., each mapped to a textual meaning.  
   – COUN (Country Code): used only for certain codes (e.g. EN1990 variants in Hong Kong “HK/852”, Israeli load trains “IL/972”).  

4. How Defaults Are Resolved  
   – On project start, the user issues a single NORM record with optional COUNTRY code and CAT.  
   – SOFiSTiK loads the corresponding INI‐file: DC_NDC.INI (where DC = NORM, NDC = designation).  
   – That INI file contains all boxed values, material definitions, partial‐factors, combination rules, altitude/wind/snow parameters.  
   – Changing NORM after loads or materials have been input is not recommended. Temporary redefinition is allowed only if load parameters stay constant.  

5. Implementation Notes for RAG Indexing  
   – Treat each row as a “DesignCode” entity with attributes:  
     • code_family (NORM), code_name (NDC), description_text, default_unit, implemented_in (list of modules), optional categories, optional country.  
   – Key terms for embedding: Eurocode part numbers, national annex identifiers, module names (AQB, BEMESS), and CAT enumerations.  
   – Also index cross‐references to other code families (e.g. US AASHTO → US ACI 318).  

This structured overview captures every column’s semantics, example values, and the loading logic via INI files, providing a compact yet comprehensive specification suitable for downstream retrieval‐augmented generation.

The input “NORM” table is the master‐record by which SOFiSTiK selects default materials, superposition rules, load combinations and design rules.  It is intended to be provided at the very start of any project; redefining it later (or hacking the INI files) is strongly discouraged.  Below is a structured overview of its content, columns and the kinds of rows it contains.

1. Columns / Items  
• DC  
  – Design code family (e.g. EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, BS, IS, US, CSA, GB, NF, UNI, UNE, SS, DS, NS, SP, NZS, SFS, NEN, NBN, NBR, ZA).  
• NDC  
  – The exact designation of the code within that family (e.g. EN 1992-1-1, DIN 1052-1988, OENORM B 4750).  
• COUN  
  – Optional country code; used to pick national “boxed values” or annex variations (e.g. HK/852 for Hong Kong, IL/972 for Israel).  
• CAT  
  – Category or class within that code (e.g. A/B/C/D, safety‐classes, bridge classes).  The valid entries come from the matching INI file.  
• LON, LAT  
  – Geographical longitude/latitude in degrees; some codes adjust wind, snow or seismic coefficients with location.  
• G  
  – Gravity acceleration (m/sec²); normally taken from the code unless a true local value is required.  
• UNIT, LANG, PAGE  
  – (Processed only in AQUA / TEMPLATE) allow global unit sets, language files or page setups.  

2. How Defaults Are Loaded  
• Each combination DC + NDC + (COUN) yields an INI file named “DC_NDC.INI”  
• This INI contains all default material properties, load factors, partial safety factors, combination rules, national variations, etc.  
• If a code has no INI file (typically older or very new standards), AQB/BEMESS modules may still implement it in program code; in such cases materials are referred to generically (e.g. BOE = concrete, BSOE = steel).  
• Categories (CAT) must be chosen where the code allows/disallows them.  Historic or custom codes can use “USER” to define a free‐text category.

3. Representative Rows (Illustrative, not exhaustive)  
• DIN FB102-2009  
  – Code: DIN  
  – NDC: FB102-2009 (Fachbericht 102)  
  – UNIT: Design  
  – CAT: 0, A, B  
• DIN 1052-1988 (Holzbau)  
  – Steel & timber design per 1988 edition.  
• OENORM B 4750 (prestressed concrete) & B 4300 (steel)  
  – Austrian Standards from 1994/2000, CAT = A.  
• US / AASHTO-2004 → US ACI 318-14 (reinforced concrete)  
  – Implemented features:  
    • DESI = bending & shear design  
    • PUNC = punching shear check  
    • CSIG = crack width by permissible stresses  
    • CT = crack width by table values  
    • CW = crack width by calculation  
• CSA S6-19 (Canadian Highway Bridge)  
• SP (Russian), IS (Indian), UNE (Spanish) instructions  
• SS (Sweden)  
  – Building annex (BFS 2022:4 EKS 12) & Bridge annex (TSFS 2018:57)  
  – Categories A1–A3 (buildings), B1–B4 (roads), C1–C4 (footbridges), D1–D4 (railways).  
• DS (Denmark) EN-NA series  
  – Categories reflecting safety vs. control level: LE, NE, HE, LN, NN (default), HN, LR, NR, HR.  
• NZS (New Zealand)  
  – CAT A for buildings; CAT 0 for “no prestress.”

4. Key Usage Notes  
• Changing NORM mid‐project invalidates many downstream defaults—avoid doing so.  
• If you truly need a local gravity or altitude effect, override G or LAT explicitly.  
• All code‐specific parameters (boxed values, partial factors, combination rules) live in the matched INI file.  Consult that file to see possible CAT values, default units, material suites, etc.  
• When a code includes multiple modules (concrete, steel, composite, timber, masonry, aluminium), each is listed as a separate NDC with the same COUN/CAT scheme.

The input “NORM” table is the master registry of all structural‐design codes, national variants and configuration options supported by the software.  It is used to set up defaults for materials, load combinations, units, language and environmental parameters based on a chosen design code and (optionally) a country code.  A brief breakdown follows:

1.  Core Fields  
   •  NORM / Item:  Identifier of the record (always “NORM”).  
   •  DC:  Design-code family, e.g. “EN”, “DIN”, “US”, “NZS”.  
   •  NDC:  Specific designation or version of that code family, e.g. “1992-1-1”, “1052-1988”.  
   •  COUN:  Country code for any boxed (national) values within Eurocodes or other codes, e.g. “HK/852” for Hong Kong, “IL/972” for Israel.  

2.  Configuration Keys  
   •  CAT:  A category or class selector required by some codes (e.g. safety class, usage class).  Its allowable values and their meaning are defined in the matching INI file.  
   •  LON / LAT:  Geographical longitude and latitude (in degrees).  Some codes adjust wind, snow or seismic loads by location.  
   •  ALT:  Altitude (not shown in snippet but supported).  
   •  G:  Local gravity acceleration (m/s²).  By default the code’s value is used; only override if precise local g is needed.  
   •  UNIT:  Global unit system (e.g. metric, imperial).  Affects input and output across modules.  
   •  LANG:  Language selection for menus and reports (processed by AQUA/TEMPLATE modules).  

3.  INI-File Mechanism  
   •  For each combination of DC + NDC + COUN, an INI file named “DC_NDC.INI” is loaded to supply default parameters – material properties, combination factors, national annex values.  
   •  Eurocode families (EN 1990–1999) and many other standards ship with these INI files.  If you redefine the design code after you’ve already created actions or load cases, you risk inconsistency; redefine NORM only when actions remain unchanged.  
   •  Boxed (national) values from the country code can also be manually tweaked at run time via record TVAR.

The input table is part of the SOFiSTiK “NORM” record system, which defines the design‐code environment for subsequent actions, load cases and material definitions.  Each row in the table corresponds to one design standard (or family of standards) and carries a small set of fields that the various SOFiSTiK modules use to pick up default parameters, national annex values and program‐specific code fragments.  A retrieval or RAG system should index each row by its code name and capture the following key pieces of information:

1.  Code Identifier  
    •  The short name used in input (first column). Examples:  
       –  “OEN EN199X-200X”  
       –  “OEN EN199X-200X-BRIDGE”  
       –  “OEN 4700”  
    •  This identifier is also the stem of the INI‐file that holds the defaults (e.g. OEN_EN199X-200X.INI).

2.  Description  
    •  Multi‐line text listing all parts of the standard family and national annex where applicable.  
    •  For building codes it enumerates concrete (EN 1992-1-1), steel (EN 1993-1-1), composite (EN 1994-1-1), actions (EN 1990, EN 1991-1-x) and material parts (timber EN 1995-1-1, masonry EN 1996-1-1, aluminium EN 1999-1-1).  
    •  For bridge codes it similarly lists EN 1992-2, EN 1993-2, EN 1994-2, the relevant EN 1990/EN 1991 parts and material standards.  
    •  Some descriptions include an inline CAT specification to subdivide by bridge type and safety class (e.g. “CAT B/C/D Straßenbrücken / Fußgängerbrücken / Eisenbahnbrücken mit Einwirkungen und Bemessungswerte für Brücken (boxed values)”).

3.  UNIT  
    •  A small integer code (column “UNIT”) that tells SOFiSTiK which global set of units to apply for input and output.  
    •  The actual unit definitions are in the matching INI-files.

4.  Design Flags  
    •  One or two letters (column “Design”) indicating where the code is implemented:  
       –  “A” means supported in the AQB (concrete design) module.  
       –  “B” means supported in the BEMESS (steel/composite design) module.  
       –  “A,B” means both.  
    •  In some cases additional letters (e.g. “C”, “D”) mark sub-modules or program variants.

Contextual fields that live outside the snippet but belong to the same record include:  
–   NORM: the main record type (“NORM”) that activates design code selection.  
–   DC: the code family (EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, etc.).  
–   NDC: the designation or version (e.g. “EN1992-1-1:2011”).  
–   COUN: country code for national variants (e.g. “HK/852”).  
–   CAT: category or class where codes differ by usage (buildings vs. bridges, safety classes, inspection levels).  
–   LON, LAT, altitude (Lt4) and gravity (“G”) to trigger location-specific defaults in snow/wind/earthquake provisions.  

Because SOFiSTiK relies heavily on INI-files derived from NORM + DC + NDC (named DC_NDC.INI), any post-definition change of NORM or NDC can invalidate material and action defaults.  The table thus forms the backbone for automatically populating design parameters, national annex values (“boxed values”) and selecting the right subset of code clauses in each analysis or design module.

The snippet you’ve provided is one row from SOFiSTiK’s NORM‐record lookup table—specifically the entry for the Swiss Standards family “SIA 26X.” This table drives the automatic defaulting of material, action and combination parameters whenever you select a design code in an INI file or via the NORM command. Below is a breakdown of each column and the meaning of all fields in that one row:

1. Row key (leftmost column, often hidden)  
   • “SIA 26X”  
     – This is the design‐code family identifier (DC + NDC). In SOFiSTiK parlance, “SIA” is the Swiss design‐code family (DC), and “26X” is the specific variant (NDC), covering all SIA standards in the 200–299 range.  

2. Description (second column)  
   • Title line: “Schweizer Normen” (literally “Swiss Standards”)  
   • Constituent standards included under SIA 26X:  
     – SIA 262 “Betonbauten (2013)” – Concrete structures standard (2013 edition)  
     – SIA 263 “Stahlbau (2013)” – Steel structures standard (2013 edition)  
     – SIA 264 “Stahl-Beton-Verbundbau” – Composite steel-concrete design standard  
   • Related action and combination rules (all part of SIA 26X):  
     – “einschließlich Einwirkungen, Kombinationen nach:”  
       • SIA 260 “Grundlagen der Projektierung” – Basics of structural design, including actions and load combination rules  
       • SIA 261 “Einwirkungen auf Tragwerke” – Actions on structures (wind, snow, seismic, etc.)  
   • Related material specifications:  
     – “einschließlich Materialien nach:”  
       • SIA 265 “Holzbau mit Serviceklassen 1, 2, 3” – Timber design standard with service classes, user must specify the exact class in the material definition  

3. UNIT (third column)  
   • “0”  
     – This numeric code picks the default set of unit definitions (length, force, stress‐units, etc.) for all modules. The actual mapping “0 → some unit system” is defined in the matching INI-file (DC_NDC.INI). If you override UNIT via the UNIT record in AQUA or TEMPLATE, you force a different global unit set.  

4. Design (fourth column)  
   • “A,B”  
     – These are the allowed category codes (CAT) for this design code.  
     – CAT A and CAT B cover different “safety classes” or “levels of combination rigor.” For many Swiss projects, you would choose A (normal building design) or B (special loading or higher safety requirements). The actual meaning (e.g. which partial factors differ) comes from the INI file for SIA 26X and must be cross‐checked with the SIA non-ANSI annex.  

How it fits into the bigger picture:  
• When you start a new model and enter  
   NORM DC=SIA NDC=26X CAT=A UNIT=0  
  the software reads “SIA_26X.INI,” loads all the default material strengths, partial factors, snow/wind parameters, load combinations (from SIA 260/261), and service‐class rules for timber (SIA 265).  
• If you later change NORM or reassign CAT, you must ensure no existing load cases or materials get invalidated; SOFiSTiK strongly discourages redesign code changes once you’ve defined materials or actions.  
• If you need a custom CAT—for instance a historic Swiss code not shipped in the standard INI—you can still use CAT=USER and then set up your special rules manually (via TVAR records or by editing the INI).  

In summary, this table row tells SOFiSTiK exactly which Swiss SIA sub‐standards to activate under the umbrella “SIA 26X,” what unit system to apply by default, and which safety‐class options (A or B) are valid.

The table is a registry of implemented design‐code packages in SOFiSTiK, each row defining one “NORM” entry (i.e. one code sequence plus its national annex or variant).  It is used by the software’s modules (AQB, BEMESS, AQUA, TEMPLATE, etc.) to pick default materials, load combinations, unit sets, country variants and implementation flags.  Below is a breakdown of its structure and semantics:

1. Columns  
   • NORM (leftmost column)  
     – This is the code identifier to be entered in the SOFiSTiK input (record `NORM`).  
     – Typically composed of a standard family (e.g. BS EN199X-200X) and, where relevant, a suffix like “-BRIDGE” to distinguish building vs. bridge annexes.  
   • Description  
     – A multiline text field that lists:  
       • The scope (e.g. “National Annexes BS building construction”)  
       • The individual parts of the EN standards with their national annex references, for example:  
          – BS EN 1992-1-1/NA:2005 Design of concrete structures  
          – BS EN 1993-1-1/NA:2008 Design of steel structures  
          – BS EN 1994-1-1/NA:2008 Design of composite steel and concrete structures  
          – followed by the overarching combination standard (BS EN 1990/NA:2009), the loading parts (BS EN 1991-1-x/NA:200x), and the material parts (Timber, Brickwork, Aluminium).  
   • UNIT  
     – Integer code referencing a predefined set of units for all input/output in modules (unless overridden).  
     – In the example rows, “6” refers to the unit‐set matching British/Eurocode conventions (kN, m, MPa, etc.).  
   • Design  
     – Flags (letters) indicating which design subprograms have built–in support for that code:  
       • A = implemented in AQB (reinforced concrete/steel design)  
       • B = implemented in BEMESS (timber/steel–timber design)  
       • Other letters (not shown here) might indicate additional modules.  
     – A comma‐separated list allows a single code to drive multiple design engines.

2. Example entries from the snippet  
   • BS EN199X-200X  
     – Description: National Annex for general BS building construction  
       followed by the parts EN 1992-1-1, EN 1993-1-1, EN 1994-1-1 plus EN 1990 and EN 1991 loading parts, and the material parts EN 1995-1-1 (Timber), EN 1996-1-1 (Brickwork), EN 1999-1-1 (Aluminium).  
     – UNIT = 6  
     – Design = A,B  
   • BS EN199X-200X-BRIDGE  
     – Description: National Annex for BS bridge construction  
       followed by EN 1992-2, EN 1993-2, EN 1994-2 and the same combination hierarchy (EN 1990, EN 1991-2, plus materials).  
     – UNIT = 6  
     – Design = A,B

The input table is the master definition of the “NORM” record in SOFiSTiK’s RAG-style input. It tells the system which design code to use, which national annex or variant, and which global defaults to apply. Below is a structured breakdown of its components, their meaning and interrelationships, and the special conventions you need to know when constructing or parsing such a record:

1. Header and Record Name  
   • NORM: The record name. Must appear once at the very start of a project to set up all subsequent defaults.  
   • Warning: Changing NORM after loads or materials have been defined is unsupported and may cause inconsistent results.

2. Key Fields  
   • DC (Design Code Family): A two-letter code identifying the code family (e.g. EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, BS, IS, US, CSA, GB, NF, UNI, UNE, SS, DS, NS, SP, NZS, SFS, NEN, NBN, NBR, ZA).  
   • NDC (Specific Designation): A sub-designation under the chosen code family—often the part or section, normally matching an INI-file name suffix.  
   • COUN (Country Code): For EN codes (Eurocodes) or other families that have national annexes or boxed values. Examples: “00” general EN, “HK/852” for Hong Kong, “IL/972” for Israel.  

3. Category/Class Selection (CAT)  
   • CAT lets you choose a subclass or safety/usage category where codes allow it.  
   • Values are defined per code in the matching INI-file (e.g. “A1”, “A2”, “B1”, etc.).  
   • Historic or user-defined codes can use CAT=USER to supply an arbitrary name.  

4. Location and Environmental Parameters  
   • LON, LAT: Geographic longitude and latitude in degrees—used for wind, seismic, snow load mapping.  
   • LT4 (Altitude): Elevation above sea level, in meters, for snow-load adjustments.  
   • G: Local gravitational acceleration in m/s² (defaults to 9.81 m/s² but may be overridden).  
   • If you do not want a parameter considered at all, set it to “NONE.”  

5. Units and Language (UNIT, dLANG)  
   • UNIT: Global unit system for input/output (processed by AQUA/TEMPLATE). Defaults come from the code’s INI-file, but this field can override it.  
   • dLANG: Optional language switch, mostly for AQUA/TEMPLATE.  

6. INI-File Mechanism  
   • The name of the INI-file used to supply defaults is constructed as DC_NDC.INI (e.g. EN_1992-1-1.INI).  
   • Most material properties, load factors, combination rules, and “boxed values” for national annexes reside in these INI-files.  
   • The auxiliary record TVAR can be used to manually override any boxed value after reading the INI-file.  

7. Examples of Available Codes and Categories  
   – Eurocodes (EN): NDC parts EN1990 through EN1999, country codes 00, HK, etc. CAT = A/B/C for building/bridge classes.  
   – German (DIN): DIN_1052-1988 (wood), DIN-FB102-2009 classification with CAT A,B.  
   – Austrian (OEN): OEN B 4750 (pre-stressed concrete), OEN B 4300 (steel).  
   – British/Commonwealth: BS or UBC families not explicitly listed in the snippet but follow the same pattern.  
   – Canadian (CSA S6-19 for highway bridges).  
   – Swedish (SS EN 1992–1–1/EKS 12:2022 etc.): CAT A1–A3 for buildings; bridge annexes SS EN199X-200X-BRIDGE with CAT B1–B4 (road), C1–C4 (foot), D1–D4 (rail).  
   – Danish (DS EN 1990/NA:2007 etc.): CAT LE, NE, HE (extended control), LN, NN, HN (normal control), LR, NR, HR (reduced control). Bridge tables similarly subdivided.  
   – New Zealand (NZS): CAT A for buildings; CAT 0 for no prestress.  
   – US AASHTO to ACI mapping: AASHTO-2004/2010/2014/2020 design routed to ACI 318-14. Supported checks: DESI (bending & shear), PUNC (punching), CSIG (crack width by permissible stress), CT (crack by tabulated values), CW (calculated crack width).  

8. Usage Guidelines  
   • Always define NORM up front.  
   • Do not redefine code families mid-project unless you intend to rebuild all dependent records.  
   • Check module manuals: not all modules automatically honor every aspect (e.g. seismic zoning, snow-altitude coefficients).  
   • After setting NORM, read and, if necessary, override boxed values via TVAR before defining load cases or material sections.  
   • UNIT and dLANG only affect AQUA/TEMPLATE; record PAGE only affects the current module’s layout.  

This table thus serves as the single point of truth for code selection, national annex parameters, environmental conditions and global defaults in SOFiSTiK’s design workflow.

The input “NORM” table is the central registry of all code‐related parameters used by SOFiSTiK’s design modules (AQB, BEMESS, etc.).  It drives every default setting for materials, load combinations, country-specific boxed values and even global units or language selection.  Below is a structured breakdown:

1. Primary Columns  
   • NORM: Identifier for the record (always “NORM”).  
   • DC (Design Code family): Short acronym for the code system (EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, BS, IS, US, CSA, NF, UNI, UNE, SS, DS, NS, SP, NZS, SFS, NEN, NBN, NBR, ZA).  
   • NDC (Designation Code): Full number/year of a specific standard (e.g. 1990-1-1 for Eurocode 2, 1988 for DIN 1052, etc.).  
   • ITEM DESCRIPTION: Human-readable title of the code (e.g. “Design of concrete structures,” “Holzbau (1988)”).  
   • UNIT: Module scope to which this applies (most often “Design,” occasionally “UNIT Design,” meaning unit‐system selection).  
   • CAT (Category/Class): Allows picking sub-variations or safety classes defined per country annex (e.g. A1–A3 for Swedish buildings, B1–B4 for Swedish road bridges, LE/NE/HE … for Danish codes, etc.).  

2. Location and Environmental Defaults  
   • LON (Longitude, default 0°)  
   • LAT (Latitude, default 45°)  
   • G (Gravity acceleration, default 9.81 m/s² or “*” meaning code default)  
   These can be overridden if a user wants true local values or to suppress a parameter (“NONE”).  Note that wind, snow, altitude and seismic parameters implied by latitude/altitude may not be fully enforced unless checked in module manuals.

3. Country-Specific Boxed Values  
   • COUN: Country code (e.g. “HK/852” for Hong Kong, “IL/972” for Israel).  
   • Within EN‐family codes, national annex deviations are pulled from files named EN_NDC_COUN.INI (e.g. EN 1992-1-1_HK.INI).  If no INI exists (older OEN 4200-4253), AQB falls back on built-in defaults.

4. Code Implementation Flags  
   • A / B markers indicate whether a code is implemented in AQB (A) or BEMESS (B).  
   • Many codes (US AASHTO, US ACI 318-14, Canadian CSA S6-19, Russian SP, Indian IS, Spanish UNE, French NF, Brazilian NBR, South African ZA, etc.) have been partially or fully coded.  Check module HTM‐files for details.

5. Special Cases  
   – Old Austrian OEN 4200-4253 have no INI; user supplies “BOE” for concrete, “BSOE” for steel.  
   – US AASHTO versions (2004, 2010, 2014, 2020) all map to US ACI 318-14 for bending/shear (DESI), punching (PUNC) and crack checks (CSIG, CT, CW).  
   – For some bridge standards (SE, DK, NO, NZ etc.) multiple categories (road, foot, rail) each with safety class and control level.

6. Workflow Notes  
   – Specify design code, country code and geodata at project start.  Redefining code after load cases exist or editing INI by hand is unsupported and risky.  
   – Temporary code changes for specific materials (e.g. steel only) are possible but must be handled with care.  
   – UNIT or dLANG only processed in AQUA/TEMPLATE; PAGE only affects current module.

This table defines the “NORM” input record for SOFiSTiK’s code‐checking and default‐selection engine. It is used at the start of a project to select all material, action, combination and unit defaults via a combination of design code identifiers, country variants, geographic parameters and optional category‐classes.  Whenever you change the design code after having defined load cases, or hack the INI‐files manually, you risk inconsistent results—SOFiSTiK expects you to lock in NORM at the outset.

1.  Core Fields  
    • NORM: Keyword for the record.  
    • DC (Design code family): e.g. EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, BS, US, CSA, GB, etc.  
    • NDC (Designation): Specific code identifier within the family (e.g. EN1992-1-1, US ACI 318-14).  
    • COUN (Country code): Two‐ or three‐character variant to pick national annex (e.g. “00”=General EN, “HK/852”=Hong Kong, “IL/972”=Israel).  
    • CAT (Category/Class): Optional sub‐classification (A, B, C, … or user‐defined) to capture building type, safety class or load‐train definitions.  

2.  Geographic & Physical Defaults  
    • Lt4, Lt16, etc.: Local length or code‐specific load type defaults.  
    • LON, LAT: Longitude/latitude (degrees); used for wind/snow/seismic zone lookup.  
    • G: Local gravity (m/s²); only needed if you want the true geoid value instead of code default.  

3.  Units & Language  
    • UNIT: Global unit‐system selection (overrides INI‐file default).  
    • dLANG: Data‐language for AQUA/TEMPLATE modules.  
    • PAGE: Module‐specific page‐layout settings.  

4.  INI-File Mechanics  
    • INI‐files are named DC_NDC.INI (e.g. EN_1992-1-1.INI).  
    • They store national “boxed values” (e.g. snow load coefficients vs. altitude) and defaults that the software applies behind the scenes.  
    • Missing or modified values can be overridden manually via the TVAR record, but this is advanced usage.  

5.  Code Families & Examples  
    Eurocodes (EN 1990–1999) with national annexes for many countries  
      – EN1992 (Concrete), EN1993 (Steel), EN1994 (Composite), etc.  
      – Country annex examples:  
         • SE/EKS 12:2022 (Sweden – building & bridge categories A1–A3, B1–B4, C1–C4, D1–D4)  
         • DS/NA 2007–2017 (Denmark – safety & control categories LE, NE, HE, LN, NN, HN, LR, NR, HR, and bridge‐specific CAT BNE–BHE, CNE–CHE, DNE–DHE)  
      – Historical national codes like DIN 1052-1988, OEN 4300/4750, etc., each implemented in AQB/BEMESS.  

    Other National Standards  
      – US: AASHTO 2004–2020 mapped to ACI 318-14 checks (DESI, PUNC, CSIG, CT, CW).  
      – CSA S6-19 (Canadian highway bridge code).  
      – SP (Russia), IS (India), UNE (Spain), NZS (New Zealand), NBR (Brazil), ZA (South Africa), etc.  

6.  Category‐Class Usage  
    • “CAT USER” allows free‐form names for legacy or non‐supported codes.  
    • Bridge vs building classes control load definitions, safety factors and inspection levels.  
    • Example classes:  
       – A–C for buildings (normal/extended control, low/normal/high safety)  
       – B–D for road, foot, railway bridges (multiple classes 1–4)  

7.  Key Warnings & Best Practices  
    • Set NORM before defining actions/load cases—changing it later may violate code consis­tency.  
    • Geographic parameters (altitude, zones) are only applied where the specific module implements them. Always verify in the module manual.  
    • To suppress an environmental factor entirely, use “NONE.” The self‐weight load case G remains automatic unless overridden.  

In summary, this table is a master‐switch that steers virtually every default in SOFiSTiK’s structural‐design toolchain. Properly selecting DC, NDC, COUN and CAT—together with LON, LAT and G—ensures that all subsequent analyses, combinations and code‐checks align with the chosen national/regional standards.

1.  Record Fields  
    •  DC (Design‐Code Family)  
       ­– Two‐letter code indicating the standard series (EN, DIN, OEN, SIA, AS, BS, IS, US, CSA, GB, NF, UNI, UNE, SS, DS, NS, SP, NZS, SFS, NEN, NBN, NBR, ZA).  
    •  NDC (Designation)  
       ­– Specific version or part number of the code (e.g. EN1992‐1‐1, DIN1052‐1988).  
    •  COUN (Country Code)  
       ­– Used for “boxed” national variants within EN‐series or for special rules (e.g. HK/852 for Hong Kong; IL/972 for Israeli load trains).  
    •  CAT (Category/Class)  
       ­– Optional subclass within a code (e.g. bridge‐safety classes, building safety levels).  The valid entries are defined in the corresponding INI‐file or coded lists (e.g. A1/A2/A3 for Swedish buildings, B1–B4 for road bridges).  
    •  LT (Load Type)  
       ­– Default load generation (e.g. “Lt16 – – *”).  
    •  LON, LAT  
       ­– Geographic coordinates in degrees.  Used where climate or seismic parameters (wind, snow, earthquake) are code‐driven.  
    •  G  
       ­– Gravity acceleration in m/sec².  Normally the code’s default (self‐weight) is applied; override only if local value is critical.  
    •  UNIT, LANG, PAGE  
       ­– Unit system, language, and page formatting: only AQUA/TEMPLATE modules act on these; elsewhere global units come from the matching INI‐file.  

2.  Default Selection and INI‐Files  
    On project start, you must specify NORM fully so that SOFiSTiK can pull in defaults from DC_NDC.INI.  Changing DC/NDC after defining load cases or materials can lead to inconsistent settings.  Many code fragments are hard‐coded, but most parameters (e.g. material partial factors, combination coefficients, snow altitudes) come from INI‐files named by DC and NDC.  If your design code includes “boxed values” (national options within Eurocodes, e.g. Hong Kong or UK variants), you must supply a country code so that DC_NDC_COUN.INI is found and read.  

3.  Categories, Zones, and Suppression  
    •  CAT entries allow finer classification in special codes (historic or non‐standard codes may use CAT USER with a free‐form label).  
    •  Altitude, wind/snow, and earthquake zones get converted to internal parameters by the active design modules; you must verify compliance yourself.  
    •  To suppress an environmental factor entirely, set its value to NONE.  
    •  Self‐weight (G) is always applied per the code; only define G explicitly to override defaults.  

4.  Available Code Packages  
    Each listed design code shows: country/coun- try code, code designation, unit enforcement, module support flags A (AQB) and B (BEMESS), and CAT options.  Examples include:  
    –  DIN FB102-2009 (Fachbericht 102, cat A,B)  
    –  DIN 1052-1988 Holzbau (cat A)  
    –  OENORM B 4750/4300 (concrete/steel; cat A)  
    –  US AASHTO 2004/2010/2014/2020 –> US ACI 318-14 (features DESI, PUNC, CSIG, CT, CW)  
    –  Canadian CSA S6-19 Highway Bridge (cat 5 A)  
    –  SS EN1992-1-1/EKS12:2022 concrete, SS EN1993-1-1/EKS12:2022 steel, plus timber/brick/aluminium, with CAT A1–A3 for buildings, B1–B4 for bridges.  
    –  DS EN1990/NA:2007 with layered CATs LE,NE,HE,LN,NN,HN,LR,NR,HR plus special BNE/BHE for road bridges, CNE/CHE for footbridges, DNE/DHE for rail.  
    –  NZS New Zealand Standards with CAT A for buildings and CAT 0 for no prestress.  

5.  Concrete Design Features  
    For US AASHTO codes mapped to ACI 318-14, the following checks are implemented:  
    •  DESI – Bending and shear design  
    •  PUNC – Punching shear check  
    •  CSIG – Crack‐width by permissible stresses (ACI method)  
    •  CT – Crack‐width from tabulated values  
    •  CW – Crack‐width calculation by explicit crack‐analysis

 • UNIT, dLANG  
   – (Processed in AQUA or TEMPLATE) Selects global unit system and language for input/output.  
 • PAGE  
   – (Module‐local) Influences formatting in printouts.

– Tokenize key fields (“ZA TMH7”, “South Africa”, “1989”, “prestress classes”, “UNIT 6”, “Design A”, “AQB”)  
– Embed the relationship: NORM→Description→CAT mapping  
– Tag this record with “bridge design”, “culvert design”, “South African Standard”, “SOFiSTiK INI‐file”  
– Store field/value pairs for quick retrieval by queries like “Which unit set does South African bridge code use?” or “What CAT options exist for ZA TMH7?”

The table under review is a “feature‐implementation matrix” for the concrete design modules in the SOFiSTiK suite, showing at a glance which analysis and verification capabilities have been coded for each supported design code. It is intended to guide users in selecting a valid NORM record (the “Design Code” entry) and to set realistic expectations about which checks will actually run. Below is a structured description of its content and how to interpret it:

1. Overall Structure  
   - There are six columns.  
     1. Design Code  
     2. DESI  
     3. PUNC  
     4. CSIG  
     5. CT  
     6. CW  
   - Each row corresponds to one design code or design‐code family (including national annexes and older standards).  
   - Cells contain either:  
     • “X” meaning that the given feature is implemented for that code,  
     • “→ Another Code” meaning that this code is not directly supported but is mapped internally to another code’s implementation, or  
     • blank, meaning no support.  

2. Column Definitions  
   1. Design Code  
      – The identifier passed in the NORM record. Examples: “EN 199X-200X,” “DIN 1045-1 (2001),” “OEN EN199X-200X-BRIDGE,” etc.  
      – Bridge‐specific variants always carry the suffix “-BRIDGE.”  
   2. DESI  
      – Bending and shear design routines.  
   3. PUNC  
      – Punching shear check.  
   4. CSIG  
      – Crack‐width checks by permissible‐stress method (permissible σ).  
   5. CT  
      – Crack‐width checks by table lookup (tabulated values from the code).  
   6. CW  
      – Crack‐width checks by full calculation of crack width.  

3. Row Highlights and Special Cases  
   - EN-family codes  
     • EN 199X-200X (general building) and EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE (bridge annex) both have “X” in every column, indicating full support.  
     • DIN EN199X-200X and the bridge variant also show full support (all X).  
   - Older DIN codes  
     • DIN 1045 (1988) – full support (all X).  
     • DIN 4227+A1 (1995) – not directly implemented; the table shows “→ DIN 1045 (1988),” meaning the software actually treats it as the 1988 DIN 1045 code.  
     • DIN 1045-1 (2001) and DIN 1045-2008 (2008) – full support.  
   - DIN FB and FB104 series (reports/fachberichte)  
     • DIN FB102-2009 (2009) → DIN EN1992-2004  
     • DIN FB102-2003 (2003) → DIN 1045-1 (2001)  
     • DIN FB104-2009 (2009) → DIN EN1992-2004  
     • DIN FB104-2003 (2003) → DIN 1045-1 (2001)  
     – All these rows are blank in the feature columns because the actual implementation is inherited via the arrow mapping.  
   - Austrian OEN codes  
     • OEN EN199X-200X and OEN EN199X-200X-BRIDGE – full support (all X).  
   - US AASHTO variants  
     • Although not shown in the screenshot, preceding text suggests each AASHTO edition (2004, 2010, 2014, 2020) is mapped to the American ACI 318-14 implementation.  
     – Features in those cases follow the ACI implementation.  
   - Other codes (e.g. CSA, SP, IS, UNE, SS, DS, NZS) are not shown in the cropped table but would follow the same pattern if present.  

4. Interpretation Guidelines  
   – An “X” in column DESI means the software will automatically perform bending and shear design checks per that code.  
   – If PUNC is blank, punching checks are not available under that code, and the user must either switch codes or perform a manual check.  
   – Mapping entries (arrows) guarantee backward compatibility with legacy standards but do not add new features beyond the target code.  
   – Users redefining NORM mid‐project should verify that any remapped code still meets their national requirements, especially for crack‐width calculations (CSIG, CT, CW).  

5. Contextual Notes  
   – This table links directly to the NORM record in SOFiSTiK input. The record selects defaults (material properties, load combinations, safety factors) via an INI‐file (${DC}_${NDC}.INI).  
   – Bridge variants trigger special boxed values for actions and combination coefficients as defined in the matching ‑BRIDGE annex.  
   – The presence or absence of CT vs. CW influences whether crack widths come from static tables or are computed dynamically.  

Summary  
This feature matrix is an essential quick‐reference for users setting up concrete design in SOFiSTiK via the NORM record. By reading across a given design code row, one immediately knows which of the five major checks (DESI, PUNC, CSIG, CT, CW) will be carried out, or if the code is internally mapped to another standard’s implementation.

The input table is a summary matrix showing which aspects of reinforced-concrete design are implemented in the software for each supported design code. It appears in SOFiSTiK’s documentation and cross-references the concrete design module’s capabilities (bending & shear, punching shear, crack-width checks by stress or by table, and crack-width calculation) against a long list of national and international standards.

Structure  
• First column (“Design Code”) lists the standard or code designation, often including publication year in parentheses. Bridge-specific national annexes appear immediately below their parent EN-based design code. Some older or superseded codes are linked by arrows (→) to the current implementation.  
• Remaining five columns label the implemented checks:  
  – DESI: Bending and shear design  
  – PUNC: Punching shear check  
  – CSIG: Crack-width by permissible-stress method  
  – CT: Crack-width by table lookup  
  – CW: Crack-width by explicit calculation  

Entries  
• An “X” indicates full support of that check under the given design code.  
• A hyphen (“–”) means that the check is not implemented for that code.  
• Arrow rows (e.g. “OEN 4750 (2000) → OEN 4700”) show that the older standard is treated as equivalent to the newer one.  
• For bridge annexes (e.g. “BS EN199X-200X-BRIDGE”), the same set of checks often mirrors the building-code row immediately above.  

Key patterns and highlights  
• Most modern Eurocode-based national annexes (e.g. NF EN1992-2004, SS EN1992-2004, NS EN199X-200X, DS EN199X-200X, NEN EN199X-200X, NBN EN199X-200X) show full implementation (X across DESI, PUNC, CSIG, CT, CW). Bridge variants of these annexes also carry complete coverage.  
• Several non-Eurocode European standards (OEN 4700, SIA 262, BS 8110, SP 63-13330, UNE EHE, UNI DM-2018, NF BAEL) support the three checks DESI, PUNC, CSIG but lack table or calculation-based crack checks (CT and CW are “–”).  
• Swiss SFS EN199X-200X and its bridge variant defer to the generic EN199X-200X row (indicated by “→ EN 199X-200X”).  
• British Highway code BS 5400 (1990) is mapped to BS 8110 (1997).  
• US AASHTO bridge codes (2004, 2010, 2014, 2020) all map to US ACI 318-14; only the bending, punching, and stress-based crack checks are available (DESI, PUNC, CSIG = X, CT and CW = “–”).  
• Older US ACI references (ACI 318-08) redirect to the 318-14 implementation. Recent ACI versions (318-14, 318-19) follow the same pattern of supporting DESI, PUNC, CSIG only.

Contextual notes  
• The table is one piece of the larger “NORM” record, which in SOFiSTiK controls default selections for materials, superposition rules, load combinations and code-specific parameters via INI-files named by DC_NDC.INI.  
• When a code has national or regional variants (boxed values), these are loaded from separate INI-files (for example EN 1992-2004/CN or EN 1993-2005/HK).  
• Users may temporarily override the chosen design code or suppress parameters by specifying “NONE,” but doing so requires caution and manual verification of resulting combination coefficients and local parameters like gravity acceleration, altitude, wind/snow zones or seismic zones.  
• This implementation table helps automated workflows (AQUA, BEMESS modules) decide which concrete checks can be executed under the active code without raising errors or requiring manual intervention.

In summary, the table is a concise cross-reference for RAG or API queries to determine whether a specific code supports bending/shear checks, punching shear, crack-width checks by stress, tables or calculation, and how older codes are aliased to current implementations.

This table summarizes which aspects of reinforced‐concrete design are implemented natively for various national design codes in the SOFiSTiK RAG environment. It has six columns and nine rows (excluding the header). Here is a breakdown of its structure and content:

1. Columns  
   • Design Code: The national or regional code name and edition year.  
   • DESI (Bending and Shear Design): Indicates if the module can perform flexure and shear checks.  
   • PUNC (Punching Check): Indicates if punching‐shear checks are implemented.  
   • CSIG (Crack Width by Permissible Stresses): Whether crack‐width limits based on permissible stress methods are available.  
   • CT (Crack Width by Table Values): Whether crack‐width limits based on tabulated values (per code tables) are available.  
   • CW (Crack Width by Calculation): Whether crack‐width calculation via stress‐based formulas is implemented.

2. Notation  
   • “X” means the module has a native implementation of the check for that code.  
   • “→ …” (arrow) means that when this code is selected, the software actually delegates that check to a fallback code (for which there is a dedicated implementation). For example, “→ EN 199X-200X” means the module uses the Eurocode implementation for that part of the design.  
   • “–” (dash) means not implemented or not applicable.

3. Rows (per code):  
   1. **CSA S6-19 (Canadian Highway Bridge Code 2019)**  
      • DESI: → EN 199X-200X (bending and shear use Eurocode routines)  
      • PUNC, CSIG, CT, CW: none  

   2. **AS 3600 (2009) (Australian Concrete Structures Code)**  
      • DESI: → AS 5100 (delegates bending/shear to the Australian Bridge Code module)  
      • PUNC, CSIG, CT, CW: none  

   3. **AS 5100 (2001) (Australian Bridge Design Code)**  
      • DESI: X (native bending & shear design)  
      • PUNC: → EC2 EN (punching-shear uses Eurocode 2)  
      • CT: X (native table‐value crack‐width checks)  
      • CSIG, CW: not implemented  

   4. **NZS 3101 (1995) (New Zealand Concrete Structures Standard)**  
      • DESI: → EN 199X-200X (uses Eurocode routines)  
      • others: none  

   5. **GB 50010-2010 / GB 50010 (Chinese Code for Concrete Structures)**  
      • DESI: → BS 8110 (bending/shear use British Standard 8110)  
      • others: none  

   6. **IS 456 (2000) (Indian Standard for Plain and Reinforced Concrete)**  
      • DESI: → BS 8110  
      • others: none  

   7. **NBR 6118-2003 (Brazilian Concrete Code)**  
      • DESI: X (native bending & shear design)  
      • PUNC: → EN 199X-200X (punching uses Eurocode 2)  
      • CT: X (native table‐value crack checks)  
      • CSIG, CW: not implemented  

   8. **ZA TMH7 (1989) (South African Bridge Code)**  
      • DESI: → BS 8110  
      • others: none  

Key observations:  
– Only AS 5100 (2001) and NBR 6118-2003 support native implementations of crack‐width checks (CT).  
– Punching‐shear checks are not widely available; they are delegated to Eurocode 2 for AS 5100 and NBR 6118, and not provided for most other codes.  
– Where a code lacks its own module for a given check, the software falls back to a better-supported code (Eurocode or BS 8110) via the arrow notation.
