The table shown is a classic “command‐definition” lookup used by the BEMESS post‐processing module in a RAG‐vector‐store context.  It defines two control keywords (ITEMs) that users enter literally (Unit = LIT) to steer the type of design run and how results are stored.  Below is a breakdown of its structure and contents:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns:  
     – Item: the control keyword you type (case‐insensitive).  
     – Description: what that keyword does and any sub‐options.  
     – Unit: input type—here always “LIT” (literal strings).  
     – Default: the setting used if you omit this command.  

2. ROW 1: TYPE  
   • Purpose: selects the overall design task or analysis mode.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (i.e. determined by the system or preceding context)  
   • Sub‐options (you supply one of these immediately after TYPE):  
     – ULTI  
       Reinforced‐concrete design for ultimate limit states (ULS).  
       For serviceability (SLS) load cases an averaged safety factor may be input via LC FACT.  
     – ACCI  
       Reinforced‐concrete design for accidental loading situations (per EN 1992-1-1 §6.2.2).  
     – EARQ  
       Reinforced‐concrete design for seismic (earthquake) situations.  
     – SLS  
       Serviceability‐limit‐state design checks only.  
       (No shear design or punching checks are done here—see MREI, CRAC or NSTR for crack/span checks.)  
     – STRE  
       Linear stress analysis based purely on elasticity theory (no design).  
   • Notes: if TYPE is omitted the program picks a default in dependence on the current system configuration.

3. ROW 2: RMOD  
   • Purpose: determines how reinforcement or stress results are saved or accumulated across runs.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (internally “SAVE” for ULS runs, “SUPE” for SLS runs)  
   • Sub‐options (one of these follows RMOD):  
     – SING  
       Single analysis only; do not store any results.  
     – SAVE  
       Store reinforcement/stress tables, overwriting any previous data.  
     – SUPE  
       Superpose: compute the maximum between the newly calculated and already stored reinforcement/stress, then store that maximum.  
     – DELE  
       Delete the stored results for this distribution number (see CTRL LCR).  
   • Notes:  
     – SUPE is especially useful when you want the envelope of several load‐case designs.  
     – To combine REDN/REDM (reduced normal force or moment runs) or to do pure superposition runs, pair RMOD with CTRL LCRI and CTRL LCR.

4. Cross‐References and Context  
   • MREI, CRAC, NSTR: modules for crack‐ and serviceability‐limit checks invoked under TYPE SLS.  
   • CTRL LCR / CTRL LCRI: controls linking and superposing different design runs; interacts directly with RMOD DELE, SAVE, SUPE.  
   • LC FACT: used under ULTI if mixed ULS/SLS load cases supply an average safety factor.  

By structuring CONTROL input this way, BEMESS lets you flexibly switch between analysis modes (TYPE) and manage how intermediate or final reinforcement/stress results are recorded (RMOD), all in a concise, tabular format that integrates with other command blocks (e.g. CTRL PUNC for punching, CTRL RO_V for shear‐reinforcement limits, etc.).

The table is an extract from the SOFiSTiK‐BEMESS input deck that defines the keywords and numeric parameters needed for punching‐shear and related checks in slab and wall elements.  It is organized in four columns—Item, Unit, Default, and Description—and lists only those parameters whose primary function is to control punching shear, shear reinforcement, tendon effects and sector‐method eccentricity factors.  (For other slab‐related parameters see the companion tables MREI, CRAC, NSTR, MAT and PUNC.)

1.  Columns
   •  Item: the name of the control keyword or parameter  
   •  Unit: physical unit or indication “–” when unitless  
   •  Default: the value used if the user omits the parameter  
   •  Description: what the parameter does, valid ranges and code references  

2.  Rows (selected entries)

   2.1  RO_V (–; Default 0.2)  
        Maximum reinforcement ratio for shear in a “normal” slab region (outside punching zones).  Enter as percent.  If a bending‐only design cannot resist the factored shear, the program will increase longitudinal bar area up to RO_V before providing discrete shear links.  Used in EN 1992-1-1 and many other codes.  

   2.2  V2 (–; Default 0.3 when used with CTRL RO_V)  
        Complementary value for “upper” reinforcement ratio in the punching region.  When punching shear requires a two‐layer shear design, V2 sets the top‐face reinforcement ratio.  

   2.3  COTT (–; no default in table)  
        Upper and lower bounds of cotangent(θ) used in the shear‐force inclination (θ) calculation.  Permissible between 1.00 and 3.00.  

   2.4  VLEV (–; no default in table)  
        Maximum lever arm factor for shear design (z/d ratio limit).  

   2.5  BETA (–; Default depends on code, see below)  
        Eccentricity factor β for punching design per EN 1992-1-1 Clause 6.4.3(6) and national provisions (NDP).  Integer or decimal inputs select among:  
        •  0, 1, 2, 3: pre-defined application scopes (corner/edge/internal columns, flat β vs. sweeping β)  
        •  10: German/Austrian NDP—always use EN eqn (6.39) if it yields a larger β for high e/c (>1.2)  
        •  –0.1, –1, –2: “exact” β even if below sweeping β (–0.1 means allow zero)  
        •  +0, +1, +2: β not smaller than sweeping one, exact meaning lesser of sector method or eqn (6.39)  
        Default: 0 for most EU codes, 10 for DE/AT, 2 for DK/ES/others.  

        Sub-controls:  
          – V2: sector method override for wall corners and ends (default 3 ► do not use sector β)  
          – V3: sector method override for all columns (default 0 ► use sector β if controlling)  

   2.6  RADP (–; Default 6.0)  
        Factor to modify the “punching check radius.”  By default, sectors closer than 6·d to an opening or boundary are inactive.  RADP scales that distance.  

   2.7  VPDC (–; Default 0.12)  
        Factor for creep and shrinkage losses considered in the punching check.  Default corresponds to 12 % prestress loss.  Input 0.0 to switch off.  

   2.8  SIGZ (N/mm²; Default 0)  
        Switch tendon‐force influence on punching shear.  0 ► tendon effect off; 999 ► special case, set bond stress = 0.45 N/mm².  

   2.9  WTEN (–; Default 2.0)  
        Distribution width factor W for QUAD tendons, entered as a multiple of slab thickness.  

   2.10 V3 (–; no default in table)  
        A “third” checkbox value used by some CTRL commands (e.g. CTRL BOUN) to select among discrete sub‐options.  

3.  Usage notes  
   •  Every CTRL keyword may have multiple numeric “values” (V2, V3, …) to fine-tune algorithm choices.  
   •  Unless overridden, defaults are chosen to comply with EN 1992-1-1 or national annex rules.  
   •  These parameters feed directly into the punching‐shear envelope calculation (β·V_ed), sector method checks, prestress loss modeling, and radial cut‐off definitions.  

This structured overview of the input table will help you construct your RAG vector store entries by identifying each keyword’s role, valid range, default behavior and underlying code reference.

The input table defines a series of control‐parameters (items) for the SOFiSTiK BEMESS design program.  It is organized in four columns—“Item,” “Description,” “Unit,” and “Default”—and each row documents one parameter.  Below is a detailed, row‐by‐row description suitable for ingestion into a RAG‐driven vector store:

1.  Column Headings  
    • Item: the short command‐name or keyword used in the input file (e.g. LAY, LCR).  
    • Description: a brief textual explanation of the parameter’s purpose and usage.  
    • Unit: the physical unit or qualifier (if any) associated with the parameter. A dash (“–”) indicates no explicit unit.  
    • Default: the default value applied when the parameter is not explicitly set by the user.

2.  Row 1 – LAY  
    • Description: Selects the concrete slab layer design procedure.  
      – 0: ULS design by the Baumann method; SLS by Capra–Maury approach.  
      – 1: Layer design via strain iteration.  
      – 2: Sandwich‐model approach per draft EN 1992-1-1, Annex G.  
      – Default behavior: in ULS and crack design, LAY = 0; for prestressed slabs or skew reinforcement, LAY = 1; in stress checks, LAY = 1.  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: –  (the program picks 0 or 1 depending on design context)

3.  Row 2 – LCR  
    • Description: Assigns the reinforcement‐distribution number for the current design.  Users can delete existing sets by referencing LCR in conjunction with CTRL RMOD DELE (e.g. “CTRL RMOD DELE LCR 31,32”).  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: 1  

4.  Row 3 – LCRI  
    • Description: Specifies a design run whose results will be used to determine the maximum reinforcement demand.  LCRI allows one analysis to feed forward its maxima into subsequent designs.  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: –  

5.  Row 4 – LCRP  
    • Description: Imports punching‐shear reinforcement results from another design case, typically referenced by an LCRI number.  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: same as LCRI  

6.  Row 5 – DMOM  
    • Description: Activates storage of “woodarmer” design bending forces (offsets) for use in later superposition or detailing.  See the bending‐design theoretical principles.  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: –  

7.  Row 6 – TENS  
    • Description: Reduces the permissible concrete compressive stress when concrete is under transverse tension (i.e. T‐section cracks).  The default reduction is 25 %.  Note that EN 1992-1-1 Clause 6.5.2(2) is specific to beam‐strut design and not applied to general slabs/shells.  The 25 % factor originates from a German national annex applicable when cracks run perpendicular to compression zones in finite‐element quadrilateral shells.  A special keyword “TENS ’prEN’” invokes the draft EN 1992-1-1 Annex G (G.9) provision.  
    • Unit: %  
    • Default: 25  

8.  Row 7 – PFAI  
    • Description: Chooses the compression‐failure checking method for shell and disk elements.  
      – 1: Mechanical‐correct analysis (default for ULS design).  
      – 2: Transforms any failure case into an equivalent compression‐reinforcement requirement (default for serviceability checks).  
    • Unit: –  
    • Default: *  (an asterisk indicates a program‐determined default, typically 1 for ultimate‐limit checks)

Each entry in this table must be invoked via the corresponding “CTRL” command syntax in the BEMESS input deck (e.g. “CTRL LAY 2” or “CTRL TENS 20”).  Parameters with no explicit default are inherited from the program’s code logic or from higher‐level control keywords.  This structured description captures the semantics, units, and default behaviors essential for any automated retrieval‐augmented design assistant.

The input table defines a set of control parameters (“CTRL” switches) used to steer shear‐ and punching‐design checks in a reinforced‐concrete slab or wall model.  Each entry in the table consists of

•  Item name (the keyword used in the input deck)  
•  A brief description of what it controls  
•  Units or format  
•  Default and permissible values  
•  Any code‐specific notes or variants (e.g. Eurocode vs. German NDP)

Below is a structured summary of the main parameters:

1.  RO_V  
    – Maximum reinforcement ratio (percent) that may be assigned as “shear reinforcement” in a normal slab region when bending reinforcement alone is insufficient.  
    – Unit: %  
    – Default: 0.20  
    – V2 (upper bound for certain regions): 0.30 or 0.40 in specific cases.  
    – See also PUNC RO_V for punching‐region reinforcement.

2.  COTT  
    – Cotangent limit (θ) used in shear‐design formulas.  
    – Unitless  
    – Permissible input: [1.00 … 3.00]

3.  VLEV  
    – Maximum internal lever arm used in shear design.  
    – Unitless  
    – No explicit default; chosen per code requirements.

4.  BETA  
    – Eccentricity‐factor for punching‐shear (“β” in EN 1992‐1‐1 §6.4.3).  
    – Unitless  
    – Default:  
      • 0 for most Eurocode countries  
      • 10 for Germany / Austria (their NDP requires eqn 6.39 whenever β calculated by perimeter‐sector or flat methods exceeds sweeping‐value)  
      • 2 for Denmark, Spain, and other nations where special provision applies  
    – Sub‐switches:  
      • V2: Controls wall‐corner and wall‐end β (0 = sector min sweeping; –0.1 = even if below sweeping; 3 = ignore sector method).  
      • V3: Globally disable (3) or permit (0) the sector‐method check vs. eqn 6.39.

5.  RADP  
    – Multiplier for the “check radius” in punching‐perimeter generation.  
    – Unitless  
    – Default: 6.0 · d (slab thickness‐based perimeter); internals adjust for thick sections.

6.  VPDC  
    – Flag/factor to include creep and shrinkage losses in the punching check.  
    – Unitless  
    – Default: 0.12 (i.e. 12 % prestress loss if prestressed tendons are present; 0 = turn off).

7.  SIGZ  
    – Bond‐stress control for prestressed strands in punching perimeter.  
    – Unit: N/mm²  
    – Default: use code‐calculated bond law (SIGZ 0 = off).  
    – Special override: “CTRL SIGZ 999 V2 0.45” forces σ₀ = 0.45 N/mm².

8.  WTEN  
    – Distribution width (W) factor for QUAD‐pattern tendons.  
    – Unitless factor relative to slab thickness.  
    – Default: 2.0 · thickness

9.  CTRL TYPE  
    – Defines whether ULS or SLS checks are performed:  
      • ULTI (default if superposition from MAXIMA with design combinations)  
      • SLS (service‐limit only—no shear/punching unless SUPE option is active).

10.  REDN / REDM  
    – Scale factors (<1.0) to reduce normal force (REDN) or bending moment (REDM) for special design cases (e.g. cracked‐section tension checks).  
    – Must be used together with “CTRL RMOD SUPE” and require a preceding base run without reduction.

11.  VF70  
    – Factor to increase shear capacity for accidental or power‐plant design (per DIN 1045‐1 eqn 70/105).  
    – Unitless multiplier (e.g. 1.15).

12.  BUBB  
    – Reduction factor for bubble‐deck (voided‐slab) shear capacity.  
    – Default: 0.55 · VRDc  
    – No shear links allowed; V_ED ≤ V_RDm(=0.55·full‐section capacity).

13.  BOUN  
    – Controls shear‐reduction at supports and shell‐edges according to EN 1992‐1‐1 §6.2.1(8) and national rules:  
      • BOUN 0: no reduction  
      • +1, +2, +4, +8: apply linear drop to x_VED·d at direct, shell, or indirect support edges  
      • V2 override (default 0.7) keeps 70 % shear at face of support.

14.  CTRL LCRI / CTRL LCR  
    – Keys to store and re‐use reinforcement or stress maxima from earlier design runs (enabling “superposition” of reinforcement envelopes).

15.  CTRL CORE  
    – Number of threads for parallel processing.  
    – Default: auto‐detect physical cores; override via SOF_NUM_THREADS or “CTRL CORE NN[%]”.

See also related tables or sections for material (“MAT”), punching (“PUNC”), cracking (“CRAC”), non‐steel ratios (“NSTR”), and reinforcement input (“MREI”).

The table below defines the optional “CTRL”‐commands and parameters that govern shear and punching‐shear design of slabs and wall supported elements in BEMESS (SOFiSTiK).  Its four columns are:

• Item: the keyword (always used with the “CTRL” prefix)  
• Description: what the switch/factor controls  
• Unit: the physical or non‐dimensional unit  
• Default: the value assumed when no input is given  

1. CTRL  
 – Prefix that activates any of the following commands.

2. RO_V (with optional V2)  
 • Description: Maximum shear reinforcement ratio (in lieu of stirrups) for a normal slab region.  If the bending‐determined stirrups are insufficient, BEMESS will raise the longitudinal reinforcement up to RO_V (%) rather than add shear links.  
 • Unit: %  
 • Default: 0.2  
 • V2: an upper cap on that ratio (e.g. “CTRL RO_V 0.4 V2 0.3” limits reinforcement to 0.3 %).

3. COTT  
 • Description: Limit the cotangent of the shear‐flow angle φ in shear design.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Input range: 1.00…3.00  
 • Default: code‐specific (no explicit input → uses standard EN-1992 value).

4. VLEV (with optional V2)  
 • Description: Maximum lever‐arm factor z/d in shear checks.  Example: “VLEV 0.9” → z = 0.9·d.  You can also control the maximum shear‐flow angle via V2, or switch the entire limit off by “CTRL VLEV 0 V2 0.”  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: code‐specific.

5. BOUN (with optional V2 & V3)  
 • Description: Shear reduction at supports (“direct” and “indirect”): the shear force is linearly reduced from the support face out to xVED·d.  Bit‐flags 1,2,4,8 enable reduction at direct edges, shell edges, wall corners, hanging slabs, respectively.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: flags 1+2+4 (EN and DIN codes use xVED=1.0; older codes 0.5).  
 • V2: retention factor at the face (EN-1992-1-1 6.2.1(8) prescribes ≥70 % → default V2 0.7).  
 • V3: custom override of xVED.

6. VMIN  
 • Description: Minimum shear‐capacity coefficient vmin per EN 1992-1-1 6.2.2(1).  Not applied to punching checks.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: code‐specified (often ~0.233·fck^0.5).

7. MINS  
 • Description: Minimum shear‐reinforcement ratio per EN 1992-1-1 9.3.1.  Slabs may use a fraction (<1) of beam minima.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: 0.6 for Germany/ÖNORM, otherwise 1.0.

8. WINT (with optional V2)  
 • Description: Integration method for punching shear at wall corners/ends.  
  – 0: integrate slab‐shear force (default)  
  – 1 or 1.5: integrate support reaction (per theoretical principle)  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: 0  
 • V2: setting V2 0 suppresses the 15 % “stud-rail” increase.

9. WEND  
 • Description: Leg length of the punching perimeter at wall ends.  A negative input (e.g. –1.0) invokes the theoretical rule based on adjacent spans.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: –1.0

10. BETA (with V2 & V3)  
 • Description: Eccentricity factor β for punching‐shear per EN 1992-1-1 6.4.3 or national derogations (NDP).  β scales the active shear perimeter and may be computed by:  
  – eq.(6.39) (German/Austrian rule)  
  – sweeping value (flat, per edges or corners)  
  – sector‐method (if controlling)  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: 0 (Eurocode default), 10 (DE/AT), 2 (DK/ES/others)  
 • V2: wall‐corner/ends override (e.g. 0=sweeping‐min; –0.1=exact even if lower)  
 • V3: sector‐method switch (0=use if lower; 3=never use).

11. RADP  
 • Description: Multiplier of the standard 6·d punching‐perimeter radius to include/exclude sectors with openings or boundaries closer than 6 d to the column.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: 6.0 (internally reduced for very thick slabs)

12. VPDC  
 • Description: Factor for creep/shrinkage losses in punching‐shear checks.  Default corresponds to 12 % prestress loss.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: 0.12

13. SIGZ (with V2)  
 • Description: Tendon‐bond stress in shear.  
  – SIGZ 0: ignore tendons (no shear contribution)  
  – SIGZ 999 V2 x: set bond stress = x (N/mm²)  
 • Unit: N/mm²  
 • Default: 0 (tendons switched off)

14. WTEN  
 • Description: Distribution‐width factor W for QUAD tendons (shear transfer in tendon troughs).  Input as multiple of slab thickness: “WTEN 2.0” spreads tendon shear over 2·d.  
 • Unit: –  
 • Default: 2.0

Below is a structured, detailed description of the input‐table parameters used in SOFiSTiK’s RAG/BEMESS shear and punching checks. Wherever possible, the “Item” name corresponds to the CTRL command, followed by its purpose, acceptable input, units, and default.

1. Shear‐reinforcement controls  
   • RO_V (CTRL RO_V V2 x.x)  
     – Purpose: Defines the maximum percent of shear reinforcement allowed in a normal slab region when bending reinforcement alone cannot resist the applied shear.  
     – V2: A secondary value for “upper reinforcement,” e.g. CTRL RO_V V2 0.3 limits additional stirrups.  
     – Input: percentage ( % ).  
     – Default: 0.2 % (as per Eurocode default).  
     – See also PUNC ro_v for punching‐region shear.  

   • COTT (CTRL COTT θ_max)  
     – Purpose: Caps the cotangent of the shear‐force inclination angle θ in the shear‐design formulas (V3 method).  
     – Input: any real number between 1.00 and 3.00.  
     – Units: – (dimensionless).  
     – Default: not set (user must supply within permissible range).  

   • VLEV (CTRL VLEV z_max)  
     – Purpose: Sets the maximum internal lever arm z used in shear‐capacity calculations.  
     – Input: factor (–).  
     – Default: not set (consult national annex or user input).  

2. Punching‐shear and prestress‐loss factors  
   • BETA (CTRL BETA mode [V2 v2] [V3 v3])  
     – Purpose: Eccentricity factor β governing punching‐shear perimeter shape. Conforms to EN 1992-1-1 §6.4.3 and national deviations (e.g. Germany/Austria NDP).  
     – Modes:  
       · 0: flat “sweeping” β for all columns (Eurocode default).  
       · –0.1, –1, –2: exact β from sector method or Eq. (6.39), even if smaller than sweeping.  
       · +0, +1, +2: enforce at least sweeping β (never smaller).  
       · 10: always use Eq. (6.39) for boundary/edge columns (Germany/Austria).  
       · 2: Denmark+Spain national annex.  
     – V2 override: controls wall corners/ends (default V2 = 3 disables sector method).  
     – V3 override: controls all columns (default V3 = 0 uses sector if controlling).  
     – Units: – (dimensionless).  
     – Default: 0 (EC), 10 (DE/AT), 2 (DK/ES), 2 (others).  

   • RADP (CTRL RADP f_rad)  
     – Purpose: Scales the punching‐shear check radius (normally 6·d from column edge).  
     – Input: factor (–).  
     – Default: 6.0.  

   • VPDC (CTRL VPDC f_loss)  
     – Purpose: Accounts for prestress loss (creep/shrinkage) in punching‐shear checks.  
     – Input: fraction of prestress force lost (e.g. 0.12 for 12 % loss). 0.0 = no loss.  
     – Units: – (dimensionless).  
     – Default: 0.12.  

3. Tendon‐bond and distribution settings  
   • SIGZ (CTRL SIGZ τ_bond [V2 τ2])  
     – Purpose: Sets the average bond‐stress τ between prestressing strands and concrete for shear/punching checks.  
     – Input: τ in N/mm². SIGZ 0 disables tendon influence. Special: “999” sets τ_bond = 0.45 N/mm² via V2.  
     – Units: N/mm².  
     – Default: 0 (off).  

   • WTEN (CTRL WTEN w_factor)  
     – Purpose: Defines the width of the tendon‐force distribution W for QUAD‐tendon elements, expressed as a multiple of slab thickness.  
     – Input: factor (–).  
     – Units: – (dimensionless).  
     – Default: 2.0.

The table in question is a catalog of “CTRL”‐type input parameters and associated variables used by the SOFiSTiK/BEMESS punching‐and‐shear module (often in a RAG vector‐store context for Retrieval‐Augmented Generation). Each row of the table defines one configurable quantity, its meaning, allowed range or special notes, units (where applicable), and its default value. In practice these controls tune aspects of slab shear check, punching check, tendon losses, bubble‐deck behavior, and the treatment of edge/corner effects. Below is a structured description of the key items:

1. CTRL RO_V  
   • Name: Maximum reinforcement ratio for shear in a “normal” slab region (non-punching)  
   • Description: If the slab fails the shear check without stirrups, BEMESS may boost the flexural (bending) reinforcement up to this ratio (in %). Useful around points of zero bending moment.  
   • Unit: percent (%)  
   • Default: 0.2  
   • See also: PUNC RO_V for the punching (column) region  

2. COTT  
   • Name: Limitation of cotangent θ used in shear design equations  
   • Description: Upper/lower bounds for the θ parameter in the shear‐resistance formulas.  
   • Range: input between 1.00 and 3.00 (no unit)  
   • Default: not explicitly given, user must supply if deviating from code recommended  

3. VLEV  
   • Name: Maximum lever arm for shear design (often z ≤ d·VLEV)  
   • Description: Applies the eccentricity value β from EN 1992-1-1 §6.4.3.  Selects how β is computed for corner, edge, internal columns or walls.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0.12 (or sometimes 6.0 for the creep/shrinkage factor context—see VPDC below)  
   • Special modes via CTRL BETA:  
     – 0: exact for all columns but at least the sweeping (flat) value  
     – 1–3: various restrictions on use of “exact” vs. “flat” β depending on e/c ratio  
     – 10: German/Austrian NDP: always use the higher from Eq. (6.39) when span‐difference >25%  
     – Negative or positive suffixes (–0.1, +1, +2) lock the β to minimum/maximum of sector method or EC equation  

4. BETA  
   • Name: Eccentricity (β) factor in punching design  
   • Description: Overrides the flat‐sector or code equations (6.39–6.46).  Multiple sub‐controls (CTRL BETA …V2/V3) let you force sector‐method usage or force code equation usage for wall corners/ends or for all column types.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0 (flat or sector‐min), 10 (German/Austrian), 2 (Denmark/Spain/others)  

5. RADP  
   • Name: Factor modifying the punching check‐perimeter radius  
   • Description: By default, sectors closer than 6·d to a column edge are excluded.  RADP scales that 6·d distance up or down, adapting for thin vs. thick slabs.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 6.0  

6. VPDC  
   • Name: Factor for reduction of punching capacity due to creep & shrinkage  
   • Description: Accounts for time‐dependent prestress loss.  Default assumes a 12% loss of prestress force in the tendon.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 0.12 (i.e. 12% loss)  
   • Special input: 0.0 means “no loss”  

7. SIGZ  
   • Name: Influence of tendon normal force on slab shear capacity  
   • Description: Switching off tendon bond stress contribution by input SIGZ 0.  A special switch SIGZ 999 V2 0.45 will set the bond stress to 0.45 N/mm².  
   • Unit: N/mm²  
   • Default: active (non-zero) unless overridden  

8. WTEN  
   • Name: Distribution width W for QUAD (quadrilateral) tendon layout  
   • Description: Input as a multiple of the element thickness; defines how wide the tendon “bundle” is spread in the finite‐element slab.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: 2.0  

Additional context notes:  
- CTRL TYPE ULTI/SLS select ultimate vs. serviceability‐only design workflows.  
- CTRL LCRI, LCR enable superposition of prior design runs to accumulate maximum reinforcement or stresses.  
- CTRL VF70, REDN, REDM scale design forces for accidental loading or simulated reduced normal/bending loads.  
- CTRL BOUN adjusts shear‐force reduction at direct supports and shell edges per EN 1992-1-1 §6.2.1(8).  
- CTRL BUBB modifies shear capacity for bubble‐deck slabs, capping VRd,c to a fraction (default 0.55) of a full‐section capacity.  

In a RAG/vector‐store setting, each of these parameters becomes a dimension or key‐value entry you can query. For example, “What is the default punching‐perimeter radius factor?” returns RADP = 6.0. Or “How do I force the sector method for all columns?” returns CTRL BETA V3 = 3.

The table on the previous page is a master list of user‐control switches (“CTRL” commands) for SOFiSTiK’s concrete‐design module (BEMESS).  Each row in the table defines one “Item” (a keyword you type), a short “Description” of its purpose, the physical “Unit” (if any), and the “Default” setting.  Below is a detailed walk-through of each entry:

1. BRIC  
  • Description: Turns on the design check of 3D volume (brick) elements.  If you invoke DI3D and set BRIC=0, BEMESS skips any volume‐element design.  
  • Unit: — (dimensionless flag)  
  • Default: “–” (off)

2. BUBB  
  • Description: Activates “bubble‐deck” design.  In bending, the concrete compression zone is limited to the outer solid layers.  In shear, the slab’s punching/shear capacity is reduced to CTRL BUBB × (full-section capacity).  Links are disallowed so any V_ED must be less than V_RD,bbbe = 0.55·V_RD,c of a solid slab.  Within punching perimeters the normal shear check is also applied.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 0.55

3. REDN  
  • Description: Factor for reduced axial (N) force in design.  Use when you want to reduce service or ultimate normal force (for staged construction, etc.).  Note: a “pure” run without REDN first is required if you want to capture the true maximum tension or compression.  Always use with CTRL RMOD SUPE.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 1.00

4. REDM  
  • Description: Factor for reduced bending moment (M) in design.  Same workflow comments apply as for REDN.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 1.00

5. SNIP  
  • Description: Safety factor for short-term/long-term loading per the Russian code.  By default, 0.9 for long-term loading.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 0.9

6. VF70  
  • Description: Increases shear capacity when designing for accidental loading (e.g. power plants).  It scales V_RD,c per DIN 1045-1 Eq. 70/105 or EN 1992-1-1.  Typical use: VF70=1.15 to reflect a reduced partial‐safety factor.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 1.00

7. WALL  
  • Description: Enables “deep‐beam” (wall) treatment of slabs when they act like one‐way walls.  If YES, imposes minimum reinforcement rules (e.g. 0.075% each face per EN 1992-1-1, 0.10% per Austria B 4700, 0.15% for older codes).  If NO, no minimum is enforced (default for shell/3D systems).  See also MAT AM3.  
  • Unit: LIT (literal “YES”/“NO”)  
  • Default: * (contextual default: NO for shells, YES for disks)

8. CORE  
  • Description: Controls parallel computation.  By default, SOFiSTiK auto-detects hardware and license (HISOLV) to parallelize solve or element loops.  You can explicitly set the thread count via CTRL CORE.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: * (automatic)

9. WARN  
  • Description: Switch off selected warning or error messages by specifying their IDs.  Useful to suppress non-critical alerts in batch runs.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: * (no suppression)

10. V2  
  • Description: A generic “second value” for commands that take two parameters.  For example, CTRL RO_V V2 1 sets the max shear‐reinforcement ratio, or CTRL SLS V2 1 adjusts SLS stress combination.  Consult “Theoretical Principles: SLS stresses.”  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: “–” (not applicable unless used)

11. V3  
  • Description: A generic “third value” for commands with three parameters, e.g. CTRL BOUN V3 … adjusts the span‐related shear‐reduction length at supports.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: “–”

See also related control records MREI (mesh refinement), CRAC (crack‐width checks), NSTR (non-structural loads), MAT (material definitions) and PUNC (punching‐perimeter switches).  Each of those tables follows a similar “Item – Description – Unit – Default” format, so you can cross-reference parameters across the concrete‐design workflow.

The image is a full-width extract from a SOFiSTiK “Input Description” manual (specifically the BEMESS module) describing how shear forces at direct supports are handled by default and how they may be modified with the CTRL BOUN command. It combines two short explanatory paragraphs with a schematic diagram (Figure 3.1) and its caption. Key elements are:

1. Header 
   • Top left: SOFiSTiK logo in blue.  
   • Top right: “Input Description | BEMESS”.

2. Text block 1 – Default shear reduction at direct supports  
   • Explains that, unless overridden, the software linearly reduces the design shear force from 100 % at the controlling section (distance xVED · d from the face of the support) down to 0 % at the face of the support.  
   • Defines xVED · d as the “controlling shear cut” distance per DIN 1045-1 § 10.3.2(1) and EN 1992-1-1 § 6.2.1(8).  
   • Notes that xVED is set to 1.0 · d for EN and DIN 1045-1 (and all new EC codes), otherwise 0.5 · d, and that CTRL BOUN V3 can be used to change this value.

3. Text block 2 – EN 1992-1-1 requirement to continue shear reinforcement to the support  
   • Quotes EN 1992-1-1 § 6.2.1(8): “Any shear reinforcement required should continue to the support.”  
   • Explains that, since Version 2016, the reduced shear at the face of the support is not driven to 0 % but held at 70 % of the full shear.  
   • States that CTRL BOUN V2 may be used to set this face‐of‐support factor (default: CTRL BOUN 1+2+4 V2 0.7).

4. Text block 3 – Check of VRd,max  
   • Clarifies that for the ultimate shear capacity check (VRd,max) the linear reduction is only applied between the support axis and the face of the support; from the face of the support back to the controlling section (xVED · d) the unreduced shear values are used.  
   • References DIN 1045-1 § 10.3.2(3) and EN 1992-1-1 § 6.2.1(8).

5. Figure 3.1 – Schematic of reduced shear VED (in red) near direct supports

     – A red line showing the reduced shear: vertical drop to 70 % at the face of the support, then sloping down in parallel.  
   • Labels: “V = 100 o/o” at the black line, “Ved = 70 o/o” at the red vertical.

Throughout the page, fixed-width font highlights commands and code references (e.g. CTRL BOUN, xVED *d, DIN 1045-1, EN 1992-1-1), and the narrative explains both the default behavior and how to override it for compliance with Eurocode requirements.

The table presented is a compact four-column reference for the SOFiSTiK “CORE” control directive, which governs parallel computation threading. It is intended to be parsed into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) store so that, when a user or program requests information on parallel processing or thread control, this record can be matched and returned efficiently. The key elements of its structure and content are as follows:

1. Table Structure  
   • Column 1 “CORE”  
     – Holds the specific keyword or sub-command of the main control directive (“CORE”).  
     – Here it appears only once, indicating that the only available sub-directive under this heading in the current release is “VAL.”  
   • Column 2 “Description”  
     – A concise human-readable description of what the corresponding sub-directive does.  
     – For “VAL,” it reads “Number of used threads,” i.e. it specifies how many parallel threads should be allocated.  
   • Column 3 “Unit”  
     – Defines the measurement or type of value the sub-directive expects. In this case it is a dash (–), signifying “unitless” or an integer count.  
   • Column 4 “Default”  
     – Shows the built-in fallback value if the user does not explicitly set one. An asterisk (*) implies that the default is determined dynamically (see underlying program logic) rather than a fixed literal.

2. Contextual Role in SOFiSTiK Workflows  
   – The “CTRL CORE” instruction lets modelers and analysts finely control the number of threads used for parallelizable tasks (solver routines or element‐wise operations).  
   – By default, SOFiSTiK queries the operating system for the count of available physical cores. That becomes the default “VAL.”  
   – This asterisk default allows the software to adapt automatically to the hardware environment, ensuring efficient utilization.  
   – Users can override it by issuing “CTRL CORE N” (or “CTRL CORE N[%]”) to lock in a specific thread count, which in turn guides subsequent computations (e.g., matrix solvers, element loops).

3. Advantages of Including This Table in a RAG Vector Store  
   – Precision: Each column is a potential retrieval key. Queries for “CTRL CORE,” “parallel threads,” “unitless,” or “default” can directly locate this entry.  
   – Disambiguation: The four-column structure clearly separates the command name, its behavior, expected input, and default handling, which improves semantic indexing.  
   – Extensibility: As new sub-directives get added under “CORE” (for example, “CTRL CORE MODE” or “CTRL CORE AFFINITY”), they can be appended as new rows without altering the schema.  
   – User Guidance: By embedding the default logic (asterisk) and linking it to the broader description (automatic detection of cores, environmental override via SOF_NUM_THREADS), the RAG system can answer “What happens if I don’t set THREADS?” or “How do I force single-threaded execution?” by returning this record plus the supplemental notes.

4. Suggested Metadata for Vector Embeddings  
   – Keywords/tags: “parallel computing,” “thread count,” “SOFiSTiK solver,” “CTRL CORE,” “performance tuning.”  
   – Contextual pointers: link to environment variable “SOF_NUM_THREADS,” license requirement “HISOLV,” and overriding syntax “CTRL CORE NN[%].”  
   – Category: “Resource Control,” subcategory: “Compute Configuration.”  
   – Usage scenario: “Explicit thread assignment,” “Automatic core detection,” “Suppress parallelism by setting VAL to 1.”  

By representing this table in the vector store with these annotations and structured fields, downstream retrieval will be both accurate (exact command lookup) and contextually rich (explaining default behavior, overrides, and system dependencies).

The table summarizes the options available in SOFiSTiK for selecting and controlling the linear-equation solver via the CTRL SOLV command. It associates each solver name with its numeric code, indicates whether a special license (HISOLV) is required, and shows if parallel execution is supported.  Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1. Solver  
   – The name of the algorithm used to solve the system of equations. Four solvers are listed:
   • Skyline Gauss/Cholesky  
   • Iterative  
   • Sparse LDL (default)  
   • Sparse Parallel (also known as Pardiso)

2. CTRL SOLV  
   – The integer code passed to the CTRL SOLV command in the input file to select the corresponding solver:  
   • 1 = Skyline Gauss/Cholesky  
   • 2 = Iterative  
   • 3 = Sparse LDL  
   • 4 = Sparse Parallel (Pardiso)

3. License  
   – Indicates whether a HISOLV license granule is needed for serial and/or parallel runs:  
   • Skyline Gauss/Cholesky (code 1)  
     – Serial: no special license required  
     – Parallel: not applicable  
   • Iterative (code 2)  
     – Serial: requires HISOLV  
     – Parallel: requires HISOLV  
   • Sparse LDL (code 3, the default)  
     – Serial: no special license required  
     – Parallel: not applicable  
   • Sparse Parallel / Pardiso (code 4)  
     – Serial: requires HISOLV  
     – Parallel: requires HISOLV

4. Parallel  
   – Notes whether the solver can be executed in parallel (multi-threaded) mode:  
   • Only the Iterative (2) and Sparse Parallel/Pardiso (4) solvers support parallel processing—provided a HISOLV license is available.  
   • The Skyline Gauss/Cholesky and Sparse LDL solvers execute in a purely serial fashion.

Additional context (from the “CORE Parallel computation control” section):  
– By default, SOFiSTiK automatically decides to run in parallel when the selected solver and license permit it, and when adequate hardware is detected.  
– The environment variable SOF_NUM_THREADS or the command CTRL CORE NN can override the number of threads.  
– Specifying CTRL SOLV 1 or 3 will lock the run into serial mode, since those solvers do not offer parallel execution.

Usage example:  
– To use the default sparse LDL solver (serial):  
  CTRL SOLV 3  
– For a parallel Pardiso solve (with HISOLV):  
  CTRL SOLV 4  

In practice, the “Sparse LDL” solver (code 3) is the standard choice for most analyses. Users who need large-scale or very sparse systems may opt for the parallel Pardiso solver (code 4) or the iterative solver (code 2), remembering to secure a HISOLV license for both serial and parallel executions.

 3.4.1 CORE Parallel computation control
 SOFiSTiK supports parallel computing for selected equation solvers. Additionally, some pro- grams offer parallel element processing capabilities – independent of the chosen equation solver (CTRL SOLV).
 By default parallel computing is triggered automatically where it is feasible.
 Parallel computing requires corresponding hardware and operation system support. In addi- tion, availability of an adequate SOFiSTiK license is obligatory.
 Hint
 Parallel computing requires availability of a HISOLV license (ISOL granule).

Additionally, some pro- grams offer parallel element processing capabilities – independent of the chosen equation solver (CTRL SOLV).. By default parallel computing is triggered automatically where it is feasible.. Parallel computing requires corresponding hardware and operation system support. In addi- tion, availability of an adequate SOFiSTiK license is obligatory.. Hint. Parallel computing requires availability of a HISOLV license (ISOL granule)..
 If parallel computing is active, the number of adopted threads is determined as follows (listed with increasing priority):
 a) The software retrieves the information about the number of available physical processor cores on the system. This number defines the default number of threads that are used when a parallel computation is activated.
 b) This default can be modified via the environment variable SOF_NUM_THREADS, which is also available as sofistik.def parameter.
 c) Finally, an explicit statement CTRL CORE NN (or as relative input CTRL CORE NN[%]) temporarily assigns the number of available threads for the respective run.
 Hint
 Neither option b) nor option c) state an explicit parallel computation request. The deci- sion if a parallel computation is triggered, depends on the actual analysis option (parallel processing must be supported for the specific task) and the availability of an adequate license. Parallel computing can be suppressed by explitly setting the number of available threads to 1 (or 0).

Below is a structured, detailed description of the “CRAC” table and its fields. This record governs crack-width checks in reinforced concrete designs, interfacing with other records (CTRL, MAT, GRP, ELEM, NODE) to select between simple tabular checks and precise calculations.

1. Purpose of the CRAC Record  
   • Defines parameters and options for crack-width analysis in slabs, walls or silos.  
   • Works in tandem with control record CTRL, material data MAT, and element/group/node assignments (GRP, ELEM, NODE).  
   • Offers two main modes:  
     – Simple tabular check (via field TAB)  
     – Precise calculation (via fields PARA, BET1…K1)

2. Key Fields and Their Meanings  
   • XMIN  
     – “Minimum thickness of compressive zone.”  
     – Only valid for slab systems (not for Baumann detailing or multi-layer reinforcement).  
   • WK  
     – Computed crack width (primary result of calculation).  
   • TAB  
     – Switch to tabular crack-width check.  
     – Cross-references environmental class (DDES) and table lookups via GRP/ELEM/NODE.  
     – Setting WK=TAB forces this mode.  
   • PARA  
     – Activates precise crack calculation (per DAfStb-Heft 400 or EN 1992-1-1).  
     – Overrides concrete tensile stress BETZ in MAT (automatically set to zero in precise mode).  
   • BOND  
     – Bond quality indicator of reinforcement surface:  
         • RIB – Ribbed  
         • PROF – Profiled  
         • PLAI – Plain/smooth  
   • BET1  
     – β₁ coefficient (bond factor) used in crack formula for WK.  
     – Defaults: RIB=1.0, PROF=0.75, PLAI=0.5  
   • SILO  
     – Special option for silos: sr,max = 2·c + (1/(2·1.8))·d/ρo,p,eff  
     – Any numerical override is permitted.  
   • BET2  
     – Load-duration factor:  
         • SHOR (short‐term) ⇒ BET2=1.0 (or kₜ=0.6 per EN1992-1-1)  
         • STAT (long-term) ⇒ BET2=0.5 (or kₜ=0.4)  
   • WKB  
     – Computed crack width on the lower side (if different from WK).  
   • Units & Defaults  
     – Inputs in millimetres [mm].  
     – Default WK, WKB = 0. [mm]  
     – Default XMIN, AIMA unspecified unless overridden.

3. Simple Tabular vs Precise Calculation  
   a) Simple Tabular Check  
      – Controlled by DDES (exposure class) + WK=TAB.  
      – Can also be driven by a preset crack width in PARA or records GRP/ELEM/NODE.  
      – PARA-SSU allows user to override steel stress used in table lookup.  
      – If no steel stress is defined, design uses table diameters only.  
   b) Precise Crack-Width Check  
      – Activated by providing PARA or a numeric WK in CRAC.  
      – Ignores MAT.BETZ (set to zero).  
      – Requires parameters WK…K1 for full formula.

4. Country-Specific & Special Options  
   • CRAC CODE – Switch to another EN-country’s national annex.  
   • Special option “–8” for Denmark (2023-3).  
   • AIMA – Effective depth adjustments:  
       – Positive value (e.g. AIMA 140 [mm]) defines a max lever arm.  
       – AIMA 999 sets aimax = “outer to innermost reinforcement distance +0.5·Φᵢ,max + c_inside.”  
       – hc_eff = MIN{2.5·(h–d), h/2, MAX[(h–x)/3; aimax +0.5·Φᵢ,max + c_outside]}.  
       – Negative AIMA (–10): hc_eff unchanged, but steel stress taken from tension‐force center.  
       – AIMA –999: allows hc_eff increase as above.  
   • Warning: Negative AIMA yields significantly lower crack widths than positive or no AIMA.

By populating and combining these fields appropriately, the CRAC record flexibly supports both quick checks and detailed crack-width verifications in compliance with EN 1992-1-1 and various national annexes.

content:
The snippet you provided is part of the CRAC (crack-width) input table in a concrete‐design or crack‐analysis module.  The table has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and defines three user-selectable parameters (SAND, AIMA and CODE) that control how crack widths are computed.  Below is a detailed breakdown.

1) Item: SAND  
   – Description: “Sandwich model” interaction of two orthogonal reinforcement directions, per prEN 1992-1-1_202x.  It governs whether and how strains from one direction (esmx–ecmx, esmy–ecmy) are added to the other, and whether a transition region is enforced.  
     • 0: No addition of cross-strains (this was the pre-2023-6 default behavior).  
     • 1: Add cross-strains except when the two moments (ml and mll) differ by less than 5 % (e.g. midspan in a four-sided supported slab).  Transition region is 5 %–20 %.  
     • 2: Same as 1, but with a tighter transition region of 2.5 %–7.5 % (resulting in abrupt “jumps” in midspan).  
     • 11: As 1, plus the absolute strain component |e2| per commentary clause G.26.  
     • 12: As 2, plus |e2| per G.26.  
     • –1: As 0, but remove the crack‐width limit by applying a 0.9 factor.  (EN 1992-1-1 clause 7.15 often overly reduces sr,max, so here at least 90 % of the unconstrained crack width is used.)  On SAND>0, the strains are added and the 0.9 factor is not enforced.  
   – Unit: — (dimensionless selector)  
   – Default: 0  
   – Notes: A sample input file “a1_single_span_girder.dat” shows SAND usage in a one-span girder with 90°/45° bars.

2) Item: AIMA  
   – Description: Option to override or compute the effective concrete height hc-eff for crack calculations.  You can supply:  
     • A positive value in [mm] (e.g. AIMA 140) to set aimax = AIMA.  
     • 999 to trigger “automatic” aimax = (outer cover to innermost bar) + 0.5·Φi,max + c-inside, where c-inside equals the outer cover.  
     • A negative value (e.g. –10 or –999): –10 leaves hc-eff unchanged but uses a sandwich-model stress level taken from the tension‐force centroid; –999 may also increase hc-eff.  Negative AIMA tends to yield significantly lower crack widths.  
   – Formula used (when automatic):  
     hc-eff = MIN { 2.5·(h–d) ; h/2 ; MAX [ (h–x)/3 ; aimax + 0.5·Φi,max + c-outside ] }  
   – Unit: mm  
   – Default: none (user must supply if special behavior is needed)

3) Item: CODE  
   – Description: Choose which national annex or code version to use when computing crack widths under EN 1992-1-1.  Mapped integers are:  
     1 = Original (no annex)  
     2 = German NA  
     3 = British Standard (BS 8110 style)  
     4 = Italy  
     7 = Austria  
     8 = Denmark  
     9 = Netherlands  
     10 = Norway  
     11 = France  
     12 = Belgium  
     13 = Sweden  
     Special: “–8” selects the Denmark 2023-3 update.  
   – Unit: LIT (literature code selector)  
   – Default: none (if omitted, the software uses its internal default, typically the Original EN)

How these feed into the overall CRAC calculation:  
• SAND adjusts how biaxial bending strains interact in the crack‐width formula.  
• AIMA fine-tunes the lever arm or effective depth used in stress‐based crack control.  
• CODE ensures the correct national coefficients and limit states from the selected annex are applied.

content:
The table defines four key parameters that control the calculation of minimum and robustness reinforcement in a reinforced‐concrete section according to EN 1992-1-1 and associated national parameters. These inputs are read by the BEMESS module (or in the design parameter dialog) and govern how cracking moments, minimum steel areas and ductility checks are performed.

1. FFCT  
   ­ Description: “Factor for effective tensile strength”  
   ­ Role: Multiplies the mean tensile concrete strength fctm to obtain the effective tensile strength fct,e used in crack‐moment calculations. According to EN 1992-1-1 clause 7.3.2, fct,e = FFCT · fctm. A minimum of 3.0 N/mm² is enforced for lightweight concretes when FFCT = 1.0.  
   ­ Default: 1.0 (commonly used for bending‐constrained members; yields fct,e = fctm)  
   ­ Notes: If no FFCT is specified, the code assumes FFCT = 1.0. For members subject to restrained shrinkage or thermal effects, a lower factor (e.g. 0.5) may be chosen to reflect earlier cracking.

2. KC  
   ­ Description: “Coefficient for stress distribution during first cracking”  
   ­ Role: Accounts for the three‐dimensional stress state and axial force effects on the moment at first crack (Mcr). KC modifies the stress block used in cracking‐moment expressions.  
   ­ Default: 0.4 (typical for bending‐constrained condition without axial load)  
   ­ Notes: If KC is omitted, it is automatically derived from the axial load interaction in a 3D analysis. A value of 1.0 is often used for members under centric constraint (e.g. pure shrinkage restraint without bending).

3. K  
   ­ Description: “External constraint coefficient”  
   ­ Role: Captures the stiffening effect of support or settlement restraints on cracking and minimum reinforcement. It adjusts the calculated crack moment and thus the steel area required.  
   ­ Default: 1.0 (for bending‐constrained members or column‐settlement restraints)  
   ­ Notes: In German national practice (DIN-NA), a depth‐dependent K may be specified per Figure 7.1d of EN 1992-1-1. Where tendon reinforcement is present, its contribution is omitted; instead, the crack moment feeds directly into the normal reinforcement check.

4. ROBU  
   ­ Description: “Robustness reinforcement”  
   ­ Role: Provides ductility and continuity under accidental or extreme loadcases. When set, a dedicated check per clause 9.2.1.1 of EN 1992 ensures that a minimum steel area is present to prevent brittle failure.  
   ­ Default: none (must be explicitly input to activate the robustness check)  
   ­ Notes:  
     • If you specify “MREI ROBU FCTM,” the robustness check uses fctm; specifying “MREI ROBU = 2.50” replaces fctm with 2.50 N/mm².  
     • The robustness bars are always placed at the bottom fiber; top reinforcement is only added if tensile stresses occur in permanent loads. You must define a near‐constant load case (e.g. FACT 0.001) for that check.  
     • German practice uses a fixed lever arm kz = 0.9 and the yield strength fyk from the Nationally Determined Parameters (NDP).

Additional Remarks  
- Crack‐width limits (clause 7.3.3) and explicit width inputs (clause 7.3.4) are handled via the CRAK record or the crack‐control dialog. If you choose tabulated crack width control (CRAK WK TAB), you must still supply WKU and SIGU in GRP so that minimum reinforcement and stress limits are enforced without direct table lookup.  
- The table defaults assume a standard bending‐constrained beam without axial load. For heavily restrained members (thermal, shrinkage, or early‐age effects), both KC and FFCT may be reduced to reflect lower effective tensile resistance.  
- You cannot assign different MREI settings to multiple group IDs within a single run. To vary parameters across member groups, launch multiple BEMESS runs and filter by GRP selections.

By carefully setting these four parameters, the software will automatically compute the crack moment, derive the necessary minimum steel area (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.2), and—if requested—check for robustness reinforcement in accordance with EN 1992-1-1 clause 9.2.1.1.

MREI
 The minimum reinforcement according to EN 1992-1-1 7.3.2 is defined with the record MREI FFCT, KC and K. In Germany the increase of hc,ef acc. figure 7.1d is taken into account. A tendon reinforcement is not taken into account, the MREI crack moment is calculated into a necessary normal reinforcement.
 The factor of the effective tensile strength results as follows:
 ƒct,eƒƒ = FFCT · ƒctm
 Minimum 3.0 N/mm2 (leightweight concrete) are used for FFCT = 1.0.
 Without an input for KC the coefficient is determined from the axial force for three-dimensional systems. Reasonable inputs are:
 MREI FFCT 1.0 KC 0.4 K 1.0 for bending constraint MREI FFCT 0.5 KC 1.0 for centric constraint from hydration heat
 The item K is calculated in dependence of the depth. For external constraint (column settlement or bending constraint) it should be input with k=1.0.
 The determination of the minimum reinforcement requires an input of the crack width WKU and WKL in record GRP respectively in the design parameter dialog! For a parallel explicit crack width input in CRAK WK (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.4), this is used also for the minimum rein- forcement. If the limitation of the crack width according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3) is desired simultaneouslywith CRAK WK TAB, WKU and SIGU can be input in record GRP (or the design parameter dialog)! Then WKU is used for the minimum reinforcement and SIGA is used for the limitation of the crack width without a direct calculation according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3).
 Example: see bemess6_design.dat

If the limitation of the crack width according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3) is desired simultaneouslywith CRAK WK TAB, WKU and SIGU can be input in record GRP (or the design parameter dialog)! Then WKU is used for the minimum reinforcement and SIGA is used for the limitation of the crack width without a direct calculation according to tables (EN 1992-1-1 7.3.3).. Example: see bemess6_design.dat.
 ROBU: the check of a minimum reinforcement for the safety of a ductile member behaviour (ro- bustness reinforcement) occurs with an input for ROBU. With MREI ROBU FCTM the check is performed with the concrete tensile strength fctm, with MREI it is performed with fctk. However, a different tensile strength may be input with ROBU, e.g. MREI ROBU=2.50 (N/mm2).
 The minimum reinforcement is then calculated according EN 1992 9.2.1.1(1) equation (9.1N). Only for german design codes a crack moment is calculated and designed with a fixed lever arm value kz=0.9 and the steel yield strength fyk according (NDP) 9.2.1.1 (1). The robutsness reinforcement is always applied at the bottom of a section. On top only in case of appearing tensile stresses. To recognize this it is necessary to define a permanent loadcase for this check may be with a little factor only, e.g. LC (2721 2726 1) FACT 0.001. Usually the robustness reinforcement on the top has to be placed over a length of up to a quarter of the span length.
 Varying MREI input for different groups is not possible in one run, but you can make multiple PROG BEMESS runs with different GRP selection.

The table shown is a configuration fragment for the “SHFT” (shift-rule) module of a reinforced‐concrete design program. In this module, when SHFT is set to 1, an additional axial (normal) force is assumed, which produces a shift in the bending‐reinforcement requirement and leads, in the regions close to supports, to a reduction in design shear force by up to 0.5·z·cot θ. To prevent an excessive increase in longitudinal reinforcement at midspan, the minimum compression‐strut angle θ is reduced according to a default control ratio (CTRL COTT = 7/4). A full example input file is provided in the German data file versatz.dat.

Below is a detailed breakdown of the table’s structure and meaning:

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – The name of the parameter or keyword to be specified in the input deck.  
   • Description  
     – A concise explanation of what the parameter controls, including the meaning of each valid code or numeric value.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical unit or notation in which the parameter is expressed. If the entry is “–”, it indicates a dimensionless code or an option list rather than a numerical quantity with units.  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed by the program if the user does not explicitly specify this parameter.

2. Table Row  
   Item: TYPE  
   – This keyword activates or deactivates the consideration of the offset (“shift”) rule in the shear‐reinforcement design.  

   Description:  
     • 0 – “does not consider”  
       When TYPE = 0, the additional normal force and the resulting shift of bending‐reinforcement/shear‐force diagrams are ignored. Shear design is performed without the EC 2 shift rule.  
     • 1 – “Consideration according to EC 2 method”  
       When TYPE = 1, the program applies Eurocode 2’s provisions for including an axial load effect that shifts the shear‐force diagram. In supported spans, this reduces the design shear force up to 0.5 · z · cot θ, and midspan uses a modified minimum compression‐strut angle to avoid over‐reinforcement.

   Unit: –  
     Since TYPE is a discrete option (0 or 1), no physical unit is associated.

   Default: 0  
     If the user omits a TYPE entry, the module assumes TYPE = 0, i.e. no shift‐rule offset is applied.

3. Contextual Notes  
   – The “shift‐rule” adjustment originates from EC 2 Clause 6.2.3 or a national annex.  
   – When activated, it modifies internal force envelopes before computing the required shear reinforcement, especially near supports.  
   – The default compression‐strut angle control (CTRL COTT = 7/4) reduces θ by a factor of 7/4 to limit extra reinforcement at midspan.

This precise description ensures that a retrieval‐augmented generation system can match user queries about “SHFT 1 behavior,” “shear reduction near supports,” or “EC 2 shift rule,” associating them with the TYPE parameter, permissible values, defaults, and related design consequences.

content:
This table defines the key NSTR input items that control stress‐range checks and reinforcement adjustments in a BEMESS slab design. Each row lists an Item code, its functional Description, the expected input Unit, and its Default setting. In use, these parameters integrate with commands such as ECHO, CTRL BMOD SUPE or MAXIMA‐generated load-case sets to perform fatigue and serviceability checks in accordance with EN 1992-1-1 and related standards.

1. SIGS  
   – Description: Specifies the stress range (Δσ) of longitudinal (tensile) reinforcement across all relevant load cases. If the computed range exceeds the specified value, BEMESS will automatically increase steel area to satisfy the requirement.  
   – Special note: “NSTR SIGS 999” suppresses any reinforcement increase and only reports the computed stress range.  
   – Unit: N/mm²  
   – Default: none (user must supply a value when a range check is desired)

2. SIGT  
   – Description: Defines the stress range required for shear (link) reinforcement. By default it is set to 0.454×SIGS, reflecting the reduced diameter‐related fatigue capacity in punching‐shear links. If the range is exceeded, transverse steel is increased, but punching reinforcement is never amended by SIGT. Special negative inputs (e.g. SIGT = –120) force a stress‐range calculation in every element, enabling comparison against a fixed minimum reinforcement.  
   – Unit: N/mm²  
   – Default: 0.454 × SIGS

3. SIGP  
   – Description: Sets the fatigue stress range for prestressing steel. BEMESS will attempt to meet this range by adding longitudinal non‐prestressed reinforcement; if it cannot, a warning is issued.  
   – Unit: N/mm²  
   – Default: none

4. CHKC  
   – Description: Maximum allowable compressive stress in concrete. Three operating modes:  
     • 0.45 → check against 0.45·fck,l  
     • 0 → no control performed  
     • >1.5 → interpret input directly as N/mm²  
     In “layer design” (default NSTR), reinforcement is increased if necessary. Under CTRL LAY 0 checks only (no increase); on CTRL LAY 1 a pure check (no increase) can be forced with a negative input (e.g. NSTR CHKC –0.45).  
   – Unit: n/a or N/mm²  
   – Default: 0

5. CHKR  
   – Description: Maximum steel stress control. Modes analogous to CHKC:  
     • 0.8 → limit to 0.8·fyk  
     • 0 → no control  
     • >1.5 → interpret directly in N/mm²  
     Exceeding the limit triggers automatic reinforcement increase.  
   – Unit: n/a or N/mm²  
   – Default: 0

6. DECO  
   – Description: Sets the check distance for decompression strain according to EN 1992-1-1 § 7.3.1. The default (100 mm) is read from the configuration file; it may be overridden (e.g. “NSTR DECO 120[mm]”) without the h/10 limit. During any NSTR stress check the program computes the maximum decompression strain in tendon directions over this distance above/below the duct and stores results for graphical output in WinGRAF.  
   – Unit: mm  
   – Default: none (use the .ini default)

Usage Context  
• Typically, an ultimate‐limit‐state design is run first.  
• A subsequent serviceability/fatigue check is invoked via CTRL BMOD SUPE in tandem with pre-generated MAXIMA load cases.  
• After the first stress‐range check, any reinforcement increases feed into a follow-up calculation, reducing computed stress ranges (“control of reinforcement increase”).  
• SIGS, SIGT, SIGP drive fatigue capacity checks per EN 1991-1-1 and DIN-FB 102.  
• CHKC/CHKR enforce compressive/stress limits in concrete and steel respectively, with optional pure‐check modes.  
• DECO governs decompression verification around prestressing ducts.

The excerpt you provided is part of a larger input‐parameter table used to control fatigue and stress‐range checks in a concrete‐design module (often referred to as BEMESS or AQUA CONC). Below is a detailed description of its structure, the specific entries shown, and how they interact with other commands (ECHO, CTRL, MAT, LC) to perform reinforcement design and serviceability checks.

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns (implicit in the excerpt):  
     – Keyword: the input command or code (e.g. NSTR, FATC, G_SD)  
     – Parameter Name/Title: often repeats the keyword or gives a short label  
     – Description: what the parameter controls or how it is used  
     – Default/Value: default numerical setting if any (e.g. 1.00 for G_SD)  
     – Remarks/Cross‐References: notes on deprecated items, alternative syntax, related commands  

2. “See also” References  
   • ECHO: controls printing of intermediate stresses and lever arms  
   • CTRL: various switches (e.g. BMOD SUPE to trigger stress‐range reinforcement updates)  
   • MAT: material definitions (e.g. FFAT for concrete fatigue properties)  
   • LC: load cases (e.g. LC14 for concrete fatigue checks)  

3. Entry: FATC  
   • Keyword/Name: FATC (Fatigue Age of Concrete)  
   • Status: Deprecated (“No longer used”)  
   • Function: originally specified the concrete age at which fatigue properties were taken  
   • Replacement: rather define fcd‐fat in the material card (AQUA CONC FFAT)  
   • Alternative syntax: via AQUA CTRL REST (restart feature)  

4. Entry: G_SD  
   • Keyword/Name: gamma-sd (partial safety factor for fatigue)  
   • Context: Applied to LC14 fatigue check per EN 1992-2 (clause 6.4.5)  
   • Default Value: 1.00  
   • Note: the standard uses symbol γEd,fat rather than γSd.  

5. Entry: NSTR  
   • Keyword/Name: NSTR (stress‐range check for normal reinforcement)  
   • Purpose: checks reinforcement stress ranges Δσ = σmax–σmin over a set of service load cases  
   • Required Inputs:  
     – SIGS: flexural stress range  
     – SIGT: shear‐link stress range  
     – CHKR: check‐switch for R‐value, decompression etc.  
     – LS_U, LS_L, LS_V: upper/lower stress limits for fatigue steel checks  
     – FAKU, FAKL, FAKV: safety factors for steel fatigue  
   • Workflow:  
     1. Perform a normal ultimate‐limit‐state design (“BEMESS”).  
     2. Use CTRL BMOD SUPE to invoke stress‐range check: the program re‐reads saved reinforcement areas and recomputes stresses for each load case (with and without live loads generated in advance by MAXIMA).  
     3. Compute min/max stresses, determine Δσ and, if Δσ exceeds allowable, automatically increase reinforcement to satisfy the fatigue requirement.  
     4. Printing:  
        – ECHO NSTR FULL: prints elements needing no increase  
        – ECHO SIGS NSTR: prints individual load‐case stresses and updated lever arms  
   • Special Features:  
     – Re‐running BEMESS under CTRL BMOD SUPE yields smaller Δσ because it uses the already‐increased reinforcement from the previous run (iterative control).  
     – SIGT negative input (e.g. SIGT –120) forces a shear‐range check everywhere, useful to verify minimum shear links against actual requirements.  
     – Punching checks do not increase shear reinforcement; link‐stress ranges for graphic output are stored for WinGRAF.  

6. Decompression Check (DECO)  
   • Purpose: verify concrete isn’t cracked in post‐tensioned elements (EN 1992-1-1 §7.3.1)  
   • Default Check Distance: 100 mm (from .ini file) or h/10  
   • Override: NSTR DECO 120[mm] to set custom check distance  
   • Output: maximum decompression strain above/below duct stored for WinGRAF  

7. Fatigue Check (Concrete and Steel)  
   • Concrete: controlled via LC14 (DIN-FB 102‐4.188 or EN 1991-1-1) using σc,perm from a permanent load case; the program computes λc0 and performs the check.  
   • Steel: triggered when any of LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, FAKU, FAKL or FAKV are input. According to 4.3.7.5 DIN-FB 102/EN 1991-1-1:  
     SGS = ΔσRsk(N*)  
   • Examples: prestressed_slab.dat or csm32_slab_design.dat illustrate typical data files.  

By understanding these three key table entries (FATC, G_SD, NSTR) and their interplay with ECHO, CTRL, MAT, and LC commands, you can configure and automate both ultimate‐limit and serviceability (fatigue, decompression, shear‐link stress) checks within the concrete‐design software.

The table is a parameter‐definition catalog for fatigue and serviceability checks (chiefly in prestressed‐slab design) and is organized into four columns – “Item,” “Description,” “Unit” and “Default” – and several logical groups of related inputs. Below is a breakdown of its structure and semantics:

1. Column‐Headings  
   • Item: the keyword used in input decks (e.g. NSTR, CTRL) or in the program’s .dat files.  
   • Description: a concise explanation of what the parameter controls or how it is to be interpreted.  Often includes normative references (DIN‐FB 102, EN 1992-1-1, EN 1992-2) or cross-references to other inputs (e.g. LC14, MAXIMA).  
   • Unit: the physical unit or a dash “–” for dimensionless quantities.  
   • Default: the value assumed when the item is omitted.

2. Group 1 – Fatigue “λ” Correction Coefficients  
   All four parameters are dimensionless correction factors λs from DIN-FB 102 Annex A.106.2 or EN 1992-2 NN.2.1/3.1:  
   • LS_U – upper reinforcement correction λS for fatigue check.  
   • LS_L – lower reinforcement correction λS.  
   • LS_V – shear (link) reinforcement correction λS.  
   • LS_P – prestressing steel correction λS.  
   • LC14 – multiplies concrete fatigue product λc1⋅λc2⋅λc3⋅λc4; λc0 is auto-computed.  
       – Without any LC14 entry, the concrete fatigue check falls back to EN 1992-1-1 cl. 6.8.7 (6.77) using a permanent loadcase and NSTR SIGS with 100% permanent factor (e.g. NSTR SIGS 999 LS_U 1 1).  
       – LC14 = 0 disables concrete fatigue check altogether.  
       – With LC14 specified, the check is done with σ_c,perm in accordance with EN 1992-2 NN.3.2 (NN.112).  
   Unit: –  Default: “–” for LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, LS_P, LC14.

3. Group 2 – Axle‐Load Increase Factors (Load Model 3)  
   These four dimensionless factors scale the fatigue spectrum for the relevant reinforcement under traffic loading:  
   • FACU – upper reinforcement factor (default 1.0)  
   • FACL – lower reinforcement factor (default 1.0)  
   • FACV – shear reinforcement factor (default 1.0)  
   • FACP – prestressing steel factor (default 1.0)  
   Unit: –  Default: 1.0

4. Group 3 – Tendon Direction Control  
   • LOCP – “Local directions of tendons on CTRL LAY 0.”  
       – Only valid on control layer 0 where tendons are modeled exactly.  
       – LOCP = 0: stress‐range uses the maximum of main and transverse reinforcement ranges (default).  
       – LOCP = 1: stress‐range uses only the main reinforcement range.  
       – LOCP = 2: stress‐range uses only the transverse reinforcement range.  
   Unit: –  Default: “–”

5. Group 4 – Fatigue Safety Factor for Concrete (γ_sd)  
   • G_SD – the partial safety factor γ_sd, applied to fatigue checks controlled by LC14 in EN 1992-2 (NN.112).  
       – In the EN text it is often written as γ-Ed,fat.  
       – Default 1.00.  
   Unit: –  Default: 1.00

Cross‐References and Notes  
– NSTR SIGS, SIGT, CHKR, LS_U/L/V, FAKU/FAKL/FAKV feed into a two‐step process: a ULS design first, then serviceability stress‐range checks. Pre-computed load‐case sets (with/without live loads) must be generated (e.g. via MAXIMA) to calculate Δσ across all load cases. Only 100 % permanent factor is allowed for fatigue range checks.  
– SIGT (shear link stress‐range) uses the square‐root of the strut inclination per EN 1992-1-1 6.8.2(3). Alternating shear directions trigger decompression checks.  
– A negative SIGT input forces a shear‐range check everywhere, useful to confirm that any computed shear is below the minimum provided reinforcement. Punching shear is not amended by SIGT.  
– DECO distances for decompression (default 100 mm) are drawn from the .ini file or can be overridden via e.g. NSTR DECO 120 (mm).  
– For slab examples see prestressed_slab.dat or csm32_slab_design.dat in CSM DESI.  
– Steel fatigue (if LS_U/L/V or FAK… inputs present) follows SGS = ΔσR_sk(N*) per DIN-FB 102 4.3.7.5 or EN 1991-1-1.

 ment stress in computed. The minimum and maximum value of all load cases then give the stress range. To avoid misunderstanding, only an input of 100 % permanent factor (LC...PERC used for other checks) is allowed using NSTR. The set of load cases with/without live load part has to be produced with MAXIMA in advance. If the stress range is to large, the reinforcement is increased correspondingly.
 Also the elements that do not require any reinforcement increase are printed with ECHO NSTR FULL. ECHO SIGS NSTR produces the stresses of the single load cases as well as the used updated lever arms. If a further calculation is started with CTRL BMOD SUPE after a BEMESS calculation with a stress range check, smaller stress range are determined in this second calculation, because the reinforcement increased in the previous calculation is used for the stress determination (= control of the reinforcement increase).
 At first a design in the ultimate limit state should be performed usually. Then an separate BEMESS stress range check occurs with CTRL BMOD SUPE for possible other serviceability load cases from the program MAXIMA.

If a further calculation is started with CTRL BMOD SUPE after a BEMESS calculation with a stress range check, smaller stress range are determined in this second calculation, because the reinforcement increased in the previous calculation is used for the stress determination (= control of the reinforcement increase).. At first a design in the ultimate limit state should be performed usually. Then an separate BEMESS stress range check occurs with CTRL BMOD SUPE for possible other serviceability load cases from the program MAXIMA..
 For the shear link stress range (SIGT) the square route of the strut inclination is used according to EN 1992-1-1 6.8.2(3) (6.65). It is also checked whether the direction of the shear force alternates in the different load cases, because it is an indication for decompression: E.g. if LC 1 has Vx=+100 and LC 2 has Vx=-100, then both load cases have the same shear stress but the shear force changes through zero from LC 1 to LC 2!
 With spezial input of a negative SIGT e.g. -120 always a stress range in shear reinforcement is calculated. This automatically causes shear reinforcement in every element. With this feature you can check if the then necessary shear reinforcement is smaller than an anyway placed minimum shear reinforcement (that you cannot input up to now).
 A stress range is not considered for the punching check! Over punching nodes no shear rein- forcement will be increased due to SIGT! For graphical checks, the link stress range computed from the real slab shear force is calculated and stored for WinGRAF.
 DECO: for the decompression check according EN 1992-1-1 7.3.1 the check distance (default 100mm) is taken from the .ini file and thus adjusted to the design code. Via input e.g. NSTR DECO 120[mm] the check distance can be changed individually (without h/10 limitation). In every stress check with NSTR (also pure input NSTR) the maximum decompression strain in the direction of tendons in the check distance above and below the duct surface are calculated and stored for WINGRAF.
 Example prestressed_slab.dat or in CSM DESI: csm32_slab_design.dat
 Fatigue check
 The fatigue check for concrete according to DIN-FB 102-(4.188) or EN-1991-1-1 is con- trolled via LC14. With additional input to LC14 and a permanent loadcase the check is done with sigma_c,perm. λc0 is calculated by the Programm. The simple check is then done in addition for comparison reasons.

 A fatigue check for steel is realized, if at least an input for LS_U, LS_L, LS_V, FAKU, FAKL or FAKV is done. Here SIGS means according to 4.3.7.5 DIN-FB 102 or EN-1991-1-1:
 SGS = ΔσRsk(N∗)
