The table under review defines the full set of input parameters required by the RAG‐based reinforced‐concrete module. Every row is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—so that downstream processes can pick up both the semantic meaning of each variable and a sensible fallback value if the user does not explicitly supply one.

1. Material Class Definitions  
   • CONC (–) – Specifies which concrete class is to be used. Must be chosen from the project’s AQUA or SSD databases.  
   • STEE (–) – Specifies which reinforcing‐steel class is to be used, likewise sourced from AQUA/SSD.  

2. Shear‐Design Control Parameters  
   • K (LIT; default K1S) – Governs how transverse (shear) reinforcement is checked:  
      – “K1” indicates that span reinforcement is continuous (>50% coverage).  
      – “K1S” indicates stepped or segmented span reinforcement.  
   • MINC (–; default 0.0) – Sets the minimum transverse reinforcement ratio as a fraction of the main (longitudinal) reinforcement. In effect, Ax,transverse ≥ MINC·Ax,main.  
   • MSTA (LIT; default YES) – Characterizes the nature of the loading:  
      – “YES”: primarily stationary (static) loading,  
      – “NO”: includes significant dynamic or variable components.  
      This flag also activates the shear‐reduction algorithm in zone 3 (in accordance with DIN 1045-1988).  

3. Minimum Pressed‐Section Reinforcement (AM3)  
   • AM3 (%; default ‘*’) – The minimum ratio of reinforcement in compressed (pressed) sections, expressed as a percentage of the statically required steel area.  
     Default values depend on the code selected (see also CTRL WALL):  
       – 0.8% for DIN 1045-1988  
       – 0.0% for DIN 1045-1, EN 1992, BS, ACI, ÖNORM  

4. Fundamental Material Strengths  
   • FC (MPa; default ‘*’) – Effective design strength of concrete. Can be adjusted up to ±30% from database default.  
   • FY (MPa; default ‘*’) – Steel yield limit. Also adjustable up to ±30%.  
   • FYS (MPa; default ‘*’) – Yield limit for shear and punching‐shear reinforcement.  

5. Material‐Safety (Partial‐Safety) Factors  
   • SC1 (–; default ‘*’) – Concrete safety factor in bending.  
   • SC2 (–; default ‘*’) – Concrete safety factor in compression members.  
   • SS1 (–; default ‘*’) – Steel safety factor for tension and bending.  
   • SS2 (–; default ‘*’) – Steel safety factor for compression reinforcement.  

6. Optional Strain Limits (not shown in the main four-column extract but referred to in adjacent text)  
   • C1 (‰; default ‘*’) – Maximum allowable concrete compression strain, used only in layered‐section designs.  
   • S2 (‰; default ‘*’) – Maximum allowable steel tensile strain in reinforcement.  

Annotations:  
– A dash (–) in the Default column indicates “no default” (mandatory user input).  
– An asterisk (*) means “default varies with CTRL REIN/ULTI and the design code in force.”  
– Units “LIT” denote literal (string) inputs.  

See also: CTRL, CRAC, NSTR for related control flags and material‐database linkage.

The input “Defaults of the safeties” table is a concise lookup of the partial‐safety factors applied to concrete and steel in ultimate‐ and reinforcement‐design checks, keyed by the selected design code.  It feeds directly into the module’s MAT and SS2 parameters (where SS2 is the steel compression‐reinforcement safety factor), and its values are used unless the user overrides them from the material‐property database (e.g. to change concrete strength fʹc, steel yield fʹy or the safety factors themselves).  MSTA, separately, controls shear‐stress reduction in shear zone 3 per DIN 1045‐1988, but does not affect this table of partial‐safety factors.

Table structure  
• Columns  
  – SC1  : partial safety factor γ₁ for concrete resistance (compression, service/ultimate)  
  – SC2  : partial safety factor γ₂ for concrete (secondary checks or specific limit states)  
  – SS1  : partial safety factor γ₁ for reinforcement tensile strength  
  – SS2  : partial safety factor γ₂ for reinforcement compressive strength  

• Rows (Design Codes & Application States)  
1. DIN 1045-1 (REIN+ULTI)  
   • Both reinforcement‐limit (REIN) and ultimate‐limit (ULTI) checks use:  
     SC1 = 1.50, SC2 = 1.50, SS1 = 1.15, SS2 = 1.15  

2. DIN 1045-1988 (REIN)  
   • Older German standard—in reinforcement‐state only—uses more conservative values:  
     SC1 = 1.75, SC2 = 2.10, SS1 = 1.75, SS2 = 2.10  

3. DIN 1045-1988 (ULTI)  
   • For the ultimate‐limit checking branch of the same standard, all partial factors default to 1.00, effectively no additional safety beyond material strains and strengths.  

4. ÖNORM (REIN+ULTI)  
   • Austrian standard, same factor set for both limit‐state checks:  
     SC1 = 1.50, SC2 = 1.50, SS1 = 1.15, SS2 = 1.15  

5. EN 1992-1-1 (REIN+ULTI)  
   • Eurocode 2, identical to ÖNORM values in this table:  
     SC1 = 1.50, SC2 = 1.50, SS1 = 1.15, SS2 = 1.15  

6. British Standard (REIN+ULTI)  
   • UK code—again same γ for concrete, slightly lower for steel:  
     SC1 = 1.50, SC2 = 1.50, SS1 = 1.05, SS2 = 1.05  

7. American ACI (REIN+ULTI)  
   • ACI uses a pair of values, typically LSD/ULS or φ/unfactored basis, denoted here as X/Y:  
     SC1 = 1.0 / 0.9, SC2 = 1.0 / 0.65, SS1 = 1.0 / 0.9, SS2 = 1.0 / 0.65  

Key notes for interpretation  
• “REIN” rows apply when designing reinforcement at service or characteristic load combinations; “ULTI” rows apply to ultimate‐limit (strength) verifications.  
• In the code implementations, CTRL REIN/ULTI switches between the two sets.  
• The table’s default values can be overridden per‐material via the material database (for advanced codes or special steels/concretes).  
• C1 (maximum concrete compression strain, in ‰) and S2 (maximum reinforcement tensile strain, in ‰) are separate inputs—C1 is only used in layer design—so they do not appear here but must be provided if required by the chosen code.  
• Together with MAT (material selection), SS2 and MSTA settings, this table fully determines the safety factors used throughout bending, shear and axial checks in accordance with the selected standard.

The table shown defines the GEOM input record for positioning concrete-plate thickness and the various layers of orthogonal mesh reinforcement.  GEOM remains in effect until a new GEOM record appears and is used in a dedicated design run (not in a parameter-definition/PARA run) whenever any of H or HPRE is specified.  If the seven “HU…DDHB” entries (H, HA, DHA, HB, DHB, DDHA, DDHB) are provided, they override any values previously read from a PARA run or the SSD-design dialog.  Conversely, when HU-DDHB are omitted, the software will fall back on PARA values for that run.  Note that none of HA, DHA, HB, DHB, DDHA or DDHB affect disk‐type structures; for those, GEOM together with DIRE UPP and PARA DU/ASU/ASU2 is applied to one side and mirrored on the other, producing area reinforcements ASU and ASL (in WINGRAF only ASU is shown and must be duplicated).  

Column headings  
•  Item: parameter symbol in the GEOM record  
•  Description: what the parameter controls  
•  Unit: always millimetres (mm)  
•  Default: value assumed if the field is left blank  

Parameters  
1.  H  
 – Plate thickness  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: database value (marked “*”)  
 – Notes: cannot be mixed inside a PARA run; if specified, triggers a separate design run  

2.  HA  
 – Centre-to-edge distance of the upper main (support) reinforcement  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: 35  

3.  DHA  
 – Centre distance between the upper transverse (middle) bar and the main upper bar  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: 10  

4.  HB  
 – Centre-to-edge distance of the lower main (span) reinforcement  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: HA (i.e. same as upper main by default)  

5.  DHB  
 – Centre distance between the lower transverse (middle) and the lower main bar  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: DHA  

6.  DDHA  
 – Centre distance of the upper inner (secondary) reinforcement from the middle layer  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: DHA  

7.  DDHB  
 – Centre distance of the lower inner reinforcement from its middle layer  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: DHB  

8.  HPRE  
 – Limitation of the concrete compression-zone thickness; used to model hollow or double-deck plates via GEOM…HPRE  
 – Unit: [mm]  
 – Default: none (blank)  
 – Notes: cannot be combined inside a PARA run; when set, a shear check must still be performed separately as no shear‐design is carried out here  

Cross references  
•  DIRE: orthogonal two‐course mesh reinforcement directions  
•  THRE: skew (two‐ or three‐course) reinforcement definition  
•  MAT: material parameters (e.g. MINC) used in skew mesh  
•  PARA: default design parameters for spacing, bar areas (DU, ASU, ASU2)  

Usage notes  
•  GEOM’s eight parameters define the vertical layout of reinforcement layers in a single design invocation.  Changing any of H, HA…DDHB, or HPRE requires running a new design (separate from PARA).  
•  In disk or shell problems, HA/DHA/PARA DU/ASU/ASU2 apply symmetrically to both faces; output shows ASU/ASL, but only ASU is graphed.  
•  Use GEOM together with DIRE (or THRE) for final reinforcement design.

sections: 3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section

content:
The image is a schematic, labeled “Geometry of the reinforced concrete cross section (O = upper side, U = lower side),” showing a straight‐through section of a rectangular concrete member with its reinforcement layers and key dimension annotations. In a right‐hand legend the top three ticks and labels (from outside in) are HO, DHO and DDHO, indicating successive cover and bar‐location distances on the upper (O) side; the bottom three ticks are DDHU, DHU and HU, indicating the analogous distances on the lower (U) side. On the left the overall effective depth “D” is dimensioned between the centrelines of the outermost upper and lower reinforcement layers.

Main graphic elements, from top to bottom:

  1. Two nearly coincident horizontal heavy lines at the very top represent the uppermost concrete cover surface (top face) and the outermost upper reinforcement bar layer (support reinforcement).  
  2. Immediately beneath these lines—and separated by the small cover distances labeled HO, DHO and DDHO in the legend—there is a single row of small circular “dots,” each aligned horizontally, denoting the “main” or longitudinal bars of the upper mesh layer.  
  3. Below that row of dots, a single row of short, thick, slanted rectangles (approximately at a 45° angle) represents the transverse (or shear) reinforcement bars of the upper mesh.  
  4. At the mid‐height of the section, a pair of dashed‐line vertical boundaries (one on each side of the concrete body) enclose the reinforced region; between these dashed lines is the interior concrete (no reinforcement drawn), indicating the clear web or unreinforced core.  
  5. Beneath the center, the lower layer mirrors the upper but in reverse order: first a row of slanted rectangles (transverse bars), then a row of circular dots (longitudinal bars), and finally two heavy horizontal lines marking the lower‐most reinforcement bars and the lower concrete surface.  

Dimension call‐outs and labels:

  – On the right side, three upward‐pointing ticks with leader lines define: (1) DDHU (distance from the bottom face up to the first reinforcement layer), (2) DHU (next cover to the second layer), and (3) HU (the concrete cover thickness to the lower longitudinal reinforcement).  
  – The top right has the symmetric labeling for the upper side: HO (outer cover), DHO (first layer location), and DDHO (second layer offset).  
  – On the left side, a double‐arrow dimension labeled “D” spans from the horizontal centerline of the topmost reinforcement to that of the bottommost reinforcement, indicating the effective depth of the section.  

Styling and conventions:

  • All angles (for slanted bars) are drawn consistently at approximately 45°; the slanted bars are uniformly spaced along the length of the section.  
  • The dashed vertical lines are offset symmetrically from the outer concrete faces, suggesting an effective width or perhaps formwork limits.  
  • The figure is entirely black‐and‐white, using line weight variation (heavy lines for concrete faces and main bars, lighter lines for cover demarcations, dashed lines for boundaries) and simple geometric shapes (dots for round bars, slanted rectangles for stirrups or transverse bars) to distinguish element types.  

Overall, this diagram concisely captures a two‐layer orthogonal reinforcement layout in a rectangular concrete member, with clear annotation of cover distances, bar layer offsets, and effective section depth.

sections: 3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section

content:
The table shown is the formal parameter‐list for one of the main reinforcement‐orientation records (DIRE) in the SSD input deck.  It defines five scalar inputs—UPP, LOW, X, Y and Z—each of which controls how the two orthogonal steel mesh layers are laid out in a slab or shell element.  Below is a field-by-field breakdown suitable for populating a RAG vector store or for inclusion in a metadata catalog.

1.  Item: UPP  
    •  Meaning  
       – “Upper” main reinforcement angle. This is the orientation of the primary (support) mesh layer measured from the local x-axis.  In planar analyses the local x-axis coincides with the global x-axis; in 3D you may redefine the local axes via SOFIMSHA/SOFIMSHB.  
    •  Domain / Constraints  
       – Continuous real number, in degrees, constrained to the closed interval [0, 180].  
       – Positive angles rotate clockwise about the origin of the local coordinate system.  
    •  Unit  
       – degrees  
    •  Default  
       – 0 (i.e. parallel to the local x-axis if you do not explicitly supply UPP)

2.  Item: LOW  
    •  Meaning  
       – “Lower” main reinforcement angle. This sets the orientation of the secondary (span) layer of mesh, again measured from the local x-axis, and orthogonal to the corresponding transverse bars.  
    •  Domain / Constraints  
       – Continuous real number, in degrees, between 0 and 180.  
       – Clockwise is positive.  
    •  Unit  
       – degrees  
    •  Default  
       – 0

3.  Item: X  
    •  Meaning  
       – X‐coordinate of the centre point for a circular (radial/tangential) reinforcement pattern. When you choose UPP=0 or 90 deg (and LOW=0 or 90 deg) to invoke the “circular mesh” option, you must supply a geometric centre about which radial or tangential bars will be laid out.  
    •  Domain / Constraints  
       – Real number. Must be within the model’s coordinate range.  
       – If omitted when using circular‐mesh mode, the software cannot compute radial/tangential directions.  
    •  Unit  
       – meters ([m]_1001)  
    •  Default  
       – none (“–”)

4.  Item: Y  
    •  Meaning  
       – Y‐coordinate of the circular‐mesh center. Together with X and Z, it defines the point from which the direction vectors to each mesh element are drawn.  
    •  Domain / Constraints  
       – Real, within the finite‐element geometry’s extents.  
    •  Unit  
       – meters ([m]_1001)  
    •  Default  
       – none

5.  Item: Z  
    •  Meaning  
       – Z‐coordinate of the circular‐mesh centre, used only in three‐dimensional shell or plate analyses.  If Z = 0, the software defines the reference axis in the X–Y plane; nonzero Z locates the centre in space.  
    •  Domain / Constraints  
       – Real value; can be zero or nonzero depending on whether the circular mesh is truly 2D or a spatial pattern.  
    •  Unit  
       – meters ([m]_1001)  
    •  Default  
       – none

Additional Notes:  
– Once a DIRE record is read, these five parameters remain active for subsequent slabs or shells until another DIRE (or THRE) record is encountered.  
– If you omit both UPP and LOW, the prior PARA‐layer definitions for ASU, ASU2, etc., will still apply; but as soon as you supply UPP/LOW you override PARA for that run.  
– The special UPP=0/LOW=0 (or 90/90) combination invokes circular (radial/tangential) reinforcement, in which case X, Y, Z become mandatory.  
– All angles are relative to the element’s local coordinate system; in 3D that system can be re‐oriented via SOFIMSHA/SOFIMSHB records.

sections: 3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section

content:
The image is a schematic 2-D plot illustrating how two layers of orthogonal reinforcement (“DIRE”) are oriented with respect to a local Cartesian coordinate system. At the core of the figure sits the origin, from which two solid reference axes emanate:

  • A horizontal solid line extending to the right, terminating in an arrowhead, is labeled “X.”  
  • A vertical solid line extending downward, terminating in an arrowhead, is labeled “Y.”  

Superimposed on these axes are three dashed-and-dotted lines, each representing a distinct reinforcement direction:

  1. Main reinforcement  
     – Rendered as a long-dash, dot, dash sequence (— · — ·).  
     – Slants downwards to the left from the origin, forming an oblique angle relative to both X and Y.  
     – Annotated with the text “main reinforcement,” placed near its lower-left extension.  

  2. Transverse reinforcement  
     – Also a dash-dot style, but with a shallower angle.  
     – Slants slightly downward from left to right, roughly 10–15° below the horizontal X-axis.  
     – Marked “transverse reinforcement” to the right of the origin, along the line’s projection.  

  3. Upper-side and lower-side reinforcement (support vs. span)  
     – Two more dash-dot lines coincide at the origin and fan out:  
         • The “upper side” layer is shown as a dash-dot line leaning up and to the left (approximately 45° counter-clockwise from the vertical).  
         • The “lower side” layer is shown as a dash-dot line leaning down and to the left (approximately 45° clockwise from the vertical).  
     – A curved arrow between these two lines indicates the measured angle between upper- and lower-side orientations.  
     – The labels “upper side” and “lower side” are placed adjacent to the curved arrow to clarify which line corresponds to which layer.  

All dashed lines share the same stroke weight and pattern, emphasizing their equal status as reinforcement meshes. The solid axes contrast with the dash-dot lines to highlight the coordinate reference frame. At the bottom, the caption reads:

  Figure 3.4: Geometry of the reinforcement layers for DIRE

This diagram conveys how the main and transverse reinforcement directions, as well as support (upper) and span (lower) layers, are defined by angles measured clockwise from the local X-axis (and by extension from each other). In the context of a SOFiSTiK input deck, it visualizes the parameters you would supply via a DIRE record—namely, the direction angles for the orthogonal two-course steel mesh on both sides of a plate or shell element.

sections: 3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section

content:
The illustration is a schematic plan view of a two-layer circular reinforcement mesh, shown in relation to a local Cartesian coordinate system and a reference point M(x,y,z).  At top left a pair of orthogonal axes is drawn: the horizontal axis is labelled X (arrowhead pointing right), and the vertical axis is labelled Y (arrowhead pointing downward).  The origin is implied at the intersection of these axes.  

Some distance from the axes lies point M, annotated “M(x,y,z),” which represents the centre or a generic node of the element in three-dimensional space.  From M two straight line segments extend, each representing one layer of reinforcement:  
• The upper layer is depicted by the segment passing through a point labelled P1.  Near P1 two short solid lines (one on each side of the segment) suggest the local orientation of the reinforcing bars.  Around that region concentric dashed arcs—marked with the legend “radial”—indicate the direction of a theoretical reference circle centred at M.  The key here is that the straight bars at P1 intersect the dashed circle arcs at roughly right angles, showing they lie along the radial direction.  
• The lower layer is shown by the segment passing through a second point labelled P2, displaced slightly downward.  At P2, small ticks drawn on and adjacent to the segment mark its orientation, while a different set of dashed arcs—labelled “tangential”—trace the same reference circle.  In this case the straight segment runs roughly parallel to the dashed arcs, demonstrating that the bars lie tangential to the circle.  

Together, these two line segments and their associated dash patterns illustrate a two-layer mesh in which one course of reinforcement follows radial lines from the centre and the other course follows concentric tangential paths.  The use of distinct labels P1 (radial) and P2 (tangential) reinforces that the mesh is orthogonal in the sense of circular geometry rather than Cartesian.  

Below the graphic appears the caption “Figure 3.5: Definition of a two-layer circular reinforcement,” indicating that this diagram serves as a reference for the software input records (e.g., DIRE with UPP and LOW angles set to 0° or 90°) which automatically generate such radial and tangential bar layouts.  In three-dimensional shell or slab elements, the coordinate origin for these directions may be tied to M(x,y,z), and zero values for X and Y define the axes through opposite points on that centreline.  By alternating the defined angles for upper and lower courses in the DIRE record, the program distinguishes which layer becomes radial and which becomes tangential, exactly as sketched in this figure.

sections: 3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section

content:
The table defines six optional angle‐parameters (in degrees) that can be specified when using the THRE (Skew 2- and 3-course Reinforcement) record to control the orientation of up to three reinforcement “courses” (outer, middle, inner) on each face of a slab or shell element. These inputs are valid only for THRE and have no effect in disk‐only structures (for disks the same mesh is used on both faces, governed instead by DIRE/GEOM/PARA and always producing an ASU/ASL pair).

1. ABEX  
   • Description: Angle between the upper outer reinforcement direction and the local x-axis (clockwise positive, 0–180°).  
   • Unit: degrees  
   • Default: 0.0  

2. ABMI  
   • Description: Angle between the upper middle reinforcement direction and the local x-axis (clockwise positive, 0–180°).  
   • Unit: degrees  
   • Default: 90.0  

3. ABIN  
   • Description: Angle between the upper inner reinforcement direction and the local x-axis (clockwise positive, 0–180°).  
   • Unit: degrees  
   • Default: none (must be supplied if an inner layer is desired)  

4. BEEX  
   • Description: Angle between the lower outer reinforcement direction and the local x-axis (clockwise positive, 0–180°).  
   • Unit: degrees  
   • Default: 0.0  

5. BEMI  
   • Description: Angle between the lower middle reinforcement direction and the local x-axis (clockwise positive, 0–180°).  
   • Unit: degrees  
   • Default: 90.0  

6. BEIN  
   • Description: Angle between the lower inner reinforcement direction and the local x-axis (clockwise positive, 0–180°).  
   • Unit: degrees  
   • Default: none (must be supplied if an inner layer is desired)  

Key usage notes:  
- All angles are measured in degrees, positive in the clockwise sense, relative to the local x-axis. In planar problems the local and global axes coincide; for 3D models the position and orientation of the local system may be set via SOFIMSHA/SOFIMSHB.  
- ABEX/ABMI/ABIN control the “support” (upper) mesh layers; BEEX/BEMI/BEIN control the “span” (lower) mesh layers.  
- If you omit an inner layer parameter (ABIN or BEIN), only two courses (outer & middle) will be generated on that face.  
- These THRE records remain in force until overridden by a subsequent THRE or DIRE record.  
- No automatic SLS check of minimum compression height is performed when skewed three‐course meshes are defined; shear forces must be verified separately.  
- For disk‐type elements, these BE* inputs are ignored—both sides adopt the same mesh as defined by DIRE UPP and the GEOM/PARA settings (resulting in ASU and ASL outputs, though WINGRAF will only report ASU).

sections: 3.11 GEOM – Input of the Cross Section

content:
The figure shows a two-dimensional sketch of the local coordinate system together with the three pairs of “skew” reinforcement directions used in a THRE record (two- and three-course meshes). At its heart lies the Cartesian frame:  
• A horizontal line through the origin, with a single arrowhead at its right end, marks the positive X-axis.  
• A vertical line through the same point, arrowheads at both ends, marks the Y-axis (the upward arrow is +Y; the downward arrow shows –Y).  

Radiating out from the origin are six dash-dot rays in three symmetrically arranged pairs, each pair corresponding to one mesh layer. All rays use the same dash-dot graphic style. The angular spacing and labels are:  

1. Outer (external) layer  
   – Two rays inclined away from the Y-axis at a fairly wide angle (roughly ±60° from the vertical).  
   – A curved arrow drawn between the lower of these two rays and the negative-X to –Y quadrant is labeled “ABEX or BEEX.” This identifies the input parameters that define the skew angle of the outer reinforcement mesh.  

2. Mid (intermediate) layer  
   – Two rays at moderate slope (about ±20° from the horizontal X-axis).  
   – A curved arrow between the right-hand X-axis and its adjacent mid-layer ray is labeled “ABMI or BEMI,” denoting the parameters that set the mid-layer mesh orientation. A mirrored arrow on the opposite side would define the symmetric direction.  

3. Inner layer  
   – Two rays at a relatively small angle (roughly ±10–15°) below the X-axis, tightly clustered around the horizontal.  
   – A curved arrow between one of these rays and the X-axis is marked “ABIN or BEIN,” indicating the angles for the inner (span) reinforcement mesh.  

All angle labels follow the convention that positive angles are measured clockwise from the local X-axis. In a THRE-type design run this diagram remains in effect until a new THRE or DIRE record is issued. The outer layer (“EX”), middle layer (“MI”) and inner layer (“IN”) labels correspond directly to the input keywords ABEX/BEEX, ABMI/BEMI and ABIN/BEIN (or their transverse-bar analogs BEEX, BEMI, BEIN).  

Below the graphic, the caption reads  
   Figure 3.6: Geometry of the reinforcement layers for THRE  

Thus the sketch provides a visual reference for how the skew angles of each reinforcement mesh are defined relative to the local X–Y axes in three-course slab or shell designs.

See also: DIRE, THRE, MAT, PARA
 GEOM
 [mm]1024
 The values HU - DDHB are usually input in a separate BEMESS run or the SSD design pa- rameter dialog.
 An input H or HPRE cannot be done in a parameter definitiion run (PARA). An input H or HPRE is only allowed in a separate design run. Without input to HU-DDHB then H and HPRE can be used in combination with the PARA values for an individual design run. If HU-DDHB is input then no values are taken from a previous PARA run or the SSD design parameter dialog.
 The inputs for HA, DHA, HB, DHB, DDHA and DDHB have no effect for disk structures. The input DIRE UPP, GEOM HA,DHA and PARA DU,ASU,ASU2 count for one side of the disc, on the other side the same values are used. In the output you get an ASU and an ASL, both must be placed. In WINGRAF only ASU is served, on the other side the same reinforcement must be placed.
 This record remains effective until another record GEOM is input. More explanations are to be found in the description of the records DIRE and THRE.
 The used compression zone thickness may be limited for the design of hollow plates with the input possibility GEOM...HPRE. In this way the hollow plates or the bouble-deck plates can be calculated. However, a shear design does not occur. The shear force has to be checked separately.
 DIRE – Definition of Orthogonal Two-course Reinforcement
 See also: GEOM, THRE, MAT, PARA
 DIRE
 An orthogonal steel mesh can be laid both at the upper (support reinforcement) than also at the lower side (span reinforcement). The direction of the main reinforcement is specified and the transverse reinforcement is perpendicular to it. Clockwise angles are positive and they are defined in degrees. They are relative to the x axis of the local coordinate system, which is in the case of plane problems identical with the global coordinate system. The location of the coordinate system in three-dimensional cases can be defined in SOFIMSHA/SOFIMSHB.

In the output you get an ASU and an ASL, both must be placed. In WINGRAF only ASU is served, on the other side the same reinforcement must be placed.
 A design in ultimate limit state can be done with a symmetrical and centric reinforcement for shell systems (SYST SPAC):
 DIRE LOW SYM defines a symmetric reinforcement
 DIRE LOW CENT defines an (upper) centric reinforcement
 (without lower reinforcement)
 For hight concrete cover, the upper and lower reinforcement often are close together. Defining a symmetric reinforcement it is now taken into account that the reinforcement at the concrete compression side also gets tension and helps the tension side reinforcement. An increase of lever arm is taken into account.
 Example file: symmetric.dat
 A special option allows the design of a circular mesh reinforcement by defining a reference circle centre and the items UPP/LOW equal to 0 or 90 degrees. Then the radial or tangential reinforcement lies at the outer side.
 In the case of three-dimensional systems, Z=0 defines a Z axis through the point X,Y. If Z is not equal to 0, then X=0 defines a X axis through Y,Z, and Y=0 a Y axis through X,Z. The tangential direction has priority against the radial direction in the case of diagonally cut elements. At DIRE 0 0 the 2nd layer lies then tangential, while the 1st layer can deviate perpendicularly to the radial direction.
 In the normal case of the spiral stair the input DIRE 0 0 - 0 0 0 is correct for all elements. The stair links lie then as principal direction outside in radial direction, the structural bars are tangential in the 2nd layer (with X=Y=0 = spiral axis).

 THRE – Definition of Skew 2- and 3-course Reinforcement
 See also: GEOM, DIRE, MAT, PARA
 THRE
 The upper reinforcement mesh (support reinforcement) and the lower reinforcement mesh (span reinforcement) are selected independently of each other; thus two- and three-course reinforcement is simultaneously possible. An orthogonal two-course reinforcement laid at both sides should be specified, however, by means of the record DIRE. The angles of the reinforce- ment directions are defined in degrees and they are positive in the clockwise direction. They are relative to the x axis of the local coordinate system. The terms main and transverse rein- forcement in THRE are used analogously, e.g. in reference to the percentage parameter MINC of the input record MAT.
 The inputs for BEEX, BEMI and BEIN have no effect for disk structures. The input DIRE UPP, GEOM HA,DHA and PARA DU,ASU,ASU2 count for one side of the disc, on the other side the same values are used. In the output you get an ASU and an ASL, both must be placed. In WINGRAF only ASU is served, on the other side the same reinforcement must be placed.
 An SLS check of minimum compression height cannot be performed for skew two- and three- course meshes.
 This record remains effective until another THRE (or DIRE) record is input.

The table shown is part of the DI3D input specification for defining reinforcement directions in BRIC (brick‐type) finite‐element volume elements. It lists the parameters the user can supply, their physical meaning, units, and default values. Below is a detailed breakdown suitable for indexing in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store.

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the keyword used in the DI3D input card.  
     – Description: a concise explanation of what the item controls.  
     – Unit: the physical unit in which the input value must be supplied.  
     – Default: the assumed value when the item is omitted.  
   • Rows  
     – OAL, OAF, X, Y, Z  

2. Items and Their Roles  
   A. OAL (Meridian Angle)  
     • Description: rotation angle around the global Z-axis (i.e., a “longitude” or meridian angle).  
     • Unit: radians. Users must convert degrees to radians (e.g., 10° → 10 * π/180).  
     • Default: 0 rad (no initial rotation).  
     • Context: this is the first rotation applied when defining a reinforcement direction without a center, or prior to OAF when a center is specified. Consult the “Geology” section of the AQUA-MATE manual for the precise angular convention.  

   B. OAF (Descent Angle)  
     • Description: the angle of “descent” or tilt from the horizontal plane, measured after the OAL rotation.  
     • Unit: radians.  
     • Default: 0 rad (horizontal).  
     • Context: paired with OAL to orient a reinforcement direction in 3D space (trilinear steel behavior up to limit state in tension per Hoogenboom & de Boer, 2008).

   C. X, Y, Z (Centre Coordinates for Circular Reinforcement)  
     • Description: the Cartesian coordinates of the axis or center point when defining circular (radial/tangential) reinforcement patterns.  
     • Unit: meters [m].  
     • Default: “–” (must be provided when circular patterns are required).  
     • Context & Constraints:  
       – Standard circular reinforcement (e.g., wind‐tower or tank foundation) uses OAL = OAF = 0, with X and Y specifying the center; Z is ignored.  
       – A three‐step definition: first rotate around global Z by OAL, then tilt by OAF around the newly defined reinforcement axis, then define the circle center (X, Y).  
       – Special case: with additional Z input (only allowed if OAL = OAF = 0), users can define a rotation axis parallel to X or Y about a point specified by the other two coordinates (e.g., input Y,Z to rotate about X).

3. Usage Patterns & Examples  
   • Linear reinforcement along a global axis: omit X, Y, Z; set OAL/OAF according to desired direction.  
   • Radial/tangential patterns: OAL=0, OAF=0, supply X, Y for center; choose reinforcement type = radial (1), tangential (2), or global Z (3).  
   • Sloping circular tanks or cones: e.g., DI3D OAL 90 OAF 30 X 0 Y 0 yields a 30°-inclined circular pattern about the global Z after a 90° meridian rotation.

By capturing each field’s semantics, units, defaults, and contextual constraints, this description enables precise retrieval and interpretation when assembling DI3D input decks or answering user queries about reinforcement orientation in concrete models.

See also: PARA
 DI3D
 The design of volume elements is based on a tension force covering of the stress tensor according a paper of P.C.J. Hoogenboom and A. de Boer: ”Computation of reinforcement for solid concrete” Heron Heft 53 2008 no 4. In tension, the reinforcement steel is used up to the trilinear limit. With the new input DI3D a reinforcement direction can be defined for BRIC elements.
 Example see bric_design.dat
 Possible definitions:
 1. reinforcement direction = global-X 2.=global-Y 3.=global-Z
 DI3D OAL...OAF... without input to a centre:
 first rotation OAL around global-Z
 then rotation OAF around new 1. reinforcement direction
 DI3D with input to a centre:
 X and Y are allowed in addition to OAL+OAF. Input Z only allowed with OAL=OAF=0
 -
 circular reinforcement around X,Y (without Z input):
 Standard case OAL=OAF=0:
 e.g. wind power plant foundation or tank:
 DI3D OAL 0 OAF 0 X 0 Y 0
 1. reinforcement = radial
 2. reinforcement = tangential
 3. reinforcement = global z
 Spezial case with OAL+OAF:
 Additional rotation OAL around global-Z then rotation around new 1. reinforcement direction
 e.g. tank with 30 degree cone: DI3D OAL 90 OAF 30 X 0 Y 0
 Special input additional Z: only allowed with OAL=OAF=0:
 input Y,Z without X: rotational axis = X around point Y,Z input X,Z without Y: rotational axis = Y around point X,Z

The table shown defines the per‐layer input parameters needed by the BEMESS multi‐layer reinforcement design module (and related ASE non‐linear checks), along with their units and default settings.  Each row corresponds to a keyword (Item) that the user must supply for every reinforcement layer, and the table tells you what the keyword means, what units to use, and what value will be assumed if you omit it.  Below is a detailed walkthrough:

Columns  
• Item: the parameter name (keyword) as used in the input file.  
• Description: textual definition, restrictions and special notes.  
• Unit: physical unit (often tagged with an internal index like _1024 or _1092).  
• Default: the value assumed if the user does not specify this keyword.

1. POS (Position of the reinforcement)  
   – Description: Indicates whether this layer is placed at the top, center or bottom of the concrete cross section.  
     • UPP = measured from the upper face  
     • CENT = measured from the section centroid  
     • LOW = measured from the lower face  
   – Unit = LIT (literal token, one of the three text codes above)  
   – Default = “!” (mandatory—you must supply one of UPP, CENT or LOW)

2. Z (Centre distance of the reinforcement)  
   – Description: The perpendicular distance (in mm) from the chosen reference (see POS) to the reinforcement layer.  
   – Unit = [mm] (internal code 1024)  
   – Default = “!” (mandatory)

3. DIRE (Direction angle)  
   – Description: Angle in degrees (0–180) between the reinforcement direction and the local x‐axis of the section.  
   – Unit = Altgrad (alternative gradation for angles)  
   – Default = 0.0

4. D (Diameter)  
   – Description: Bar diameter in millimetres. A value of 0 means “do not design these elements.”  
     • You may also set D via a PARAmeter command (PARA…DU 0).  
   – Unit = [mm] (internal code 1023)  
   – Default = – (unspecified; if omitted no automatic bar sizing is done)

5. AS (Minimum reinforcement)  
   – Description: Required minimum reinforcement area per metre of width in cm²/m.  
   – Unit = [cm2/m]  
   – Default = – (no minimum enforced unless specified)

6. ASMA (Maximum reinforcement)  
   – Description: Caps the area of this layer (in cm²/m). Once this layer’s area is reached, the next inner layer gets “filled.”  
     • Do not supply ASMA for the innermost layer.  
   – Unit = [cm2/m]  
   – Default = –

7. BS (Non‐linear ASE maximum reinforcement)  
   – Description: For advanced nonlinear (ASE → REIQ) analysis, this is the maximum reinforcement per layer.  
     • Not used in standard BEMESS linear checks.  
   – Unit = [cm2/m]  
   – Default = –

8. WK (Crack width)  
   – Description: Target crack width (in mm) for serviceability limit‐state (SLS) check. Outer layers control crack width, inner layers still affect reinforcement ratio and effective depth.  
   – Unit = [mm] (internal code 1026)  
   – Default = –

9. SS (Steel stress for SLS crack check)  
   – Description: Alternative to supplying WK. You can specify the maximum allowable steel stress (in MPa; internal code 1092) instead of a crack‐width criterion, typically used with the CRAC WK TAB option.  
   – Unit = [MPa]  
   – Default = –

Additional Context  
• “See also: GEOM, THRE, PARA, LAY” in the manual for complementary geometry and parameter-setting commands.  
• Example input snippet from bemess8_multi_layer_design.dat shows how top/bottom layers report extreme stresses and strains for verification.  
• All SLS checks (serviceability) can be performed. Crack‐width design focuses on outer layers but accounts for inner layers in the effective depth calculation (see Figure 2.12 of the manual).  
• You may also employ this multilayer definition in a fully nonlinear ASE analysis, which reads BS (and ASMA if desired) to distribute reinforcement across layers.

The image is a full-page excerpt from the SOFiSTiK “Input” manual, specifically section 3.15 entitled “LAY – Definition of Multi Layer Reinforcement.” At the very top is the SOFiSTiK logo in blue, followed by the section heading and the cross-reference “See also: GEOM, THRE, PARA.” Below that is a large, two-column table delineating all of the input keywords and parameters available under the LAY card.

Left-hand column (Item) lists the parameter codes:

• POS  
• Z  
• DIRE  
• D  
• AS  
• ASMA  
• BS  
• WK  
• SS  

The middle column (Description) explains each parameter in detail:

1. POS – “Position of the reinforcement,” with allowed values UPP (Z = distance to upper face), CENT (Z = distance to center), and LOW (Z = distance to lower face).  
2. Z – “Centre distance of the reinforcement” given in [mm].  
3. DIRE – “Angle to the local x-axis (between 0 and 180°).”  
4. D – “Diameter, 0 = do not design these elements; can also be set in PARA with PARA…DU 0” [mm].  
5. AS – “Minimum reinforcement” [cm²/m].  
6. ASMA – “Maximum reinforcement. When this is reached the next inner layer will be filled. Do not input ASMA for most inner reinforcement!” [cm²/m].  
7. BS – “Maximum reinforcement for nonlinear analysis in ASE (ASE->REIQ) – not used in BEMESS” [cm²/m].  
8. WK – “Crack width” [mm].  
9. SS – “Steel stress in SLS crack check (for CRAC WK TAB alternative to WK)” [MPa].

A thin rule line encloses the table. A footnote under the table reads: “For an element maximum 40 layers can be defined.”

Below the table is a reference to an example data file (“Example see bemess8_multi_layer_design.dat”) and then a rendered, three-dimensional cutaway graphic labeled “Figure 3.7: 4 upper layer, 6 lower layer (3 in x + 3 in y = 6).” The graphic is a prismatic concrete block in a light sand-beige tone. On its top face a square grid of reinforcement bars is drawn—red bars running in one orthogonal direction and blue bars orthogonal to those—arranged in four layers near the top surface. A rectangular cutout on the block’s right side reveals six lower layers of horizontal reinforcement (alternating red and blue) embedded near the bottom of the concrete element.

Superimposed on the block are annotation boxes displaying strain results for both the top and bottom layers:

  (in case of biaxial pressure: “min. εc = (εpsl1+ψ εpsl2)/(1+ψ+2)”)  

Bottom ε:

• max. εc = 3.405 o/oo  
• min. εs = 0.053 o/oo

  (“cross direction (or skew concrete compression)”)

At the lower right of the graphic is a small legend “Stress plot element 10047 loadcase 101” and an arrow on the right face of the block indicating “stresses in direction of the max. main concrete compression strain.”

content:
Below is a structured, human‐readable breakdown of the table’s contents—its fields, meanings, units and default behaviors—as well as how it ties into the broader BEMESS/SSD input logic.  

1. General structure  
   • Four columns:  
     – Item: the keyword you type under a PARA NOG command  
     – Description: what that keyword controls in the reinforcement design  
     – Unit: the physical unit expected by BEMESS  
     – Default: the value used if you omit this keyword or rely on inheritance  

2. Grouping and element identifiers  
   • NOG  
     – “Group number.” You can subdivide by SAR (structural area) or GAR. Secondary groups are allowed, and you may restrict by an x-range (xmin–xmax). If you don’t specify NOG at all, it defaults to “*” (all groups).  
     – Unit: –/LIT (a literal integer identifier)  
     – Default: * (applies to every group)  
   • NOEL  
     – “Element number,” or in SAR mode it works like a structural area number.  
     – Unit: – (no unit)  
     – Default: – (no implicit default; you either pick elements by NOG or NOEL)  

3. Reinforcement diameters  
   • DU, DU2, DU3  
     – Bars in the upper 1st, 2nd and 3rd layers, respectively.  
     – DU=0 switches OFF design for that group.  
     – Unit: mm  
     – Default:  
         · DU  → 10 mm  
         · DU2 → inherits DU  
         · DU3 → inherits DU2  
   • DL, DL2, DL3  
     – Bars in the lower 1st, 2nd and 3rd layers.  
     – Unit: mm  
     – Default:  
         · DL  → inherits DU (upper-layer value)  
         · DL2 → inherits DL  
         · DL3 → inherits DL2  

4. Crack-width limits  
   • WKU, WKU2, WKU3  
     – Maximum crack width for upper layers 1-3.  
     – Unit: mm  
     – Default:  
         · WKU  → no default (must be set explicitly for new groups)  
         · WKU2 → inherits WKU  
         · WKU3 → inherits WKU2  
   • WKL, WKL2, WKL3  
     – Analogous crack limits for lower layers.  
     – Default: WKL → WKU, WKL2 → WKL, WKL3 → WKL2  

5. Steel stress criteria  
   • SSU, SSU2, SSU3  
     – Max allowed steel stress in upper layers 1-3.  
     – Unit: N/mm²  
     – Default:  
         · SSU  → no default  
         · SSU2 → inherits SSU  
         · SSU3 → inherits SSU2  
   • SSL, SSL2, SSL3  
     – Steel stress limits for the lower layers.  
     – Default: SSL → SSU, SSL2 → SSL, SSL3 → SSL2  

6. Minimum reinforcement areas  
   • ASU, ASU2, ASU3  
     – Required minimum steel area [cm²/m] for upper layers 1-3.  
     – Default: ASU has no default; higher layers inherit as above.  
   • ASL, ASL2, ASL3  
     – Minimum areas for lower layers. Defaults mirror ASU→ASL, ASU2→ASL2, etc.  

7. Special notes and context  
   • You only invoke these parameters once in a PARA statement under SSD-reinforcement. Then they persist in the database for all subsequent runs.  
   • Inputs from DIRE, THRE and GEOM (except GEOM-D) may be given before or after, but you must close any selection with a PARA line. The very first PARA also acts as a global predefinition.  
   • TYPE MOD mode: when you write “PARA … TYPE MOD”, you must explicitly supply every value you intend to change—no defaults or inherited values are applied, and previous DIRE/GEOM globals are not altered.  
   • Disk-structure caveat: DL, WKL, SSL, ASL inputs have no effect on disk elements; only upper-side inputs (DIRE UPP, GEOM HA/DHA, PARA DU/ASU) are used, and are automatically mirrored on the other side in output.  
   • PUNC (punching reinforcement) entries are stored globally but must be defined once via ASCII input.  

This table of “Item → Description → Unit → Default” is the master reference for all layer‐by‐layer reinforcement parameters used by BEMESS’s SSD design module. Whenever you add or modify a PARA NOG line, these rules determine what gets designed, what inherits from what, and when you need to explicitly override defaults (especially under TYPE MOD).

The input‐table in question defines a series of PARA-records that drive the SSD (Steel Stress Design) task in BEMESS. Each PARA-line assigns one or more of the following key parameters which control reinforcement checks and automatic bar-area calculations. Below is a breakdown of the table’s structure and its fields, together with the procedural rules and cross-references you need when authoring or parsing these records.

1. Table Columns  
   • Keyword (first column)  
     – Always “PARA” for these reinforcement setup entries.  
   • Parameter Codes (one or more per row)  
     – SSL3 : “Steel stress lower 3rd layer”  
     – SSL2* : (variant stress parameter, e.g. special lower-layer stress case)  
     – ASU : “Minimum reinforcement upper 1st layer”  
   • Description  
     – Free-text reminder of what each code means (e.g. “Steel stress lower 3rd layer”).  
   • Unit  
     – [cm2/m] — all AS-values (ASU, ASL, etc.) are in square centimeters per metre.  
   • Default or Flag Column (“–”)  
     – A dash “–” indicates no additional qualifier or that a parameter has no alternate status flag.

2. How and When to Input PARA Records  
   – PARA lines must be issued after the relevant GEOM, DIRE or THRE calls, to close off an element or group selection.  
   – The first PARA line in a BEMESS run also serves as the global default for all subsequent PARA calls (unless TYPE MOD is used).  
   – Any PARA lines beyond the first inherit prior global settings except for those parameters explicitly overridden.

3. Scope and Inheritance  
   – Inputs for DL, WKL, SSL and ASL are ignored for pure disc structures.  
   – For discs you only need to define DIRE UPP, GEOM HA/DHA and PARA DU, ASU (and ASU2 if differing), once per side; the same values are mirrored on the opposite side.  
   – The output will still list both ASU and ASL so that both top and bottom layers are placed in the reinforcement drawings. WINGRAF will display only ASU; users must manually mirror it for the other face.

4. Special PARA Variants  
   a) PAR-TYPE MOD  
      – When “TYPE MOD” appears on a PARA line, ONLY parameters on that line are updated for the named group/elements.  
      – Preceding global or GEOM/DIRE defaults are not carried forward; every value to be modified must be explicit.  
      – You may not issue a GEOM or DIRE call immediately before a PARA-TYPE MOD line.  
      – Example syntax:  
         GEOM … $ Exposition XC1  
         PARA NOG – DU 10 WKU 0.40 $ class F  
         GEOM … $ Exposition XC4  
         PARA NOG 3 DL 20 WKL 0.30 $ class E  
         PARA NOEL 20710,20711 DU 16 DL 14 DL2 14 TYPE MOD  
   b) Disabling a Group  
      – “PARA NOG … DU=0” switches the group off from further design checks.

5. PUNC and Database Persistence  
   – Manual PUNC entries (punching shear parameters) are saved in the database on first input and need not be reissued for subsequent runs.  
   – Once defined, PUNC parameters remain active until explicitly changed.

6. Workflow Recommendations  
   – Always issue one PARA run containing your global reinforcement design parameters before any other PARA-TYPE MOD calls.  
   – Keep your GEOM and DIRE calls grouped logically, then close each group with a PARA sequence.  
   – Use the BEMESS design output (Design-Reinforcement-loadcase) or WINGRAF-Quad report to verify that your ASU/ASL and SSL values have been properly applied.

See also the sections on GEOM (geometry settings), DIRE (load direction), THRE (thickness definitions), LAY (layer assignments), PUNC (punching shear), and MREI (material reinforcement indices) for complementary input rules and sample data files (e.g. bemess6_design.dat).

This table is part of the BEMESS SSD-task “reinforcement input” dictionary. It tells you which keywords you can feed in (via ASCII “PARA …” lines or the SSD-dialogue) to control minimum/maximum reinforcement and the spatial extent or modification of those values. Here is a structured walk-through:

1. Column Definitions  
  • Item: the exact keyword you write after “PARA” in your input deck.  
  • Description: what that keyword does, which layer(s) it affects, and cross-references to other parameters or subroutines (e.g. MREI or ASE→REIQ).  
  • Unit: the physical unit associated with that parameter. If you see a small code (e.g. “₁₀₂₁”), it points to an internal unit index in the BEMESS database.  
  • Default: a “–” means there is no built-in default; you must supply a value if you want to change it.

2. Minimum-Reinforcement Parameters  
  • ASU2 : “Minimum reinforcement, upper 2nd layer”  
  • ASU3 : “Minimum reinforcement, upper 3rd layer”  
     – Note: For usage details see the MREI PARA entry  
  • ASL  : “Minimum reinforcement, lower 1st layer”  
  • ASL2 : “Minimum reinforcement, lower 2nd layer”  
  • ASL3 : “Minimum reinforcement, lower 3rd layer”  
  Unit for all five is [cm²/m]. No defaults.

3. Maximum-Reinforcement Parameters  
  • BSU  : “Maximum reinforcement, upper 1st layer”  
  • BSU2 : “Maximum reinforcement, upper 2nd layer”  
  • BSU3 : “Maximum reinforcement, upper 3rd layer”  
     – The note clarifies that BSU/BSU2/BSU3 are not used by BEMESS’s own design routine; they are only exported to ASE for nonlinear checks (see ASE→REIQ).  
  • BSL, BSL2, BSL3 : analogous for lower layers 1–3.  
  Again units are [cm²/m], no default values.

4. TYPE / MOD  
  • TYPE : a special keyword allowing you to override any of the above design parameters on a per-PARA-line basis.  
  • MOD  : when you append “MOD” to your PARA statement, only the values you explicitly list on that same line are changed; all other parameters remain at their previous setting.  
  – Warning: TYPE/MOD lines cannot be used in combination with a prior DIRE+GEOM group; you must supply every value you want to modify, since no implicit defaults are fetched.

5. Spatial Selection Box  
  These keywords let you confine the reinforcement inputs to quads whose centers lie inside a 3D box (or rotate that box). They can be mixed with a “NOG” (group-shut-off) input if you wish.  
  • XMIN, XMAX, YMIN, YMAX, ZMIN, ZMAX : define the limits of that box in the global X, Y, Z axes.  
     – Units are [m] (internally code ₁₀₀₁). If you omit ZMIN/ZMAX, the box extends infinitely in Z.  
  • ROT : “rotation around the center of the box in the XY plane” in [degrees].

6. How It Fits Into a BEMESS Run  
  – You normally issue one full PARA statement carrying your design parameter (e.g. minimum reinforcement for a particular exposure class). That statement closes with PARA (no other PARA lines can remain “open”).  
  – Once you have defined your minimum/maximum bars, they live in the database and apply to all subsequent calculations—no need to repeat them.  
  – For disk structures, DL/WKL/SSL/ASL inputs have no effect; only the “upper” side (DIRE UPP, GEOM HA/DHA, PARA DU/ASU/ASU2) is needed and mirrored automatically.  
  – Any manual PUNC inputs (punching check) are likewise stored once and reused.  
  – If you want to disable a particular element group altogether, you can use “PARA NOG … DU=0.”

By following this table you can precisely tune minimum/maximum bar areas on a layer-by-layer basis and even restrict them to arbitrary plan regions, all under full MREI/ASE cross-checking.

See also: GEOM, DIRE, THRE, LAY, PUNC, MREI

In the output you get an ASU and an ASL, both must be placed. In WINGRAF only ASU is served, on the other side the same reinforcement must be placed.

So no (DIRE) or (GEOM) input is allowed directly before a PARA-MOD line! Also defaults e.g. for DU2=DU are not set. All values that shall be modified must be set! Usage e.g.:

Below is a structured, field-by-field description of the punching-design input table, suitable for ingestion into a RAG/vector database.  Wherever relevant, pointers to related commands (ECHO, CTRL, LC, PARA, MREI, SELE, PUNC, LC_P) are mentioned.

General notes  
• The table defines parameters for punching‐shear checks at columns, wall ends or foundation plates.  
• If no support reaction is found or shear stress is negligible, the punching check is skipped.  
• Individual nodes may be deactivated via “PUNC … HEAD OFF” or “SELE … 0.”  
• In the absence of a specific node number or coordinates, defaults apply to all punching nodes of the chosen TYPE (COL/WALL/FOUN).  
• Shear reinforcement links and longitudinal reinforcement options are governed by RO_V, RO_L and RO_M.  
• Collapse reinforcement per EN 1992-1-1 9.4.1(3) is included automatically (can be suppressed with MMOM=0).

1. TYPE (unit: LIT, default: “*”)  
   • Design mode / punching type selector. Choices:  
     – NO no punching design performed  
     – CHEK only punching check (reinforcement may only be increased to MMOM minimum)  
     – YES full input for all column nodes (default)  
     – COL same as YES but limited to column nodes  
     – WALL input for wall ends and corners  
     – FOUN input for foundation slabs  
   • Following this, a node number (No) may be provided to target subsequent inputs just at that node.

2. X, Y, Z (unit: m [index 1001], default: – )  
   • Coordinates of the punching node.  
   • If you omit the node number earlier, the program assigns the free node whose coordinates match X, Y, Z.

3. D (unit: mm [index 1011], default: – )  
   • Column or wall thickness at the punching node.  
   • Rarely needed if defined elsewhere (e.g., in SOFIPLUS).

4. B (unit: mm [index 1011], default: – )  
   • Column width. Setting B = 0 signals a circular column of diameter D.

5. HEAD (unit: LIT, default: – )  
   • Indicates whether to include an enlarged head or just perform a check:  
     – (blank) standard column-head design  
     – CHEK only punching check for an individual node (e.g. “PUNC 37 HEAD CHEK”)  
     – OFF node excluded from punching (see also “SELE … 0”)

6. DHEA (unit: mm [index 1011], default: 0)  
   • Total thickness in the enlarged head zone (usually taken from SOFIPLUS modelling).

7. RO_V (unit: %, default: 1.5)  
   • Maximum bending‐reinforcement ratio allowable when shear governs in the punching area.  
   • If a design without shear reinforcement needs more than RO_V, the solver auto-switches to a check with shear reinforcement (links/stirrups).

8. RO_L (unit: %, default: – )  
   • Longitudinal reinforcement ratio to be used when shear reinforcement is triggered.  
   • If not set, the minimum reinforcement for shear links only is applied.

9. RO_M (unit: %, default: – )  
   • Upper limit for longitudinal reinforcement at the column head check.  
   • If the required reinforcement to satisfy shear at the head exceeds RO_M, the design is flagged “undesignable” rather than pumping-up reinforcement indefinitely.

10. KPU (unitless factor, default: – )  
   • For stud-rail punching an approximate VRD,max factor.  
   • VRD,max on the critical perimeter u₁ is taken as KPU × VRD,c.  
   • Typical ETA reports permit KPU = 1.96.  
   • VRD,max is only verified; final stud-rail design must comply with the producer’s specs.  
   • Not permitted for codes lacking a VRD,max check on u₁.  
   • In WINGRAF the solver plots 9999 cm² of reinforcement to flag that a separate stud-rail design is required.

See also  
• ECHO, CTRL, LC, PARA, MREI for general control and reporting  
• SELE and PUNC for selective activation/deactivation of punching nodes  
• LC_P to link to load-case definitions  
• MMOM to disable automatic collapse reinforcement

The table under discussion catalogues all of the PUNC‐related input parameters that govern the automatic punching‐shear design checks for slab‐to‐column, slab‐to‐wall or slab‐to‐foundation‐plate connections.  It is a “keyword‐parameter‐description” listing, intended for a RAG‐vector‐store or similar rule‐driven design engine, and is organized roughly as follows:

1.  Keyword (PUNC or SELE)  
2.  Parameter name or code  
3.  Explanation of effect, default behavior or interaction with other settings  

Below is a narrative walk-through of each entry:

1.  “PUNC LC_P”  
    •  Parameter: Load case index (integer)  
    •  Description: Defines which load case is used to determine the maximum soil pressure beneath a foundation plate.  The punching check then uses the corresponding support reaction from that same load case.  If the reaction is missing or the shear stress falls below the code threshold, the punching check is simply skipped.

2.  “PUNC no. HEAD OFF”  (alternative via “SELE no. 0”)  
    •  Parameter: Node number (integer)  
    •  Description: Disables punching checks at that particular column head or node.  It can be issued either as a PUNC command (“HEAD OFF”) or via SELE with a zero‐value flag.  See also SELE for combined SSD‐task interactions.

3.  Default coverage for nodes without explicit node entries  
    •  If no specific node number or (X, Y, Z) coordinate is given, the subsequent PUNC inputs will apply to all punching‐type nodes of the listed TYPE (COL, WALL, FOUN).

4.  “PUNC RO_V”  
    •  Parameter: Target longitudinal reinforcement area [% of concrete cross‐section]  
    •  Description: When shear studs or links become necessary (i.e. when the plain‐slab shear check VRd,c is exceeded), RO_V is the longitudinal area used in lieu of full stirrups.  By default, RO_V = RO_M = RO_L sets a fixed reinforcement area for all conditions.

5.  “PUNC RO_L”  
    •  Parameter: Alternative longitudinal reinforcement area  
    •  Description: Defines the minimum longitudinal area taken when shear studs/links are used.  This prevents the very high link requirements that can otherwise result from an unbounded VRd calculation.  

6.  “PUNC RO_M”  
    •  Parameter: Maximum admissible longitudinal reinforcement area  
    •  Description: Caps the reinforcement required at the column head.  If the check would demand more than RO_M, the connection is deemed “undesignable” rather than forcing a larger bar area.

7.  Collapse reinforcement per EN 1992-1-1 §9.4.1(3)  
    •  Implicitly included even if PUNC is “NO” or “CHECK,” unless turned off via “MMOM=0.”  
    •  The collapse shear reinforcement Ved/fyk is distributed around the effective column perimeter.  (Not used at wall ends.)

8.  “PUNC KPU” (for stud-rail applications)  
    •  Parameter: kpu,sl (dimensionless factor)  
    •  Description: Multiplies VRd,c to define a new VRd,max at the critical perimeter u₁.  Many ETA approvals permit kpu,sl ≈ 1.96.  The code only checks that VRd,max is not exceeded; final stud-rail design must be done externally per manufacturer specs.  Not valid for codes without VRd,max at u₁.

9.  Plotting note (WINGRAF)  
    •  If a separate stud-rail design is required, the program plots a “9999 cm²” reinforcement symbol at the location.  

Pagination note: The table continues on the next page with further explanatory remarks and examples of usage.

The table shown is part of the “PUNC” (punching‐shear) input record set used to control punching checks in foundations, slabs or walls (TYPE=COL/WALL/FOUN) when using the RAG‐based vector store.  It defines seven adjustable parameters, each of which may be specified by the user to override default behavior.  The four columns of the table are:

  • Item: the mnemonic keyword used in the PUNC record  
  • Description: a brief explanation of what the parameter controls  
  • Unit: the measurement unit (if applicable)  
  • Default: the value assumed when the parameter is omitted  

Below is a detailed breakdown of each parameter:

1. VPD  
   – Description:  
     • “The soil pressure inside the punching circle dK reduces the maximum column load P for the punching check.”  
     • “Shear force component of tendons.”  
     – Only allowed for TYPE=FOUN (foundation plates).  When specified, VPD is subtracted from the design shear to account for pre‐compression from soil reaction or tendon force.  
   – Unit: [kN]  
   – Default: (none) – user must enter a value if reduction is desired  

2. RO_M  
   – Description: Maximum reinforcement ratio for any increase of longitudinal reinforcement due to punching‐shear.  
     • This cap prevents the algorithm from demanding an impractically large amount of rebar at the column/shell interface.  
     • If the required longitudinal reinforcement exceeds RO_M, the punching check is declared “undesignable” (no automatic reinforcement increase).  
   – Unit: % (reinforcement ratio)  
   – Default: (none)  

3. RO_L  
   – Description: Minimum longitudinal reinforcement ratio to be used when punching‐shear links (stirrups or shear studs) are triggered.  
     • If the shear check without links fails and links are added, RO_L defines the baseline rebar ratio instead of the code‐computed value (RO_V).  
     • A default “*” indicates that the code’s minimum link requirement is used unless overridden.  
   – Unit: %  
   – Default: *  

4. MMOM  
   – Description: Factor on the minimum design bending moments (per DIN 1045-1 clause 10.5.6 table 14 or corresponding EN provision).  
     – MMOM = 1.0: default code‐minimum moments plus collapse (kollaps) reinforcement are included.  
     – MMOM = 0.0: both minimum moments and collapse reinforcement are switched off.  
   – Unit: — (dimensionless)  
   – Default: 1.0  

5. HRED  
   – Description: Thickness‐reduction parameter.  The effective slab/thickness used in the punching check is min(quad_thickness, HRED).  
     – This can be used to conservatively reduce the nominal thickness in regions of high shear demand.  
   – Unit: mm  
   – Default: (none)  

6. BETA  
   – Description: Eccentricity factor for punching (see also CTRL BETA).  
     – Only values ≥ 1.0 are accepted (i.e. you may only increase eccentricity).  
     – When TYPE is omitted, BETA applies only to column punching checks (not walls).  
   – Unit: —  
   – Default: (none)  

7. KPU  
   – Description: Factor on VRD,max for studrail (shear stud) designs.  
     – When PUNC KPU=kpu_sl is set, the critical perimeter check uses VRD,max = kpu_sl·VRD,c (the code‐calculated shear resistance).  
     – ETA approvals typically allow KPU up to 1.96.  
     – The software only verifies that VRD,max is not exceeded; final studrail design must follow manufacturer’s rules.  
     – Not permitted where the applicable code does not define a VRD,max check at the first perimeter u1.  
   – Unit: —  
   – Default: (none)  

How these parameters integrate with other commands:  
  • PUNC HEAD OFF or SELE [no.] 0 can deactivate punching checks for individual nodes.  
  • When shear‐links are added, RO_L and RO_V (the code’s shear reinforcement ratio) guide longitudinal reinforcement; RO_M caps any automatic increase.  
  • Collapse reinforcement per EN 1992-1-1 §9.4.1 (3) is included automatically unless MMOM=0 or PUNC NO/CHEK is set.  
  • If separate studrail design is required, WINGRAF will plot an artificial 9999 cm² of rebar to flag it.  

Together, these seven PUNC options give the user fine‐grained control over how punching shear and associated reinforcement are calculated, limited or overridden in automated design workflows.

See also: ECHO, CTRL, LC, PARA, MREI, SELE

Below is a structured, detailed description of the four input parameters (items) in the table, suitable for ingestion into a RAG-style vector store.  It includes each field’s purpose, allowed values, units, defaults and relevant notes, together with context on how certain load-case options interact with program MAXIMA, ULS/SLS checks and punching checks.

1. Item: NO  
   – Purpose: Defines which load cases or load-case combinations are to be evaluated by the design routines, or allows direct import of a combination generated by the external superposition program MAXIMA.  
   – Allowed Values (case-insensitive keywords or single-letter codes):  
     • DESI / D  Design combination (for codes with actions—selects ultimate-limit-state combos pre-superposed by MAXIMA)  
     • ULTI    After superposition on ULS level without further actions (preferred for codes without explicit actions)  
     • ACCI / A  Accidental combination (use together with LC ACCI to trigger accidental-load safety factors; see MAT record)  
     • EARQ / E  Earthquake combination  
     • PERM / P  Quasi-permanent combination  
     • RARE / R  Rare or characteristic combination  
     • FREQ / F  Frequent combination (SLS)  
     • NONF / N  Non-frequent combination (SLS)  
     • SERV    After superposition on SLS level without actions (serviceability combos)  
   – Unit: none (“—”)  
   – Default: none (“–”)  
   – Contextual notes:  
     • When using DESI or ULTI, BEMESS automatically pulls the relevant superposed load-case set from MAXIMA.  For ultimate limit designs of structures governed by code actions, DESI is preferred; for simpler ULS checks without explicit action combinations, ULTI may be more appropriate.  Always review the BEMESS output to confirm which load-case IDs were actually selected.  
     • If ACCI or EARQ is specified, the program will apply material safety factors tied to accidental or seismic scenarios—cross-check with the MAT record.  
     • Any load-case combination flagged for maximum support reactions should also be input under NO to support punching shear checks.

2. Item: PERC  
   – Purpose: Scaling factor for the permanent (dead) load in serviceability-limit-state (SLS) checks, historically used under older design codes.  In EN-1992 fatigue and tendon checks, the literal keyword PERC=’PERM’ can be used to explicitly designate the permanent-load-case level.  
   – Unit: % per load-case (expressed as “%/LIT”)  
   – Default: 100 (% of nominal permanent load)  
   – Contextual notes:  
     • If you are working exclusively under Eurocode 2 fatigue provisions or tendon design, specifying PERC=PERM forces the program to treat the permanent load at its full (100 %) level for fatigue-life or tendon-force calculations.  
     • For legacy SLS service checks, reducing PERC below 100 automatically scales all dead loads by that percentage.

3. Item: FACT  
   – Purpose: Uniform amplification (or reduction) factor applied to each single load case when assessing ULS or SLS conditions individually (rather than as part of a combination).  
   – Unit: none (“—”)  
   – Default: none (“–”)  
   – Contextual notes:  
     • FACT is typically used when you need to override or calibrate partial safety factors on an ad-hoc basis, for example to enforce special inspection loads or temporary overload scenarios.  
     • If FACT is left blank, BEMESS uses its internal code-defined partial factors.

4. Item: SELE  
   – Purpose: Fine-tunes which component of a CSM DESI superposition load-case set should be used for cracking or punching checks.  
   – Allowed Value: “M”  
   – Unit: none (“—”)  
   – Default: none (“–”)  
   – Semantic effect:  
     • When SELE=M is specified in conjunction with a DESI (design) load-case group (e.g. LC “rare” SELE M), only the maximum bending-moment (mami) envelopes are considered.  The corresponding shear (Vz) load-cases are omitted from the crack-width or punching design, effectively deferring shear checks to a separate stage.  
   – Contextual notes:  
     • This setting is specifically for crack design in reinforced concrete slabs and members using the CSM superposition strategy.  
     • Ensure that omitted Vz envelopes are checked later under separate punching shear routines, referencing the maximum support-reaction load cases.

See also the related input records ECHO, CTRL, PUNC and S (for section properties), and MAT (for material safety factors). Always verify the automatically selected MAXIMA combinations in the BEMESS output logs and supply any additional single load cases needed for punching-shear reaction envelopes.
