The input table defines three parameters (items) that govern how the GRP‐record operates in selecting groups or structural areas and in controlling tendon activation.  GRP replaces the earlier ELEM and NODE records by applying checks to all elements and nodes of the groups you specify.  For secondary (i.e. sub-group) definitions only the elements are selected, not the nodes.  A group can also be deactivated (switched off for design) with the statement  
    PARA NOG <group> DU=0.  
By default (if you do not specify a CS value) the program assumes CS = 9998, which means “all tendons active.”  Tendons whose ICS2 flag is set to 0 or 9999 are treated as unbonded.

Below is a breakdown of each column and row in the table:

1. Column Definitions  
   • Item – the keyword you place on the GRP record.  
   • Description – full explanation of what the keyword does and any special notes.  
   • Unit – unit or literal type accepted by that field. “–” denotes unitless; “/LIT” indicates a literal (alphanumeric).  
   • Default – the default value if you omit this parameter (“*” means use the program’s built-in default).

2. Row 1: NO  
   • Item: NO  
   • Description:  
     – Specifies a group number (integer) or a secondary-group literal (text label).  
     – If omitted, all defined groups are assumed.  
   • Unit: –/LIT (you may supply either a numeric ID or a text literal)  
   • Default: * (i.e. program applies every group)

3. Row 2: SAR  
   • Item: SAR  
   • Description:  
     – Identifies a “structural area” number to which the checks should be applied instead of group IDs.  
     – Mutually exclusive with NO: you may supply either NO or SAR, not both.  
   • Unit: – (unitless integer)  
   • Default: *

4. Row 3: CS  
   • Item: CS  
   • Description:  
     – Stands for “construction stage.”  Defines at which construction stage the specified tendons become active.  
     – If you issue a record containing only “CS” (for example, GRP CS 12), the program updates only the construction‐stage setting and does not modify any group or area selection.  
     – Internally, CS=9998 is the catch‐all stage where every tendon is considered activated.  Any tendon tagged with ICS2=0 or ICS2=9999 is treated as unbonded regardless of CS.  
   • Unit: – (integer, stage index)  
   • Default: * (program uses its own default stage, 9998)

Additional notes:  
- “See also: LC, ELEM, NODE” reminds you that load cases (LC) and the former element/node records are related concepts.  
- Secondary groups only pick up element membership; node selection is omitted.  
- To completely remove a group from design checks, use PARA NOG <group> DU=0.  
- The GRP record thus centralizes group/area selection and tendon activation control in a single interface, replacing separate ELEM and NODE records.

See also: LC, ELEM, NODE
 GRP
 All elements and nodes of the defined groups are used for the checks with the record GRP. In this way GRP replaces the records ELEM and NODE.
 For secondary groups only the elements are selected, not the nodes.
 In case a group shall not be designed, a group can also be switched off from design with PARA NOG ... DU=0.
 With the default CS 9998 all tendons are active, tendons with ICS2=0 or ICS2=9999 are treated as unbonded.

The table shown defines the three positional parameters you use whenever you ask the system to run a layer‐by‐layer design or stress check over a sequence of finite‐elements.  Those parameters are FROM, TO and INC; together they tell the program which elements (or element groups) to include in the design/stress run and in what step‐size.  Below is a breakdown of each column and row in the table, followed by a short discussion of how these parameters tie in with the other keywords (LC, GRP, NODE, ELEM) mentioned in the surrounding text.  

1. Table Columns  
• Item  
  – The name of the keyword you must supply as the first word in your input record.  
• Description  
  – A concise explanation of what the keyword does, what form its argument(s) may take, and any special notes or recommended variants (for example: why you might prefer to use GRP instead of typing a group number directly into FROM).  
• Unit  
  – Indicates whether the argument is a pure number, a literal string (LIT), or whether “–” (dash) means that the field is dimensionless.  In this table, “–/LIT” means you may enter either a numeric element ID or the literal token GRP.  
• Default  
  – The value assumed if you omit that keyword from your input.  An asterisk (*) generally means “start from the first available element”; replicating FROM as the default for TO means “if you only supply FROM, then TO will automatically be set to the same value (i.e. only that one element is processed).”  

2. Row-by-Row Description  
1) FROM  
  – Purpose: Specifies the first element in the sequence to be designed or checked.  
  – Argument options:  
   • A positive integer = the ID of a single element in the model, or  
   • The literal string “GRP” = indicates that the next field (TO) holds a group number (or secondary group) rather than a single element ID.  
  – Note: If you use GRP, the program will automatically include not only all the elements in that group but also all the nodes attached to them—making it a safer way to isolate a component.  
  – Unit: –/LIT (dimensionless or literal)  
  – Default: * (the first element in the model)  

2) TO  
  – Purpose: Defines the last element (or group) to be included in the run.  If you began with FROM = GRP, this field must be the group number (i.e. the literal secondary group ID).  Otherwise, it is simply the ending element index.  
  – As soon as TO is processed, all elements from the starting ID up through this ID will form the design subset (subject to INC).  
  – Unit: –/LIT  
  – Default: FROM (i.e. if you omit TO, you only process the single element specified in FROM)  

3) INC  
  – Purpose: The increment (step size) in element numbering between successive design checks.  For example, with FROM=10, TO=20 and INC=2, the system will process elements 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, and 20.  
  – Unit: – (dimensionless)  
  – Default: 1 (every element in the FROM–TO range)  

3. How This Fits Into the Larger Context  
– LC (Load Case) must be specified elsewhere on the same record or in a preceding record so that the program knows which load‐combination to use for stresses or design.  
– CRAC, NODE and ELEM are other ways to filter or isolate parts of your model:  
  • CRAC to extract cracked or damaged elements,  
  • NODE to limit checks to a set of nodes,  
  • ELEM/ECHO FULL EXTR to force a design check on a single element and to print an extended stress‐output, or  
  • ECHO ELEM to design all elements but only report detailed results on the ones you list.  

By mastering FROM, TO, and INC, you can precisely target subranges of your finite‐element model—either individual elements, regular strides through a block of elements, or entire element‐groups—without modifying your master input deck.

See also: LC, CRAC, GRP, NODE
 ELEM
 A design or a stress analysis for the load case LC is carried out for all elements from FROM to TO in increments of INC.
 In case a group shall not be designed, a group can alse be switched off from design with PARA NOG ... D0=0.
 In input ELEM can bei used especially to check the design in one element with ECHO FULL EXTR.
 Alternatively to ELEM you can also work with ECHO ELEM, then all elements are designed but the output only prints the selected elements. Then automatically an extended output is started, the layer design stress plot is only done for the first element of the ECHO ELEM list. See example bemess.dat/english/bemess8_multi_layer_design.dat

The table below defines the four parameters you can use to drive the NODE‐based design check over a range of nodes in a given load case (LC).  These parameters let you specify which nodes in the model will be evaluated, how they are stepped through, and, optionally, how they are filtered by group membership.

1. FROM  
   – Description: The starting node number for the design run.  All checks will begin at this node.  
   – Default: If you omit FROM, the program automatically uses the smallest node number that has been saved in the current model.  
   – Unit: not applicable  

2. TO  
   – Description: The ending node number.  The design routine will proceed up through this node, inclusive.  
   – Default: If TO is not supplied, it defaults to the same value as FROM, meaning only a single node (the start node) is checked.  
   – Unit: not applicable  

3. INC  
   – Description: The increment or step size between nodes.  For example, if FROM=10, TO=20 and INC=2, nodes 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 and 20 will be processed.  
   – Default: 1 (i.e., every node in the specified range will be evaluated).  
   – Unit: not applicable  

4. GROU  
   – Description: A user‐defined set of node group IDs to be included in the run.  Only nodes that belong to one of these groups will be checked.  
   – Default: An asterisk (*) indicates “all groups,” so every node is eligible.  
   – Unit: not applicable  
   – Note: If you also want all the elements connected to those nodes to be picked up automatically, consider using the GRP command instead.  GRP applies to both elements and nodes in the same group, ensuring consistency when you need element‐based checks tied to your node selection.

Additional Context and Cross-References  
• Load Case (LC):  Because this routine performs a “design for the load case LC,” you must have defined the LC previously.  The NODE command simply applies the design checking engine to your chosen nodes under that LC.  
• ELEM:  The element design analog is driven by ELEM, which works on an element‐by‐element basis instead of node by node.  
• ECHO FULL EXTR:  If you supply a single node (by setting FROM=TO and INC=1) and want full intermediate output on results and extracted stresses, add the option ECHO FULL EXTR.  This is helpful for debugging or deep dives on one particular joint or node.  
• GRP:  As noted above, GRP will pick up both elements and nodes in a group, whereas GROU only selects nodes.  If your workflow depends on group definitions that include both, switch to GRP for convenience.

Usage Example  
  • To evaluate every fifth node from 100 to 200 in group 5 for load case 3:  
      NODE, LC=3, FROM=100, TO=200, INC=5, GROU=5  

  • To check only node 42 (and get full extraction echo):  
      NODE, LC=1, FROM=42, TO=42, ECHO FULL EXTR  

By configuring FROM, TO, INC and GROU appropriately, you gain precise control over which parts of your finite‐element model are subject to the automated design checks for any given load case.

See also: LC, GRP, ELEM
 NODE
 A design for the load case LC is carried out for all nodes from FROM to TO in increments of INC.
 In input NODE can bei used especially to check the design in one node with ECHO FULL EXTR.

The input table defines the schema for specifying which nodes in a mesh or structure are activated or deactivated when generating “punching” operations. It is typically used in conjunction with the PUNC and SELE commands described in the accompanying context. Below is a detailed breakdown of its structure, semantics and intended usage:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: Identifies the parameter name or keyword.  
     – Description: Explains the role or meaning of the parameter.  
     – Unit: Physical units if applicable; here, all entries are non-dimensional (marked “–”).  
     – Default: The initial value assumed if none is provided.  

2. Rows and Parameters  
   A. NO  
     • Item: NO  
     • Description: “Node number.”  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: – (no default; the user must supply one or more node numbers)  
     • Semantics: When using PUNC or SELE, this field lists explicit node IDs to include or exclude.  

   B. TYPE  
     • Item: TYPE  
     • Description: “Use of the selection.”  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: 1  
     • Permissible values:  
       – 0 = is not used (the node or group is turned off for punching)  
       – 1 = is used (the node or group remains active, i.e., included in operations)  
     • Semantics: Controls activation state. If set to 0, the corresponding NO or GRP entry is deactivated.  

   C. GRP  
     • Item: GRP  
     • Description: “Group number (alternative to NO).”  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: – (no group default)  
     • Semantics: Rather than specifying individual nodes, you can refer to a pre-defined group. Groups may represent sets of nodes such as all perimeter nodes or temporary supports.

3. How This Table Is Applied  
   – In a PUNC workflow, issuing “HEAD PUNC 17 HEAD OFF” directly deactivates node 17. This table underlies that capability by mapping NO and TYPE entries to the underlying engine.  
   – SELE offers a higher-level mechanism: you can pre-switch off all nodes (TYPE = 0) and then selectively switch certain nodes back on by listing them with TYPE = 1, or vice versa.  
   – Example sequences:  
     • “SELE 253” by default (TYPE = 1) takes only node 253 through.  
     • “SELE 251,255 0” removes nodes 251 and 255 from future punching operations.  
     • “SELE TYP 0 GRP 3,5” excludes all nodes belonging to groups 3 and 5 (often used for temporary supports).  

4. Relationship to TEDDY/SSD Tasks  
   – PUNC commands embedded in a “HEAD … END” block can be defined within a separate TEDDY task ahead of an SSD Task design. This table is the reference for parsing those commands.  
   – Using PUNC HEAD OFF is more explicit when only a few nodes must be deactivated—no need to redefine the entire selection logic. Conversely, SELE shines when you need complex multi-node or multi-group toggling.  

By providing a clear mapping of node IDs or group IDs (NO/GRP), an on/off flag (TYPE), and defaults, this table standardizes how downstream modules interpret punching-node modifications. It ensures both fine-grained control via PUNC and broader selection strategies via SELE.

See also: PUNC
 SELE
 Individual nodes can be deactivated for punching,
 e.g. node 17 either with PUNC 17 HEAD OFF or with SELE 17 TYPE 0
 The advantage of SELE is that you generally define the possible nodes for the automatic punch- ing node search. If only individual nodes shall be excluded from punching the input PUNC no. HEAD OFF is better (more clear).
 The advantage of PUNC no. HEAD OFF is: this input can also be made in a separate TEDDY task in front of a SSD Task design and will be used there (but not SELE). Possible SSD TEDDY Task:
 PROG BEMESS
 HEAD PUNC 16,317,712 HEAD OFF END
 HEAD
 Examples for SELE:
 SELE 253 $ take only this node (e.g. for test output)
 ( with the first input with TYPE=1, first all nodes are switched off and then the given nodes are switched on)
 oder:
 SELE 251,255 0 $ take all nodes except these
 oder:
 SELE TYP 0 GRP 3,5 $ removes punching nodes coming from GRP 3+5 (temporary supports)

The table in question defines the format and default values for a single “external‐force” record (often referred to as record S) in a BEMESS input deck.  It explicitly lists which numerical fields must be supplied for each finite‐element “panel” or “strip” when you choose to drive your design from manually entered loads rather than from information already stored in the database.  Here is a breakdown of its structure and contents:

1.  Overall Layout  
    •  Four columns are defined:  
       –  Item: the short mnemonic code for each quantity.  
       –  Description: a brief English explanation of what the quantity represents.  
       –  Unit: the physical units expected for that field.  (Bracketed units; some have superscript footnote markers.)  
       –  Default: the value assumed if you omit that field (always zero except for the element number).

2.  Record Identifiers  
    •  NO  
       –  “Element number.”  This integer identifies the particular finite‐element or strip to which the subsequent loads apply.  
       –  Unit: n/a  
       –  Default: 1  

    •  NO1  
       –  “Additional number used for distinction of several input records.”  If you need more than one S‐record on the same element (e.g. to combine load cases), you may supply a small integer index here.  
       –  Unit: n/a  
       –  Default: 0  

3.  Bending Moments  
    •  MX  
       –  “Bending moment m-xx.”  Positive corresponds to sagging about the local x–axis.  
       –  Unit: [kNm/m]  
       –  Default: 0.0  

    •  MY  
       –  “Bending moment m-yy.”  Positive corresponds to sagging about the local y–axis.  
       –  Unit: [kNm/m]¹³  
       –  Default: 0.0  

    •  MXY  
       –  “Bending moment m-xy.”  The in‐plane twisting moment per unit width.  
       –  Unit: [kNm/m]  
       –  Default: 0.0  

4.  Shear Forces  
    •  VX  
       –  “Shear force v-x.”  The out‐of‐plane shear per unit width in the x-direction.  
       –  Unit: [kN/m]  
       –  Default: 0.0  

    •  VY  
       –  “Shear force v-y.”  The out‐of‐plane shear per unit width in the y-direction.  
       –  Unit: [kN/m]¹²  
       –  Default: 0.0  

5.  Membrane (In‐Plane) Forces  
    •  NX  
       –  “Membrane force n-xx.”  The in‐plane normal force in the x-direction per unit width.  
       –  Unit: [kN/m]¹¹  
       –  Default: 0.0  

    •  NY  
       –  “Membrane force n-yy.”  The in‐plane normal force in the y-direction per unit width.  
       –  Unit: [kN/m]¹¹  
       –  Default: 0.0  

    •  NXY  
       –  “Membrane force n-xy.”  The in‐plane shear force per unit width.  
       –  Unit: [kN/m]  
       –  Default: 0.0  

6.  Notes and Context  
    •  If you use this “external‐forces” route, any internally stored loads or moments in the database are ignored for that element; you become responsible for specifying a panel thickness (via a GEOM record) as well.  
    •  Only the classic Baumann strip‐design algorithm (CTRL LAY 0) is triggered—no automatic layer‐or shear‐reinforcement design and no serviceability checks.  
    •  For a worked example of a minimal input deck with manually supplied loads, see “bemess.dat/english/special/design_of_external_forces.dat.”  
    •  Separately, the EXPO record can be used to dump any design parameters from the database back into a BEMESS‐style input file (appending to an existing file or creating “project_BEX.DAT” if none is defined).

In practice, you will issue one S‐record per element (or per load case on an element), filling out NO, NO1 as needed, then set MX, MY, MXY, VX, VY, NX, NY, NXY to the desired values in kNm/m or kN/m.  Fields you omit default to zero so you can concentrate on only the nonzero components of your external loading.

This table defines the parameters used by the EXPO record in BEMESS for exporting stored design parameters from the concrete‐design database (CDB) into an external input file. It appears in the documentation section “EXPO – Export of the Design Parameters.” EXPO is invoked when a user wishes to write current design data—fiber properties, reinforcement layout, prestress details, etc.—to a text file that can later be read by the BEMESS “bemess.dat” driver or used for special‐case batch procedures. If no file name is supplied, the system appends to the last‐opened export file or creates a default file named project_BEX.DAT.

Table Structure  
The table consists of four columns:  
• Item – the keyword or parameter name to be placed on the EXPO input line.  
• Description – a brief explanation of the parameter’s role.  
• Unit – the data type or expected literal format.  
• Default – the value assumed when the parameter is omitted.

Row Details  
1. OPT  
  – Description: “reserved.”  
  – Unit: “–” (no unit or literal expected)  
  – Default: “–” (no default value)  
  – Remarks: This slot is reserved for potential future options. Currently it must be left blank or omitted.  

2. TO  
  – Description: “Name of a file to write to.”  
  – Unit: Lit96 (a character string up to 96 characters in length)  
  – Default: “*”  
  – Remarks: If you supply a literal string here, EXPO writes to exactly that file name. If you leave it at the default asterisk (*), BEMESS will either (a) append to the file most recently opened by any EXPO command in the current session, or (b) if none exists, create a file named project_BEX.DAT in the working directory.

3. PASS  
  – Description: “Password of the CDB to be exported.”  
  – Unit: Lit16 (a character string up to 16 characters in length)  
  – Default: “–”  
  – Remarks: When the CDB has been secured with a password, this field must match that password in order to unlock the database for export. If the database is not password-protected, this field is simply omitted.

Usage Notes  
• The EXPO record is typically placed in the BEMESS input deck after all geometry, loading and reinforcement definitions.  
• No layer design or shear design is performed during an EXPO run—it only serializes existing results for reuse or inspection.  
• Serviceability and external‐force checks (per the “special” external forces mode) are not affected by EXPO. They must be handled separately using the “special design_of_external_forces.dat” example.  
• If you require a fully automated export of current design data for archiving or further batch processing, populate TO with a target path and PASS if needed, then submit the EXPO record.

The table you provided defines two related input fields for an “ECHO”‐style command in your design software:  

1.   OPT  – the primary output option you want to request  
2.   VAL  – the level or detail of output for that option  

Both fields carry an associated unit and a default value if the user does not supply anything explicitly. Below is a detailed breakdown.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
1.  OPT  (Unit: LIT, Default: FULL)  
    •  This is a literal identifier that selects one or more aspects of the design results you wish to echo (print) out. You must choose one of the following keywords (they are case‐sensitive):  
      –  PARA  : Print design parameters  
      –  MAT   : Print material data (equivalent to PARA if not separately specified)  
      –  REIN  : Print reinforcement‐related design results (bar sizes, spacing, area)  
      –  NSTR  : Print strains, stress ranges and concrete stress under Serviceability Limit State (SLS)  
      –  PUNC  : Perform punching‐shear checks  
            •  Special note: “ECHO PUNC 4” triggers a WINGRAF plot of V<sub>Ed</sub> without bedding reduction, especially useful for foundations.  
      –  RTAB  : Compile reinforcement schedules/tables only  
      –  DMOM  : Show internal forces used in the current design iteration  
            •  Warning: “ECHO DMOM” here is not the same as any “CTRL DMOM” command in other contexts.  
      –  STRE  : Perform linear stress determination (requires a preceding “CTRL STRE” setup)  
      –  ELEM  : Restrict output to a list of element numbers you supply  
      –  NODE  : Restrict output to a list of node numbers you supply  
      –  RVT   : Switch on a REVIT‐friendly output format (shorter PARA lists)  
      –  FULL  : Equivalent to requesting _all_ of the above in one go  

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
2.  VAL  (Unit: – or “/LIT”, Default: “*”)  
    •  This field controls the depth or verbosity of the data printed for the chosen OPT. You may supply:  
      –  (nothing)  
         •  Uses the system default for that OPT  
         •  Limits output to only those elements or nodes that carry the _maximum_ result values (e.g. highest moment, largest stress)  
      –  A specific element or node number (only valid when OPT = ELEM or NODE)  
      –  NO  
         •  Suppresses all output for this OPT  
      –  YES  
         •  Regular output only, no graphical plots  
         •  Still limited to elements/nodes with maximum results  
      –  FULL  
         •  Extensive tabular output for _all_ elements and nodes matching OPT  
         •  Includes any plots or graphics the module supports  
      –  EXTR  
         •  “Extreme” output level  
         •  In addition to FULL, also dumps single‐load‐case breakdowns and detailed concrete strain data  

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Additional Notes from Context Text  
–  By default (no user input), the system behaves as if you issued:  
     ECHO PARA FULL  
     ECHO PUNC YES  
     ECHO STRE YES  
     ECHO RTAB+DMOM NO  
     ECHO REIN+SIGS+NSTR *(only max‐value elements)  
–  If you supply “ECHO ELEM <list>” (instead of “ECHO ELEM no”), all elements will still be _designed_, but only those in your list are _printed_. That also triggers an extended output automatically; note that stress plots are generated only for the first listed element.  
–  To restrict to nodes, use “ECHO NODE <list>.”  
–  For stress‐range checks, “ECHO NSTR FULL” prints only those elements that _fail_ or “require reinforcement increase.”  
–  “ECHO NSTR EXTR” will dump the maximum stresses for _all_ load cases and _all_ elements. For a more visual stress‐range analysis, WINGRAF is recommended.

This table‐plus‐notes structure allows users to finely tune the reporting scope and level of detail for nearly every aspect of the concrete‐and‐reinforcement design checks performed by your software.

See also: NSTR, PUNC, LC, CTRL
 ECHO
 The default is activated without an user input:
 PARA
 FULL
 PUNC
 YES (FULL for the maximum loaded point)
 STRE YES RTAB+DMOM NO REIN+SIGS+NSTR only elements with maximum results
 On input of single elements with ELEM (not ECHO ELEM) or NODE (design test) ECHO REIN und ECHO NSTR is set to EXTR.
 Alternatively to ELEM you can also work with ECHO ELEM no, then all elements are designed but the output only prints the selected elements. Then automatically an ex- tended output is started, the stress plot is only done for the first element of the ECHO ELEM list. To select a node please input ECHO NODE. See example be- mess.dat/english/]bemess8_multi_layer_design.dat
 In the stress range check with ECHO NSTR FULL only elements that require a reinforcement increase are printed. ECHO NSTR EXTR generates the maximum stresses of all load cases and elements. Better use WINGRAF to check the stress range.
